U.S. Navy invests $50M in Shield AI’s runway-free strike drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
12:07:28 UTC
21:07:28 KST

- The U.S. Navy, PAE Aviation and the Defense Innovation Unit are investing $50 million to scale runway-independent maritime strike drones built around Shield AI's X-BAT.
- The RIMES program aims to give Arleigh Burke-class destroyers, which lack the flight decks for fixed-wing aircraft, a strike capability that can launch and land vertically.
The U.S. Navy’s Rapid Capability Office, PAE Aviation and the Defense Innovation Unit are investing $50 million to scale unmanned, runway-independent maritime strike capabilities built around Shield AI’s X-BAT aircraft, the Navy announced.
The funding falls under the Runway Independent Maritime Expeditionary Strike program, or RIMES, which the Defense Innovation Unit and Navy launched in February to develop a strike drone capable of operating from surface combatants that lack the flight decks, catapults or arrested landing systems conventional carrier-based aircraft require. The Navy’s Arleigh Burke-class destroyers, with 74 hulls currently active in the fleet, can land a helicopter but cannot deploy a fixed-wing strike aircraft, a gap the program is intended to close.
The investment builds on existing risk-reduction work led by the PAE Aviation Rapid Capability Cell with Shield AI. The award was made using the Middle Tier of Acquisition Rapid Prototype approach and an Other Transaction Authority contract, according to the Navy.
X-BAT is a vertical takeoff and landing, jet-powered aircraft Shield AI first unveiled in October 2025. The company has said the aircraft has a range exceeding 2,000 nautical miles (3,700 kilometers) with a full mission payload, a service ceiling above 50,000 feet (15,240 meters), and a wingspan of about 39 feet (11.9 meters). Shield AI has said X-BAT is designed for strike, counter-air, electronic warfare and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance missions, and that its Hivemind autonomy software allows it to operate in communications-denied or degraded environments.
“Airpower without runways is the holy grail of deterrence,” Shield AI co-founder and president Brandon Tseng said when the aircraft was unveiled. “It gives our forces persistence, reach and survivability, and it buys diplomacy another day.”
Shield AI has said X-BAT will initially be powered by GE Aerospace’s F110-GE-129 engine, with a first flight targeted for 2026. The company already supplies the Navy and other services with its smaller V-BAT unmanned aircraft, which has flown more than 170 sorties in Ukraine and supports a nearly $200 million Coast Guard contract for contractor-owned intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance services.
The $50 million RIMES investment does not disclose a timeline for X-BAT flight testing or deployment aboard Navy destroyers, and the Navy has not said how many aircraft the program is expected to procure.

Massive Drone Barrage Hits Russia as Smoke Rises From One of Its Largest Explosives Plants

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Ukraine Spots AI-Generated Russian Advance Video—Giant Soldiers and Even the Buildings Are Fake

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Spots AI-Generated Russian Advance Video—Giant Soldiers and Even the Buildings Are Fake
Russian forces are turning to AI-generated battlefield footage to manufacture evidence of advances they cannot convincingly demonstrate on the ground, according to Ukrainian OSINT group DeepState on August 18.
DeepState said Russian sources recently published a video that was presented as proof that Russian troops had infiltrated the outskirts of Oskil.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The footage, however, appears to have been generated with artificial intelligence rather than recorded at the location, according to the group’s analysis.
DeepState pointed to several visual anomalies in the video. Entire buildings appear to have been generated, while structures that should be hangars were transformed into private homes in parts of the footage.
Russian troops depicted in the clip also show distorted proportions and other visual artifacts characteristic of AI-generated imagery.
The episode appears to represent a digital evolution of Russia’s so-called “flag-planting” tactic, in which small groups are sent forward to raise a Russian flag at a location and film it as supposed evidence of territorial control, even when Russian forces do not actually hold the area.
DeepState described the emerging practice as “AI flag planting,” suggesting Russian commanders may increasingly use generative tools to create the appearance of battlefield gains without having to send troops forward to produce the footage physically.
According to the Ukrainian OSINT group, the apparent shift may reflect the growing risks associated with traditional flag-planting missions, where troops can be exposed and killed simply to create propaganda footage claiming an advance.
Usually, Russian forces send actual troops instead of generating them with AI to create propaganda videos.
Recently, Ukrainian troops captured a Russian soldier who appeared in a propaganda video presenting the Ukrainian-controlled village of Zirnytsia in the Zaporizhzhia region as having been seized by Russian forces.
Ukraine’s 142nd Separate Mechanized Brigade said the prisoner was a serviceman of Russia’s 5th Tank Brigade who had been sent to the area to display a Russian flag and record footage that could later be presented as evidence of a Russian advance.

'Something smells off': The Netanyahu backer behind two propaganda initiatives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
12:06:10 UTC
21:06:10 KST

The name Avi Gross may not be the most immediately recognizable name among Benjamin Netanyahu's supporters. Yet he is the businessman behind at least two propaganda initiatives to disseminate the Likud's messages during election campaigns, a Haaretz investigation reveals.
Gross, who had been invited as a guest of honor to a Netanyahu speech before the U.S. Congress in 2024, is the man behind the content production company New Vision Production, located in Petah Tikva, central Israel. Establishing the studios with their advanced equipment had cost millions of shekels, sources confirmed to Haaretz. Gross himself declined to respond to Haaretz's inquiries.
Founded about a year ago, NVP operates along two separate but tangential tracks. One is to provide paid content services for the Likud campaign (which the party confirmed, stating that it was done legally). The second, as revealed by Haaretz, is the distribution of viral videos taken from podcasts that the company produces for Netanyahu-supporting media personalities. The Likud stated that the party has no connection to these podcasts, which leaves the question: who actually funds them?
There is also another track, perhaps only semi-official, where the company's premises serve as a kind of production house for ostensibly private videos that align with the campaign's messages (the party denies any connection). An analysis of these reveals that at least seven "content creators" filmed independent videos that, whether by chance or not, promoted the Likud campaign's messages and attacked Netanyahu's rivals and the media.
Some of the videos were produced even before the party contracted with the company. The list of creators includes, among others, Channel 14 reporter Tamir Schneid, panelist Noam Fathi, Likud spokesman Guy Levy, and Adi Shamai Hacohen – who was behind the "coming out" video "Mom, Dad, I'm a Bibist."
Since these are ostensibly private creators, "they are not subject to legal restrictions," a legal source involved in election law told Haaretz. But when everything is done in a single complex, the dots almost connect themselves: Welcome to the propaganda studios.
The current project is not the first time Gross has acted on Netanyahu's behalf in an election campaign. In 2021, he established Lychee Productions, which was behind "The Trial," a propaganda film distributed about a week before the November 2022 election that cast aspersions on the law enforcement system, "Case 4000" against Netanyahu, and the media. Over the years, Gross also published numerous posts on his social media accounts expressing support for Netanyahu and echoing his government's messages.
Gross, a 66-year-old resident of Mikhmoret, made his fortune in textiles, got into technology companies as a partner and founded the Panda mattresses company which he recently sold to Hollandia, in which he now holds 9 percent. He had been linked to the possible acquisition of the Maccabi Netanya soccer team but no deal ensued.
Gross is not officially connected to NVP. According to the Registrar of Companies, it was founded in July 2025 as "Neve Hadar Productions" by Neve Pinchas (who is defined as the company's CEO and, sources say, is responsible for content production). Until recently, the company had not been publicly credited with any product.
But this May, things moved quickly: its name was changed to NVP, it moved to Petah Tikva, it got a website and a month later, 90 percent of its shares were transferred to an American company whose owners' identity is unknown. The company, Great Production 2026 LLC, was incorporated in April in Delaware, which does not require shareholders to be divulged.
Although Gross does not appear in the company's documents at all, two sources well-versed in the details confirmed to Haaretz that he is the businessman behind the establishment of the media initiative in Petah Tikva.
Service vendors
Possibly, the word "initiative" does not adequately reflect the project's scale and scope of influence, especially how little the time it has been operating. In just five weeks, the company published dozens of short videos with pro-Netanyahu content, some of which garnered thousands of likes and tens of thousands of views. The sources of the videos are four new podcasts with at least 15 episodes.
The hosts include Netanyahu's brother Ido Netanyahu as well as personalities associated with media outlets such as Channel 14 and Galey Israel Radio, including Efi Mordechai – who brought us the "Ulpanometer," a venture to measure leftist presence on screen.
It doesn't end there. NVP also began providing services to Gadi Taub and his podcast group "Gatekeeper," featuring among others Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz. A new podcast called "The Nationalists," hosted by Alon Malik and Bat-El Benyamin, was recently added to the gallery of locally produced podcasts.
However, the studio recordings, all edited professionally, also include less regulated initiatives, where the only thing that seems orderly is the messages: a suspicious resemblance to the Likud campaign, and primarily – an attack on the mainstream media. For example, Channel 14 personality Noam Fathi filmed a propaganda video in the podcast studio against Channel 12 News (following a libel suit filed against him by the channel and Guy Peleg over his remarks regarding the Sde Teiman affair).
"Active Info" investigators, in collaboration with Haaretz, managed to verify by by means of geolocation and image comparison that additional propaganda videos were filmed in the Petah Tikva studio complex in recent months. For example, two government-supporting content creators, Yishai Gvirtzman and Dana Cohen, popularly dubbed "Dana Banana," filmed a video attacking the media from the complex's inner courtyard, which is only accessible after a security check and by invitation from someone working there.
Two other people who appear on the list of creators working there are spokesman Guy Levy and Tamir Schneid, Channel 14's "special affairs" reporter (going by the footage, it appears that at least one of the affairs is a clash over Case 4000). Both filmed in and outside the studios. At least in Levy's case, who echoed a message that Gadi Eisenkot – Netanyahu's main rival in the upcoming election – sought to end the war, the timing is key. He did so before July 27 but also after that date, and in the 90 days preceding the elections, election laws become critical.
The advent of NVP also changed the working method of Shamai Hacohen (from the "coming out" video). In June, even before the Likud began working with NVP, he switched his usual filming location from home to the studio in Petah Tikva. From there, for example, he launched an attack against Ronen Tzur, who called for Channel 14 to be shut down, or against media outlets that did not sufficiently sing Netanyahu's praises after the day of battle with Iran about two months ago.
Beyond the unofficial recordings, NVP is also responsible for official video content in the Likud campaign. So far, it has published about 20 videos in that context, mostly against Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot, incorporating two messages: "It's them or a broad national government" and "Eisenkot is not Yashar, he's left-wing." NVP is also responsible for the AI video showing Eisenkot running with outstretched arms toward a young man resembling his son who was killed in Gaza, but at the last moment he ignores him and embraces United Arab List chairman Mansour Abbas. The creator of this video is none other than Neve Pinchas, the company's founder, who still holds 10 percent of its shares.
"Something smells off," the legal source cognizant of election law told Haaretz. But asked if it goes beyond stink, he says it's a gray area, very much so. According to him, Israel's election laws are outdated and not suitable for 2026 and the social media era. Additionally, the fact that the videos aren't published by the party itself makes it hard to show connection between it and the distribution process.
Ultimately, he says, it will be a challenge to prove that the law had been broken. All will depend on the interpretation of the Central Elections Committee chairman, Supreme Court Deputy President Noam Solberg, and the evidence presented to him. "Part of the problem with current legislation is that the law doesn't apply to unofficial campaigns," he stresses. Thus they can bypass the law. "This is not the first time this has been done, but in the past, it was much more minor and subtle," he says.
On July 19, the members of the Likud Constitution, Law and Justice Committee received an invitation signed by Minister Haim Katz, to a special meeting to discuss the reserved slots the prime minister wanted on the party's Knesset slate. The location chosen for the gathering was NVP's offices in Petah Tikva. Ultimately the meeting was moved, but this does not mean the complex was erased from the Likud's map; on the contrary. Haaretz learned that in recent weeks, the studios have become a coveted destination for the prime minister himself.
In August alone, Netanyahu was documented there three times: once as a guest on Taub's podcast, a second time to film a video in which he announced a reserved slot for Oren Dobronsky on the Likud slate, and a third time for the strange story of the Army Radio program; last week, the military station published an episode of the podcast "King of Creating Life," featuring the prime minister, and for some reason, it was not filmed at the station's Jaffa base but in the Petah Tikva studios. The station explained that Netanyahu's office told them that the filming had to be moved due to security considerations. A security source told Haaretz that the Dignitary Protection Unit had not made any such demand.
Either way, according to several testimonies, Netanyahu's frequent visits to the studios cause difficulty and inconveniences for employees in the building. They receive no prior notice and before every visit, the Dignitary Protection Unit prevents employees from leaving their offices until filming is complete.
Getting credit
Another name arising in several contexts is attorney Ophir Falk, who became the prime minister's political adviser in 2023. The year before that, he partnered in the creation of Netanyahu's book "My Story," which was part of the election campaign that year and distributed in the week preceding it, and according to a source who spoke with Haaretz, he was paid for it from Sela Meir publishing house. The second – he was a partner in Lychee Productions (and held 30 percent of its shares until it was dissolved), and joined Gross in creating "The Trial." This film, which was promoted exclusively and primarily on the Walla website and social media – and also by Netanyahu himself – reached millions of views; all this just a few days before the elections.
Yinon Magal, host of "The Patriots" on Channel 14, was also involved in the film. His voice is not heard and his face does not appear on screen, but Haaretz learned that he received payment for his participation just six months before he testified for the prosecution in the Netanyahu trial. In fact, Magal, whose name appears in the credits at the end of the film, interviewed most of the participants.
Lychee, owned by Gross and Falk, invested significantly in promoting and distributing the film. It set up social media pages, disseminated video clips and of course marketed the 40-minute film itself. It was also distributed by Netanyahu and his son Yair, as well as among opinion leaders supporting the government, such as Taub, Galit Distel-Atbaryan, spokesman Guy Levy, and Magal himself, even though he did not state that he participated in the project. In early 2025, shortly before it was finally dissolved in March of that year, Lychee released a sequel, "The Trial 2," featuring some of the original film's participants. As often happens, the sequel did not reach the heights of the original film.
In addition to Avi Gross, NVP also declined to comment but last week it stated, "NVP is a leading production company. The company is engaged in producing independent content alongside providing professional production services to diverse clients. As a policy, the company does not discuss its clients' affairs or projects in the media. The company operates in compliance with all laws, and invites entities from across Israel's business, social, and public spectrum to enjoy its professional services."
Other subjects of the article did not provide responses either. Haaretz contacted the content creators filmed at NVP's complex and asked if they paid, received payment, or were connected to the company. Dana Cohen, Yishai Gvirtzman, Adi Shamai Hacohen, Natan Solomon, and Channel 14 reporter Tamir Schneid did not respond to the inquiry. Neither did Gadi Taub or Alon Malik, who were asked if the company pays them or if they pay the company for producing the podcasts.
Haaretz also contacted Yinon Magal, who provided an irrelevant response. Ophir Falk stated that "among the multitude of false claims, the most absurd is that the prime minister's book was written by me. Prime Minister Netanyahu wrote every single word in his book, and the proof of this is the original manuscript kept in his possession." However, a Haaretz inquiry reveals that Netanyahu wrote in his book that Falk typed the content during travels across the country.
The Likud stated in response that the party "legally hired NVP in accordance with all laws for election campaign productions," but the party did not respond to Haaretz's questions regarding the connection between Gross and Netanyahu.

The cost of the plant producing solid rocket fuel for Flamingo missiles in Denmark has become known
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
15:04:49 EEST
21:04:49 KST

The cost of the plant producing solid rocket fuel for Flamingo missiles in Denmark has become known
Kyiv • UNN
The cost of the Fire Point plant in Denmark increased due to the construction of a new facility. Its launch is scheduled by the end of 2027.
The cost of the plant for producing solid rocket propellant for Flamingo missiles, which the Ukrainian company Fire Point is building in Denmark, is estimated at more than €150 million. Fire Point CEO and CTO Iryna Terekh said this during a press conference at the DALO Industry Days arms exhibition, UNN reports.
"At present, this is a very rough estimate. But the initial plan was to complete the entire project within €50 million. The cost has now risen to more than €150 million," Iryna Terekh said.
According to her, the cost tripled after it became clear that the first building purchased by the company was unsuitable for housing solid rocket propellant production, and the company was forced to build a new facility.
Iryna Terekh also added that Fire Point is already producing rocket propellant in Ukraine.
"But when it came to scaling up production, given the need for predictable capacity located in a safe place, we chose Denmark—or, more precisely, accepted Denmark's very generous invitation to establish such a plant here," she explained.
The CEO of Rocket Technology, a subsidiary of Fire Point, Viacheslav Bondarchuk, added that 100 people are working on the project, 15 of whom are executives and managers, while the rest are contractors. In the future, the company plans to hire several hundred more people for administrative positions, its engineering team, and production.
"Our first and foremost goal is to solve what is, so to speak, a common European problem (…). And we plan to open a plant here (in Denmark—Ed.) that will have enormous capacity to produce large quantities of solid rocket propellant, initially for Fire Point. We will also be able to supply other companies," Bondarchuk said.
According to him, the plant is currently under construction. The company already has all the necessary permits to build the plant and begin producing solid rocket propellant. The plant is scheduled to become operational by the end of 2027.
We remind you
As UNN reported, Fire Point is building a solid rocket propellant plant in the Danish town of Vojens, in the south of the country. This is the first case within NATO in which a member state has allowed a Ukrainian defense company to establish a production site on its territory.
For Fire Point to be able to begin producing solid propellant for Flamingo missiles, the Danish authorities removed more than 20 legislative barriers.
Locating production in Denmark will minimize the risk of a possible Russian strike on the facility.

Seven people, including six tourists and a pilot, were killed on Wednesday when a helicopter crashed at Mount Ololokwe in northern Kenya, according to local media reports citing local officials.
 
The crash occurred at Mount Ololokwe in Samburu County, about 270 kilometers (168 miles) north of the capital Nairobi.

"The Authority extends its deepest condolences to the families of the victims following this tragic incident," the KCAA said Wednesday.

The aviation authority said it is coordinating with relevant government agencies and other stakeholders in response to the accident.
 
The Air Accident Investigation Department under Kenya's Roads and Transport Ministry is leading investigations into the circumstances surrounding the crash.
 
Authorities did not immediately disclose the possible cause of the accident.
The area surrounding Mount Ololokwe, also known as Ol Donyo Sabache, forms part of Kenya's northern tourism circuit, which draws international visitors to wildlife reserves and conservancies across the region.
 
Light aircraft and helicopters are widely used to transport tourists between safari lodges, conservancies and other destinations in remote parts of northern Kenya.
 
According to the KCAA, investigators are working to establish the circumstances that led to the crash.

Israel opens criminal probes over killings of Hind Rajab and Gaza rescue workers, military says
JERUSALEM/CAIRO, Aug 19 - Israel's military will open internal investigations over its troops' high-profile killings in Gaza of 5-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab in January 2024 and 15 emergency and aid workers in March 2025, it said on Wednesday, although rights groups said such probes rarely lead to convictions.
The military said the investigation decisions followed probes by its Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism. It released decisions regarding five incidents involving the deaths of Palestinians.
They included an examination of the killings of seven aid workers with the World Central Kitchen charity in April 2024. On that incident, the military said there was "no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct that would justify the opening of a criminal investigation."
Israeli rights groups say that criminal misconduct investigations into Israeli troops over the killing of Palestinians rarely lead to convictions.
Dan Owen, a researcher in the Yesh Din rights organization, said that over the last decade only a "tiny" proportion of investigations had led to indictments while growing political pressure "further deters Israeli law-enforcement authorities from holding those responsible accountable, even when clear evidence does exist."
During Israel's offensive in response to an October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel which triggered the Gaza war, Hind Rajab was pinned down in a car for hours, begging Palestinian medics by mobile phone to send help, while her aunt, uncle and three cousins already lay dead. When an ambulance arrived, contact with the girl and the rescuers themselves was lost. Twelve days later, the bodies of the girl, her relatives and two ambulance workers were recovered from the area.
HIND RAJAB FILM
A film about Hind Rajab's death won the Silver Lion Award at the Venice Film Festival and was nominated for an Academy Award.

The bodies of two Belgian climbers who went missing in the Swiss Alps 34 years ago have been recovered from the melting Trift Glacier, police said on Wednesday.
A hiker discovered the remains on 26 July on the glacier in southern Switzerland, near the Italian border, according to police in the canton of Valais.
The remains were taken to the Institute of Forensic Medicine at Wallis Hospital in Sion for identification.
"A direct comparison of DNA profiles has formally established that these are two mountaineers who went missing in the Weissmies region in 1992," the statement said.
On 4 September 1992, the two men had set out from the Weissmies hut with the aim of climbing the summit of the Weissmies (4,017 metres) and got as far as the Almagell hut.
Caught out by appalling weather, they never reached their destination.
In the months that followed, several search operations were carried out, which led to the discovery of a rucksack, but not the hikers.
Wallis police keep records of people reported missing since 1925, mostly in mountainous areas and rivers.

Last year, the remains of a Swiss mountaineer who vanished in 1994 were discovered on a glacier on the Ober Gabelhorn mountain, also in Wallis.

How the use of artificial intelligence harms college students’ ability to learn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
12:00:43 UTC
21:00:43 KST

College students who copy answers from artificial intelligence tools without verifying the information experience declines in their ability to learn independently. These unreflective habits are associated with a weaker belief in students’ own capabilities and a reduced motivation to learn. The findings were published in Scientific Reports.
Generative artificial intelligence programs can quickly write essays, generate computer code, and solve advanced mathematical equations. These tools have become common academic aids on college campuses across the globe. When students use these systems to seek explanations or brainstorm new ideas, the technology can expand their academic perspectives and improve their studying efficiency.
But reliance on automated answers carries potential academic risks. Hui Zhao and Huijuan Gu, researchers at Zhoukou Normal University, designed a study to examine what happens when students use artificial intelligence thoughtlessly. The researchers define thoughtless use as a pattern in which users blindly adopt machine-generated text without critically evaluating, verifying, or deeply understanding the outputs.
The researchers wanted to know how this specific habit affects self-directed learning. Self-directed learning is a core educational skill in higher education. It refers to a student’s capacity to independently set goals, apply study strategies, and monitor their own academic progress. Students with high self-directed learning abilities can manage their time and actively evaluate what they do and do not understand.
To understand the relationship between technology habits and study skills, the researchers looked at two psychological factors. The first is self-efficacy, which is a person’s internal belief in their capacity to successfully complete tasks and overcome challenges. The second factor is learning motivation, which encompasses the psychological drives that push a student to initiate and persist in their coursework. The researchers based their investigation on the idea that a student’s environment, personal beliefs, and daily behaviors all shape one another in a continuous, reciprocal cycle.
Zhao and Gu recruited 487 undergraduate students from four universities in Henan Province, China, to complete an online survey. The participants answered a series of questions assessing their study habits on a five-point scale. The respondents ranged from college freshmen to seniors and represented a variety of academic disciplines, including the humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences.
The survey measured four distinct categories using established psychological scales. First, it assessed how often students engaged in thoughtless artificial intelligence use. Participants rated their agreement with statements such as “I copy learning tasks or problem statements into generative AI to seek answers or ideas” and “I feel that generative AI is more capable than I am in learning and problem-solving.”
Second, the survey measured the students’ academic self-efficacy. This section asked participants to reflect on their confidence when facing difficult materials, using prompts like “I believe that I can independently master complex learning content.”
Third, the researchers measured the students’ overall motivation to learn. This included questions about their curiosity, their desire to master new skills, and the satisfaction they gained from overcoming academic hurdles. Finally, the survey evaluated the students’ capacity for self-directed learning by asking how often they actively checked their own understanding of the material or created knowledge frameworks like mind maps.
The researchers used a statistical technique called structural equation modeling to analyze the survey responses. This analytical method allows scientists to observe complex networks of relationships between multiple different variables at the same time, rather than just looking at two variables in isolation.
The analysis revealed that the thoughtless use of artificial intelligence is strongly associated with lower levels of self-directed learning. Students who habitually relied on automated answers reported worse self-management skills and lower cognitive engagement in their coursework.
The researchers identified a specific psychological pathway explaining this decline. The authors suggest that an unreflective reliance on technology deprives students of the opportunity to struggle through complex problems. Without the experience of overcoming academic challenges through their own hard work, students reported lower levels of self-efficacy.
This lower confidence in their own abilities was in turn linked to a reduced motivation to learn. When individuals do not believe they can succeed on their own, their willingness to invest effort naturally declines. With less motivation and lower self-confidence, the students became less capable of managing their own educational progress, acting instead as dependent users of external tools.
The researchers also conducted a multi-group analysis to see if these patterns differed between men and women. This statistical test allowed the authors to compare the strength of the psychological relationships across the two demographic groups.
The analysis uncovered distinct gender differences in how thoughtless technology use relates to psychological well-being. For male students, unreflective use showed a stronger negative association with learning motivation. The researchers suggest that male students often view technology primarily as a tool for efficiency, meaning that immediate automated answers quickly replace their internal drive to engage deeply with the material.
For female students, thoughtless use was associated with steeper declines in self-efficacy and self-directed learning. The researchers note that female students tend to adopt more reflective and evaluative study strategies in their traditional coursework. When they bypass these reflective processes by copying automated answers, they miss out on the mastery experiences that traditionally build their academic confidence.
The study relies on cross-sectional data, meaning all the information was collected at a single point in time. Because the researchers did not track the students over a long period, the statistical results highlight relationships between behaviors and beliefs but cannot definitively prove cause and effect. It is possible that students who already have low self-efficacy are simply more likely to use artificial intelligence thoughtlessly.
The demographic makeup of the sample also presents some limitations. The participants were drawn exclusively from universities in a single Chinese province, and nearly eighty percent of the respondents were female. Expanding future surveys to include a more balanced demographic distribution across different regions would help verify if these patterns hold true for other student populations.
Additionally, the survey measured motivation as a single, unified concept. Future research could split this category into intrinsic motivation, such as natural curiosity, and extrinsic motivation, such as a desire for good grades. Separating these concepts would provide a more detailed picture of how automated tools influence a student’s inner drive to succeed. Future studies might also track students over an entire semester to see how their habits and self-confidence evolve as they face different types of academic challenges.
The study, “Thoughtless Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence and College Students’ Self-Directed Learning: A Multi-Group SEM Analysis of Gender Differences,” was authored by Hui Zhao and Huijuan Gu.

How to turn excess green vegetables into a vibrant Spanish soup – recipe | Waste not
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
12:00:14 UTC
21:00:14 KST

Since reading How Not to Die, by Michael Greger, I’m always looking for ways to include greens in every meal. He regularly pops into my mind when I’m cooking, whispering in my ear: “Add some spinach to that risotto,” say, or “Moringa powder will make your porridge much more nutritious.” So I’m sure today’s green gazpacho would make him proud. It’s a great way to clear out your crisper drawer and pack a meal with all sorts of greens. Anything goes, but if any of your chosen ingredients (eg, basil or mint) has a particularly potent flavour, just add it in moderation or to taste. Incidentally, the key to a great gazpacho is the quality of the olive oil, as is a nice, bold-but-balanced acidity, which is easily achieved with a squeeze of lemon or your best vinegar.
Green gazpacho
This is a really vibrant recipe, and perfect for the hot summer months. It’s best served well chilled, so make it with ice so you can enjoy it immediately or/and chill in the fridge or freezer for 30 minutes to an hour. It will keep, covered, in the fridge for up to three days, but is best eaten on the day it is made. You can also add a few ice cubes to the soup bowls, if you like.
Decorate the top with a selection of your favourite ingredients used in the soup: finely dice them and scatter on top, along with any delicate herbs and a final drizzle of extra-virgin olive oil.
Serves 4
400g green vegetables (cucumber, courgette, celery stalks and leaves, lettuce, spinach, peas, or a mix of whatever you have to hand), finely chopped – save some of your favourites to garnish
50-100g soft green herbs (parsley, basil, mint, coriander, or a mixture), leaves roughly chopped, stalks finely chopped
1 handful ice cubes 
100ml extra-virgin olive oil, plus extra to finish
 2 tbsp lemon juice, or white-wine, sherry or cider vinegar, plus extra to taste, if necessary 
1 small garlic clove (or to taste), peeled
Sea salt
Optional spices – I used cumin, ground coriander and cayenne pepper, but experiment with what you have in the cupboard
Roughly chop the green vegetables and put them in a jug blender.
Add the herbs and 200ml chilled water, drop in the ice cubes, oil, garlic and a pinch of salt, then add any spices you fancy. Blend for a minute, until very smooth, then adjust the seasoning, acidity and spice to taste.
Chill for at least half an hour, and serve cold, topped with the reserved green vegetables, finely diced, a few herb leaves and a drizzle of extra-virgin olive oil.

From spectacle to scale: why China’s robotics firms face a ‘critical juncture’
China’s robots have won global attention with a string of viral stunts. But firms now face growing pressure to generate real-world returns
At China’s annual World Robot Conference (WRC) that kicked off on Wednesday, the hall was filled with humanoid robots wowing visitors with feats of dexterity: from playing table tennis to performing drum solos.
These eye-catching displays have helped China’s robotics industry win global attention – and raise huge amounts of capital – over the past couple of years. But at this year’s summit, the overriding sentiment among executives, investors and policymakers was starkly pragmatic: the era of viral parlour tricks is over.
Across the industry, the race is now on to make the leap from small-scale trials to large-scale deployment, as firms come under pressure to generate real-world returns. Xu Xiaolan, president of the Chinese Institute of Electronics and a former vice-minister at China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, said on Wednesday that the embodied intelligence industry was at a “critical juncture”.
“The core goal over the past two years has been to push applications into the real world,” Xu said, pointing to emerging uses in public services, logistics, manufacturing, healthcare and emergency response.
The shift to mass production will also transform competition in the industry, with firms needing to deliver robots that offer “reliability, autonomy and economic value in real operating environments rather than locomotion performance alone”, Morgan Stanley said in a report published ahead of the conference.

Russia maintains regular contacts with Hamas and Hezbollah as part of efforts to promote dialogue and seek diplomatic solutions to conflicts in the Middle East, a senior Russian diplomat said Wednesday.
Aleksandr Kinshchak, director of the Russian Foreign Ministry's Department of the Middle East and North Africa, told Russian news agency Interfax that Moscow maintains contacts with a broad range of political forces.
"We regularly communicate both with the leadership of the Islamic Resistance Movement (Hamas) and with other participants in the Palestinian-Israeli conflict," he said.
Kinshchak said Moscow considers such communication important for addressing issues including ceasefires, humanitarian aid deliveries and evacuations, as well as broader efforts to resolve the Palestinian issue.
On Lebanon, he said Russia had consistently called for an end to hostilities and a transition to a political and diplomatic settlement, adding that Moscow was conveying this position to all parties involved.
He said decisions in Lebanon's direct dialogue with Israel should be based on consensus among the country's major political forces, including Hezbollah, which he said was represented in the government and parliament.
Asked about a US-announced agreement on Hamas disarmament, Kinshchak said Moscow had doubts about the prospects for its rapid implementation.
Hamas considers disarmament to be linked to a complete cessation of hostilities and the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the Gaza Strip, while Israel has publicly called for Hamas to be fully demilitarized first, he said.
“Without real mechanisms of guarantees and in the absolute absence of trust between the parties, the possibility of a speedy compromise raises doubts,” he said.
 
Assurances from Israel on weapon deliveries to Ukraine
On relations with Israel, Kinshchak said Russia-Israel ties had been affected by the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East. Although Israel had not formally joined Western sanctions against Russia, some Israeli businesses had reduced bilateral activity over concerns about secondary sanctions, he added.
Kinshchak also said Moscow had discussed reports of Israeli weapons deliveries to Ukraine with Israeli officials and received assurances that the reports were untrue.
"We promptly discuss them with the Israeli side through various channels and receive assurances that such information does not correspond to reality," he said.
Kinshchak said Russian President Vladimir Putin and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had held six telephone conversations in 2025 and two in 2026.
He added that the two countries were preparing events to mark the 35th anniversary of the restoration of full diplomatic relations on Oct. 18.

Ukraine Emerges From the Shadows of History as a Shaper of the New World Order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

I have lived on this earth long enough to become accustomed to a sense of historical continuity. Where young people see certain ruptures in Ukraine’s existence, I see only periodic transformations and the transition of society from one phase of development to another. If someone were to film this process in time-lapse, we would see a remarkable picture of the birth, growth and now spectacular rise of modern Ukraine.
The beginning of that film, for me, would date back not even to Kyivan Rus, whose imprint remained with us throughout our history. Nor would it begin with the Cossack era, whose spiritual energy Ukrainian elites scattered into the swamps of Muscovy, seeking military support there but finding instead several centuries of non-existence.
The beginning of my Ukraine was laid by that Poet to whom, by the will of Heaven, the future of his people was revealed:
And forgotten will be the shameOf bygone days,And revived will be the good glory,The glory of Ukraine,And the bright, unsetting lightWill quietly shine...Embrace one another, my brothers.I beseech you, I implore you!
His Kobzar became the gospel of a suffering people and the tuning fork from whose keynote subsequent generations measured the “tones” of their struggle for liberation. He laid the foundations of the modern paradigm of the Ukrainian people’s existence.
Then the eras changed, but there were always people who affirmed what mattered most: the spirit of the nation. Politically, it was still subdued and undefined, yet Lesya Ukrainka already saw the dawn fires of a new destiny, while Ivan Franko was already looking for the Ukrainian Moses who would lead his people out of slavery. And ever since then, Ukraine has poured – and continues to pour – its soul and heart into Mykola Lysenko’s prayer: “Great and Only God, protect our Ukraine.”
The new historical circumstances of the early 20th century flung open new windows and doors in Ukraine’s destiny. An era of revolutions and armed struggle began, bringing new trials and mistakes. Yes, our renaissance was shot down, but it was nevertheless a renaissance. Yes, attempts to establish an independent state were short-lived, but its outlines were repeatedly engraved in the historical memory of the people as a goal that had not yet been achieved, but could be achieved.
Then God granted the Sixtiers the opportunity to articulate the spiritual and cultural contours of modern Ukraine. It was like the flash of a supernova – as if dying embers and cosmic ash suddenly burst into new light. It was from the Sixtiers that the human rights activists of the Ukrainian Helsinki Group took up the baton, later passing it to the leaders of the Ukrainian Helsinki Union and the first political parties.
Yet the Ukrainian state that emerged in 1991 was only an embryo that still had to fight for its right to exist. The Russian “brake,” which suppressed the Ukrainian spirit and restrained its flourishing, continued to operate, with ever greater force. Suddenly, the Chekist instinct stirred, recalling what KGB investigators in the 1970s knew all too well: the Ukrainian “lawn” had to be periodically weeded of “Bandera weeds.” But for more than 30 years no one had weeded it – and the “lawn” had changed beyond recognition. Putin therefore had no choice but to go all in.
Yet he failed to achieve any of the goals so pompously proclaimed by the Kremlin dictator. Ukraine has become stronger and even more Ukrainian. NATO has encircled Russia more tightly. The Kremlin’s longtime friends are increasingly turning toward other partnerships. And the situation inside Russia confirms my prediction from 2022: “Ukraine is bleeding, Russia is dying.”
So, what is the meaning of this time-lapse film of Ukraine’s historical trials? Is it a heavenly curse hanging over our people, demanding new sacrifices each time? An insurmountable consequence of our fatal neighborhood – or of our national ailments?
All of this has some significance. But the main meaning of our history lies elsewhere. It can easily be derived from a formula once articulated by Yevhen Sverstiuk: “Heroically shed blood does not disappear. It is transformed into a new form of spiritual energy.” By some incomprehensible will of divine providence, Ukraine’s destiny seems to have been sealed with invisible seals – and each time, the new spiritual energy emerging from shed blood enables us to break another seal.
The end of this brutal war is not yet in sight, and no one can claim that Ukraine has drunk its cup of suffering to the bottom. Yet I know this firmly: every new suffering will give Ukraine new spiritual energy – and will weigh ever more heavily on Russia’s karma. Inevitably, a moment will come when God says to the universal evil: “Enough!”
Then the prophecy of the Ukrainian national anthem, which is sometimes met with skepticism, will be fulfilled: “Our enemies will perish, like dew in the sun.” For this prophecy echoes the biblical one: “So shall Babylon, the great city, be thrown down with violence…” (Rev. 18:21).
Then the supernova of Ukraine will flare at full strength across the geopolitical sky, and even those who today jealously watch Ukraine’s rise will be forced to acknowledge the legitimacy of its new and elevated status.
Ukraine will become one of the pillars of the future architecture of global security. This will bring to an end a long historical cycle that at times became almost unbearable. And this cycle will end with the victory of good, for which suffering souls throughout Ukraine so deeply yearn.
Then the vision of Pope John Paul II, articulated in Kyiv in 2001, will come true:
“The vision which the Apostle Andrew the First-called had does not concern only your past; it is also directed toward the country’s future. It seems to me that, with the eyes of my heart, I truly see a new light spreading across this blessed land of yours; it is the light radiated by a renewed confirmation of the choice made long ago in 988, when Christ was accepted by the Ukrainian people as the ‘Way, the Truth and the Life’ (cf. Jn. 14:6).”
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

U.S. Air Force tests portable control system for ‘fighter drones’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
11:59:27 UTC
20:59:27 KST

- The Air Force completed prototype evaluations for its portable C2E command system for Collaborative Combat Aircraft at Springfield Air National Guard Base.
- A second prototype phase testing vendors' cloud capabilities will follow before the Air Force selects a final C2E integrator.
The U.S. Department of the Air Force has completed prototype evaluations for a portable command-and-control system meant to control Collaborative Combat Aircraft in the field, the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center reported.
The system, known as the C2E, is designed to give operators a mobile way to command semi-autonomous CCA drones from austere or forward locations. The evaluation featured ground operations demonstrations from multiple industry vendors, hosted by the Ohio Air National Guard’s 178th Wing at Springfield Air National Guard Base.
Evaluators tested each vendor’s system for mobility and footprint under simulated austere conditions, then ran demonstrations focused on software agility and connectivity. The results will feed into the Air Force’s broader C2E acquisition strategy and shape the next phase of vendor selection.
“Getting prototypes into the hands of our operational and acquisitions warfighters for a swift, combined evaluation is a direct embodiment of acquisition transformation,” said Col. Eric Reagan, director of the Agile Development Office. “This partnership allows us to accelerate the fielding of the best-value capabilities to the Department of War.”
“The 178th Wing’s foundational support was key to the success of this phase, allowing our evaluators and industry partners to focus entirely on technical performance,” said Lt. Col. Gregory Bieler, materiel leader for CCA software, autonomy and teaming. “This successful collaboration establishes a strong foundation and opens the door for future integration and testing as we continue to mature the C2E and CCA program.”
This phase marks the first step toward selecting an integrator for the C2E system. Once fielded, the chosen system is intended to support Agile Combat Employment operations at the Experimental Operations Unit and integrate directly with production CCA aircraft.
A second prototype phase will follow, requiring vendors to demonstrate their C2E cloud capabilities.

====================================================================================================

Inside the slow ethnic cleansing of al-Mughayyir, a Palestinian village besieged by Israeli settlers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
11:58:34 UTC
20:58:34 KST

On a table set in the corner of the guest room, the cat belonging to Fadi Hamdallah al-Na’san, 17, climbs up and falls asleep among his belongings: his photographs, a collection of sports medals, and his school certificates. The small cat is still searching for her owner’s scent, still waiting for him to come home.
Fadi was declared a martyr on July 18, 2026, a week after being shot by Israeli forces while helping repel a settler attack on a home in his village of al-Mughayyir, east of Ramallah.
Since that day, the al-Na’san family’s home has declared open mourning for its child, hanging a large photo of him on the house. His parents cannot stop talking about the dream that he never got to fulfill.
“Despite his young age, the whole town loved Fadi and talks about him, remembering his character and how he got along with everyone,” Hamdallah al-Na’san, Fadi’s father, told Mondoweiss, his eyes wet, his voice barely holding steady. He shifted his weight on his crutches, wincing in pain from injuries inflicted by a settler attack decades ago that never fully healed.
The al-Na’san family’s home is not the only one in al-Mughayyir in mourning. Since October 2023, seven of the village’s sons have been killed and dozens arrested. Al-Mughayyir is considered one of the most prominent flashpoints of confrontation with settlers in the West Bank, given its strategic location between Ramallah and the Jordan Valley –surrounded on all sides by ten Israeli settlements and outposts.
Israeli military force and settler violence have become a daily feature of life in dozens of villages in the West Bank. According to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, settler attacks and access restrictions have displaced Palestinians across 97 communities since January 2023, most of them Bedouin and herding communities. So-called Israeli “shepherding outposts” of settler-operated farms and grazing operations backed by the Israeli military have become one of the primary instruments for seizing Palestinian land, with settlers using violence and access restrictions to empty villages of their residents. In al-Mughayyir, that process is visible in real time.
Killed while protecting his neighbors
At 10 a.m. on July 12, 2026, calls rang out from the mosque loudspeakers in al-Mughayyir, urging villagers to come to the aid of the family of Abd al-Latif Abu Alia, whose home dozens of settlers were trying to storm. “Fadi went toward Abu Alia’s house, like everyone else,” Fadi’s father told Mondoweiss. “Before he reached the house, an Israeli army patrol was standing in the road. One of the soldiers got out and opened fire at Fadi, hitting him with a bullet in the leg, in the thigh area.”
Half an hour after the confrontations began – during which seven Palestinians were shot – news of Fadi’s injury reached his family. He was taken to the Palestine Medical Complex in Ramallah, suffering from a wound caused by an explosive bullet that had severed the arteries in his leg and caused severe bleeding.
“Fadi suffered several complications,” his father said. “He developed blood poisoning, and his kidneys and liver stopped functioning. Doctors decided to amputate his leg to keep the poisoning from spreading through the rest of his body. But his small body couldn’t withstand it all, and he was killed on the morning of July 18.”
Fadi, a boy full of energy and life, stood out as a talented player at the al-Mughayyir Football Academy and later qualified for the Palestinian youth national team, representing the central West Bank region. Mourning him, the Palestinian Football Federation described his murder as a severe loss for a sports community that has lost 1,013 players in Gaza and the West Bank since the war of extermination began on October 7, 2023, including 568 footballers killed.
“Fadi’s ambition was to play for the Palestinian national team and represent it on the world stage,” his father Hamdallah said. “But even so, he wasn’t consumed by football all the time — he was also a diligent student at school and was getting ready to move up to secondary school.”
This is not the first time the al-Na’san family has suffered attacks by the Israeli army and settlers. Twenty-seven years ago, a settler ran over Fadi’s father, Hamdallah, near Alon Road, which runs alongside al-Mughayyir. He still walks on crutches today and suffers severe pain in his back and legs.
“Our suffering didn’t end with losing Fadi,” Hamdallah said. “A week after he was killed, the Israeli army stormed our home and held us in one room, and detained our son Adib alone in another room, where they beat him repeatedly while we could hear him screaming. They then took him to a nearby military camp, where they continued torturing and beating him before releasing him several hours later.”
For days after his release, 19-year-old Adib’s body was aching from bruises and wounds resulting from beatings he endured, his morale broken.
Walls that don’t protect the people inside
Fadi is the second Palestinian from al-Mughayyir killed defending the Abu Alia family’s homes. On April 12, 2024, Jihad Afif Abu Alia, 25, was killed while helping the family repel a settler attack on their home, located in the al-Mughayyir plain on the village’s eastern edge. Since then, the family has surrounded its homes with a high fence and installed a gate at the entrance.
But during the settlers’ attack on July 12, 2026, Israeli soldiers tried to tear off the gate and remove the fence. Footage showed soldiers breaking the gate’s lock and damaging it in a way that prevents it from being closed again.
“Things have been getting worse for us day after day since 2023,” Abd al-Latif Abu Alia, 56, told Mondoweiss. “But recently the attacks have become daily, in the morning and the evening. Today, the settler wants to come in and graze his sheep in my home’s courtyard, and the army protects the settlers and gives them whatever they ask for — that’s why they want to remove the fence and leave our home exposed.”
The Abu Alia family is made up of 23 members across five households, including Abd al-Latif’s parents, both over 90 years old, and his brother, who has an intellectual disability. Their homes sit on five dunams (half a hectare) of land in the al-Mughayyir plain.
“All these attacks are meant to pressure us and force us out of our homes,” Abd al-Latif said. “But that’s impossible — we will not leave our home no matter what happens, and we have no alternative to it.”
When Mondoweiss visited, the family was gathered in front of their home, braced for any settler attack, as a settler grazed his sheep next to the house. Looking out at the settler, the family described all the injuries they have suffered in recent weeks: Abd al-Latif, two of his sons, and his brother Rasmi all have broken hands and arms from beatings by Israeli forces.
“On July 8, 15 Israeli soldiers stormed our home and beat us severely, which caused fractures in my hand,” Abd al-Latif said. “We were taken to the hospital, but refused to stay overnight, out of fear of leaving our women to face a settler attack alone. Every time we defend our homes against settler attacks, the army comes and punishes us by beating us, searching the house, and destroying its contents. All of us have also been arrested and detained many times.”
Amid the escalating settler attacks, Israeli Minister of National Security Itamar Ben Gvir visited one of the newer outposts built on al-Mughayyir’s land on July 13, 2026 – the day after the assault on the Abu Alia family, a nod of legitimacy to the settler attacks on al-Mughayyir, and and a show of support by the Israeli government to the attacks that settlers are carrying out against Palestinian villages.
Israel erases al-Mughayyir’s plains
The eastern plain of al-Mughayyir looks like a barren desert today. Before August 2025, it spanned 350 dunams (35 hectares) and was one of the main sources of income for al-Mughayyir’s residents. It has since suffered wide destruction by settlers and the Israeli army. The Abu Alia family alone lost 50 dunams (5 hectares) planted with olive trees.
Ghassan Jamal, of the al-Mughayyir Agricultural Cooperative Association, told Mondoweiss that Israel and its settlers have seized all the agricultural land and grazing areas in the eastern plain, the western plain, al-Qabun, al-Dalia, Marj al-Dhahab, and al-Rafid, making up some 42,000 dunams (4,200 hectares) in total and leaving al-Mughayyir’s residents with only 1,000 accessible dunams (100 hectares) in the area covered by the village’s master plan, classified as “Area B” under the Oslo Accords.
“In the eastern plain of al-Mughayyir, 12,000 olive trees have been uprooted,” Ghassan Jamal said. “They’ve also blocked villagers from reaching thousands of trees in the village’s other plains, behind Alon Road. In other areas, settlers pour toxic substances on the trees to kill them, and bring in sheep to graze on and destroy what remains.”
“Our grandparents planted al-Mughayyir’s trees, and we never let go of them — we inherited them generation after generation,” Jamal said. “All of al-Mughayyir’s land was cultivated and cared for by its people the whole time, which is why al-Mughayyir was like paradise, and its people depended on its trees as their main source of livelihood.”
Holding on to what remains of al-Mughayyir’s land, Jamal and 15 other farmers founded a cooperative association to help each other shoulder the burdens of the loss of their land. Their first project was planting golden thistle on six dunams (0.6 hectares) in the eastern plain. “As soon as it started to yield a crop, they stopped us from harvesting it,” he said, referring to Israeli authorities and settlers. “We planted 270 grapevines seven years ago, but within a few days, the settlers brought in sheep and destroyed them completely. They also targeted the association’s greenhouses, burning and destroying them.”
The destruction of al-Mughayyir’s livestock
Al-Mughayyir was not known only for its farmland, but also for its open grazing lands, which in the past allowed residents to own thousands of sheep. Jamal Abu Alia, a local farmer, said that al-Mughayyir once had more than 18,000 head of sheep, producing 2-3 tons of cheese every day.
Today, the Abu Hammam family is nearly the only one left in al-Mughayyir that still owns a flock of sheep. The size of their flock, however, has halved in recent years, falling to only 130 heads, as a result of the family being barred from reaching grazing land.
Since October 2023, the Hammam family has been forced, due to threats from settlers, to move from their home in al-Mughayyir village to their two dunams of land in the al-Khalayel area. But in December 2025, settlers launched a violent attack on the family, beating them and driving them off the land, which they are unable to reach today.
“Today there’s no grazing land for the sheep, which stay in the pen all the time, multiplying the cost for us significantly,” Fatima Abu Naim told Mondoweiss. “We’re able to stay in our home in the middle of al-Mughayyir, but we’re afraid that settlers will reach our land here too and take it, the way they took our land in al-Khalayel and the eastern plain. But we’re trying to bear the hardship of life and stay here, so we can keep settlers from reaching this place.”
Fatima, a mother of five, voices the fears of every family in al-Mughayyir. “Every day that passes in al-Mughayyir is worse than the one before it. We live in constant fear, anxiety, and readiness for any attack,” Fatima said.
“I used to think about my children’s future and work so I could help them get an education and achieve their dreams. But today I’m consumed by fear for them, for their lives, and for their existence.”
Shatha Hammad
Shatha Hammad is a Palestinian journalist specializing in in-depth features in the West Bank, where she has reported on the ground since 2011. She holds a BA in Journalism and Political Science and an MA in Contemporary Arab Studies from Birzeit University.

Greek Cypriot politicians call for reckoning, apologies over killings of Turkish Cypriots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
11:58:00 UTC
20:58:00 KST

Muratağa and Sandallar Cemetery of Martyrs in Northern Cyprus (AA photo)
A group of Greek Cypriot politicians has called for a reckoning with the past and mutual apologies over attacks and massacres targeting Turkish Cypriots, noting that that those responsible have largely gone unpunished.
Former Greek Cypriot Foreign Minister Erato Kozakou-Marcoullis this week reposted on social media a 2016 post featuring photographs from a mass grave and issued remarks on the Turkish Cypriots massacred by Greek Cypriot armed groups in the villages of Aloda (Atlılar), Maratha (Muratağa), Sandallaris (Sandallar) and Tochni (Taşkent) on Aug. 14, 1974.
Marcoullis said that no Greek Cypriot had been punished for the killings of Turkish Cypriots, calling for the truth to be acknowledged and for both communities to apologize to one another.
“Let us acknowledge the truth and apologize to each other,” she said.
Warning that the far right continues to pose a threat on the island, Marcoullis wrote: “Unpunished crimes, unspoken truths, wounds that have not healed, pain that has not subsided.”
She stressed the need to acknowledge the facts, saying that unless the truth is confronted, crimes remain buried in silence and the suffering of both communities is acknowledged, “the divide will widen, peace will not be built, and the vision of a common homeland will forever elude us.”
Greek Cypriot lawmaker Giorgos Koukoumas also said in a written statement that the attacks against Turkish Cypriots represented one of the lesser-known chapters of Greek Cyprus’ history and could no longer be ignored by the Greek Cypriot community.
Koukoumas described the killing of 126 Turkish Cypriot women, children and elderly people by Greek Cypriot armed groups in the Famagusta area villages in August 1974, as well as the killing of a large number of Turkish Cypriot men in Tochni, as “one of the darkest pages in history.”
He said the attacks were carried out by Greek Cypriot far-right elements and stressed that most of those responsible had never been brought to justice.
“No person with a basic sense of human dignity, regardless of their political views or position on the Cyprus issue, can ignore questions such as how Turkish Cypriot children were found collectively in wells and how their remains are still being unearthed today,” Koukoumas said.
The politicians’ social media posts received support from parts of the Greek Cypriot public as well as from some politicians in the Greek Cypriot community.
Türkiye launched its 1974 Peace Operation following a coup backed by the military junta in Greece that sought to unite Cyprus with Greece. Ankara said the operation was carried out to restore constitutional order and protect the Turkish Cypriot community after years of intercommunal violence.
Following the division of the island, the Turkish Cypriot administration in the north has been recognized solely by Türkiye.

The magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck off the coast of Flores Island in Indonesia’s East Nusa Tenggara province on August 15. The Russian Embassy in Indonesia expressed condolences over the loss of life and destruction in a post on its Telegram channel.

Polish prosecutors charge a woman over an attack on Ukrainian children. Consulate says the siblings were targeted for speaking Ukrainian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
11:55:33 UTC
20:55:33 KST

Polish prosecutors have charged a 46-year-old woman over a nationality-based attack on two Ukrainian siblings in Bydgoszcz, days after police detained her and a 34-year-old man, whom they questioned as a witness, Polish Radio's Ukrainian Service reported the detentions on 18 August 2026, with the charges filed the same evening.
The detentions came four days after the alleged attack in a park near Bydgoszcz’s main railway station. The Bydgoszcz-North district prosecutor charged the woman with insulting the siblings and violating a minor's bodily integrity on nationality grounds. She denied intentionally insulting or assaulting the children and gave police a different account of the encounter.
The case comes amid rising reports of suspected hate crimes against Ukrainians and worsening relations between Warsaw and Kyiv. Police received 180 such reports in the first half of 2026—about one a day. At that pace, 2026 would end more than 30% above 2025 and nearly 35% above 2024.
Prosecutors charged only the woman; the 34-year-old man detained with her was questioned as a witness, even though the mother and the consulate described both adults as aggressors. The prosecutor placed her under police supervision, imposed a no-contact order, and set bail at 5,000 zł ($1,340). The destruction of the boy's toy drone was treated as a misdemeanor because the toy was worth just over 100 zł ($27).
The siblings—a 14-year-old girl and her 12-year-old brother—were playing with a toy drone in the park when the adults confronted them about using it, their mother told police. The Ukrainian consulate said the adults also insulted and threatened the children after hearing them speak Ukrainian.
“They twisted a child’s arm, broke a toy drone, and threw fragments at the boy,” Ukraine’s Consulate General in Gdańsk said.
The consulate said the fragments scratched the boy but caused no serious injury.
Other attacks on Ukrainians in Poland
The Bydgoszcz case is one of several recent assaults involving Ukrainian victims.
Police detained two women on 14 August over an attack on Ukrainian men outside a Poznań restaurant the previous day. A video showed one woman insulting, spitting at, and striking the men.
In July, three men allegedly beat a Ukrainian couple in Wrocław after asking whether they were Ukrainian. In Łódź, a man allegedly attacked a passerby he mistook for Ukrainian, breaking his nose and jaw.
The violence has prompted public protests. On 9 August, the Committee for the Defense of Democracy organized “Don’t be indifferent” rallies in 22 cities. Two days earlier, Warsaw organizers delivered a petition with more than 11,000 signatures calling for government action against attacks on Ukrainians.
Deepening Polish-Ukrainian rift and decline in relations
The rise in anti-Ukrainian violence in Poland has unfolded amid worsening political relations between Kyiv and Warsaw. Polish support for accepting Ukrainian refugees fell from 94% in March 2022 to 48% by early 2026, while politicians increasingly use Ukraine as a wedge issue.
Historical disputes over the Volhynia massacres and the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) have also strained relations. The rift sharpened after Zelenskyy signed a decree granting a Ukrainian special forces unit the honorary title “Heroes of the UPA.” Polish President Karol Nawrocki announced on 19 June that he had decided to revoke Zelenskyy’s Order of the White Eagle, Poland’s highest state honor.

U.S. Marine Corps holds first-ever attack drone competition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
11:54:12 UTC
20:54:12 KST

- The Marine Corps held its first Attack Drone Competition August 10-14 at Quantico, testing teams on drone strikes and survival against opposing ISR.
- FPV operators from 4th Marine Division won the event, and the Corps plans to extend engagement distances to 20 kilometers for fiscal year 2027.
The U.S. Marine Corps held its first Attack Drone Competition August 10-14 at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Virginia, testing Marines from 3rd Littoral Combat Team and 4th Marine Division on strike planning, target engagement and survival against the very drone threats they were trained to employ, U.S. Marine Corps Training and Education Command reported.
Weapons Training Battalion, part of Training Command, hosted the event. Teams conducted strike planning and execution, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance integration, urban and night operations, long-range strikes and moving-target engagements. Competitors had to synchronize multiple attack drones against separate targets at nearly simultaneous times on target.
The exercise also placed competitors on the receiving end of drone warfare. An opposing force used ISR to locate and track teams, forcing competitors to manage their signatures and respond to the threat while still completing their assigned missions.
“Being on the receiving end of the weapon system we’re trained to employ was humbling, to say the least,” said Lance Cpl. Georgino Perez, an infantryman with 3rd Littoral Combat Team and an FPV drone pilot. “It highlighted the need for more training, not only on how to employ these systems, but how to survive against them.”
The competition gave Weapons Training Battalion insight into how to sharpen current attack drone training, including long-range aerial navigation, time-on-target planning, hide-site and antenna management, emergency protective actions, escape and evasion, and signature management.
“The experience gained at the championship is important to the Marine Corps’ train-the-trainer model,” said Col. Charles E. Anklam III, commanding officer of Weapons Training Battalion. “Marines who develop proficiency through advanced training and competition can take those lessons back to their units and help build more capable attack drone teams throughout the Fleet.”
FPV operators from 4th Marine Division won the competition, which concluded with an awards ceremony.
The Marine Corps plans to expand the competition for fiscal year 2027, introducing a dedicated opposing force and electronic warfare effects while extending engagement distances to as much as 20 kilometers (12 miles). The changes are intended to build on lessons from this year’s event and further test teams operating attack drones in a contested environment.

Woman sought in Massachusetts officer’s death co-founded mental health group for first responders
WORCESTER, Mass. (AP) — Police investigating the death of an off-duty police officer in Massachusetts in what they called a domestic matter are searching for a woman who co-founded a group that focuses on suicide and mental health issues among first responders.
The officer, a 31-year veteran, was found dead at a home in Worcester, Massachusetts, on Tuesday. Police and Worcester County District Attorney Joseph Early Jr. said the 58-year woman was at the house. Police were passing out flyers with her photo to drivers in the area Wednesday morning.
Local, state and federal agencies were involved in searching for the woman, who may be armed, Worcester Police Chief Paul Saucier and Worcester District Attorney Joseph Early said at a news conference.
“I can’t get into too much of it with regards to our domestic violence rules and regulations,” Early said.
An email seeking comment on the investigation was sent to a spokesperson for Early’s office Wednesday.
Police identified the woman as Karen Solomon and did not name the officer. Thomas Duffy, the president of the local police union, identified the officer as Kurt Solomon. Police did not describe the relationship between the two. Records show the Solomons own the home and that Kurt Solomon named Karen Solomon as his wife in a 2016 bankruptcy case.
“When you serve 31 years with an individual, you become more than co-workers. You become family, and today we lost a member of our family,” Duffy told reporters Tuesday. “Just a tremendous human being. Extremely committed. Always reliable. Always dedicated to the job and to the citizens.”
He added, “It’s a very difficult time. His loss is deeply being felt by the men and women of this department right now.”
Karen Solomon is a co-founder of an organization called First H.E.L.P., the organization said in a statement Tuesday night.
The group “is dedicated to honoring the service of first responders who have died by suicide, supporting their families, reducing the stigma associated with seeking mental-health assistance, and increasing awareness of mental-health challenges within the law-enforcement and first-responder communities,” it said.
“Our first concern is for the officer who lost his life, his family, his colleagues, and the Worcester law-enforcement community,” the group said in its statement. “We extend our deepest condolences to all those affected by this tragedy.”
First H.E.L.P. said the circumstances surrounding the Worcester investigation “are an active matter for law enforcement” and the group will have no further comment on it.

Israeli strikes hit an air base hours after a Turkish delegation visit, Syrian officials say

Israeli strikes hit an air base hours after a Turkish delegation visit, Syrian officials say
DAMASCUS, Syria (AP) — A Turkish delegation had visited an air base in northern Syria the day before it was hit by Israeli airstrikes, Syrian officials said.
The Israeli strikes hit the Abu Duhur base early Tuesday, hours after the delegation had left, causing damage but no casualties. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office said in a statement that Israel had attacked the base because Syria was “on the verge of breaching” an agreed-upon “status quo in security matters” by allowing Turkish troops to deploy there.
Two Syrian officials who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly said the Turkish delegation had visited the air base in the northwestern province of Idlib on Monday to review rehabilitation work underway at the facility.
It was the first confirmation of a Turkish presence at the Abu Duhur base.
Turkish and Syrian officials have not publicly commented on Turkey’s role there but have condemned the attack, as did Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Turkey who also serves as special envoy to Syria, and a number of Arab countries.
Turkish officials on Wednesday did not comment on the reported presence of a Turkish military delegation. But Turkey’s communications directorate accused Netanyahu of making “untenable allegations ... intended to legitimize Israel’s unlawful airstrikes targeting Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.” It alleged that Netanyahu aimed “to pursue expansionist and destabilizing policies in the region ahead of the elections in Israel.”
Turkey “will resolutely continue to cooperate with the Syrian Government on a legitimate basis for the establishment of peace, stability, and prosperity in Syria, and will never allow the destabilization of Syria,” it said.
The Abu Duhur air base lies at a strategic location near the borders between Idlib, Aleppo and Hama provinces. During the time of former Syrian President Bashar Assad, who was ousted by a rebel offensive in December 2024, MiG-23 and MiG-21 fighter jets and L-39 aircraft operated out of the base.
Turkey has been supporting Syria’s effort to rebuild its armed forces by training Syrian personnel at Turkish military schools and bases, and by supplying equipment and logistical support. Officials have not disclosed the types of equipment involved. The two countries signed an agreement last year that formalized their military cooperation.
Earlier this year, Syrian troops also took part in military exercises held in Turkey.
Turkish officials have repeatedly stated that Ankara does not consider Syria’s security separate from its own.
Israel, meanwhile, has remained suspicious of the new authorities in Damascus, led by former Islamist insurgents. Syria’s interim President Ahmad al-Sharaa has said repeatedly that he does not want a conflict with Israel.
Israel carried out hundreds of airstrikes around Syria after Assad’s fall, mainly destroying assets of the Syrian army to keep them out of the hands of his successors. The Israeli military also seized control of a U.N.-patrolled buffer zone in southern Syria, which it continues to occupy.
Turkey, a NATO member that also recently signed a defense pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, gave no indication that it would respond militarily to the Israeli strikes in Syria, but the incident added further strain to already tense Turkish-Israeli relations.
Turkey and Israel once were close allies, but the relationship has been marked by deep frictions under Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s more than two-decade rule, despite brief periods of reconciliation. Erdogan is an outspoken critic of Israel’s policies toward the Palestinians, while Israel has been angered by Erdogan’s support for the Hamas militant group.
The fall of Assad’s government further strained their relations as the two rivals sought to curb each other’s influence in the neighboring country, with some analysts fearing that they could be headed toward a proxy war.
