Sybiha was born on January 1, 1975, in Zboriv, Ternopil region. He began working at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in 1997.
From 1998 to 2002, he served first as second secretary and later as first secretary at the Ukrainian Embassy in Poland. In 2002-2003, he worked as first secretary of the Legal and Humanitarian Cooperation Division of the MFA's European Integration Department.
From 2003 to 2008, he held senior positions in the MFA's Treaty and Legal Department and later in the relevant directorate. From 2008 to 2021, he served as minister-counselor at the Ukrainian Embassy in Poland, and from 2012 to 2016, he headed the MFA's Consular Service Department.
On August 23, 2016, Sybiha was appointed Ukraine's ambassador to Turkey. He was dismissed from the post on May 19, 2021, after which he became Deputy Head of the Office of the President.
On April 12, 2024, Sybiha became First Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs.
On September 5, 2024, the Verkhovna Rada appointed him Minister of Foreign Affairs following the dismissal of Dmytro Kuleba.
On July 14, the Verkhovna Rada accepted Prime Minister Yuliia Svyrydenko's resignation. The entire Cabinet automatically resigned along with her.
On July 17, with the president's approval, the government appointed Sybiha Ukraine's acting foreign minister.

Dell XPS 13 vs. MacBook Neo: A Surprising Upset
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Ever since the MacBook Neo was announced this spring, I've been looking for a serious alternative. Not a cheap knockoff that sacrifices quality for price. No, no. I was hunting for a Windows laptop with the same goal as the MacBook Neo—hiding its compromises and delivering an otherwise premium laptop at a lower cost. For months, it was crickets.
Then, the Dell XPS 13 showed up on my doorstep, and it understood the assignment. For many reasons, this was the one I'd been waiting for. But the question remains: Is it actually the better budget laptop? The answer surprised me when I dug into the testing.
Hidden Compromises
When the MacBook Neo was originally announced, it was a shocker. Apple coming in at the $599 price point for the base configuration felt unreal. Apple had never in its history brought the MacBook to such a low price. Even at its new $699 starting price, it's in unprecedented territory. Importantly, this encroached on the territory of Windows laptops, where it has traditionally had a monopoly.
And while many Windows laptops are available at this price, they suffer from many of the same problems, such as cheap materials or corners cut with low-quality displays and touchpads. Even a cheap laptop I like quite a bit, like the HP OmniBook 5 (with the Snapdragon X Plus), has a weak point in its touchpad.
But the Dell XPS 13 sought to match the MacBook Neo's premium quality in nearly every aspect. It has the same starting price of $699 (or $599 for students). It's exactly the same size at just a half-inch thick, so when the lid is closed and you're holding it, it feels just as portable. The XPS 13 weighs 2.2 pounds, half a pound lighter than the MacBook Neo. The Neo isn't heavy, but holding both in your hands, the difference is noticeable. That's the first point in favor of the XPS 13.
Despite a slightly smaller screen (13 inches, measured diagonally), the MacBook Neo sits taller than the XPS 13 when the lid is open. That's because the XPS 13's 13.4-inch display is surrounded by much smaller bezels—particularly the bottom, which gives the XPS 13 a more modern look. The white keyboard and flashier color options of the MacBook Neo certainly have their appeal, especially since the XPS 13 comes in only two shades of silver. But in general, more screen real estate and smaller dimensions are preferable, especially if you want to travel on an airplane with your laptop.
And then there's the screen itself. Most $700 laptops have mediocre screens that aren't bright enough and have poor colors. I never expected Apple to skimp on the display, of course, and it didn't. It goes up to 509 nits (as tested) and has decent color reproduction. But the XPS 13 is better in three ways. First, it has a touchscreen, which MacBooks don't (yet) have. That's a nice addition for an entry-level model. It also has a 120-Hz refresh rate, which gives the screen fast, fluid responsiveness that not even the MacBook Air has. Again, that's a feature that's exceedingly rare to find on a budget-level laptop. Lastly, the XPS 13 has better color saturation, specifically on the Adobe RGB and P3 color scales. It's actually one of the better IPS screens I've tested on a laptop, and it's as sharp as the MacBook Neo.
None of these are weak points of the MacBook Neo, but it's worth noting that the XPS 13 has it beat in a number of these areas. That's also true of the keyboard and trackpad. Both are excellent on these laptops, and I found myself comfortable using them right off the bat. Again, trackpads in particular can be a sore spot for budget Windows laptops, but Dell smartly didn't skimp on it. Apple's the one that compromised on the keyboard, both by not including Touch ID in the base model and by removing backlighting (which the XPS 13 includes).
Ports, Storage, and Videoconferencing
I already mentioned the display and the portability, but there are a few other places where the XPS 13 is the clear winner. The first is the USB-C ports. Both devices have two, but the XPS 13 splits them, so one is on the left side, and one is on the right side. I really like this decision, as it allows you to charge the device from either side. Then, there's the speed of these USB-C ports. One of the USB-C ports on the MacBook Neo is an outdated USB 2 port. Not only is it slow for file transfers, but it also can't natively output to an external display. Both USB-C ports on the XPS 13 are USB 3.2 Gen 2, which can each support a 4K display and transfer data at up to 10 Gbps.
The Neo does have an advantage when it comes to ports, though. It has a headphone jack, whereas the XPS 13 doesn't. This might be less of a big deal today than it was in the past, but I prefer laptops to keep them.
The XPS 13 comes with 512 GB of storage in both the base and upgraded models. The MacBook Neo base model comes only with 256 GB, and you'll need to upgrade to the Touch ID model for 521 GB. On top of that, Dell's laptop uses faster storage. That's a winning combination.
The videoconferencing setup is similarly good. Both webcams are 1080p. Though the image processing is a bit better on the MacBook Neo, the XPS 13 includes an IR camera for logging in without a password. The base configuration of the Neo doesn't have Touch ID, so you have to type a password to log in, change settings, and pay online.
The RAM Problem
Apple never claimed the MacBook Neo was a powerhouse. Built on an iPhone chip (the A18 Pro) and limited to 8 GB of RAM, it is clearly designed for college students and anyone with lower-level computing needs. When I tested it initially, I found that if I wasn't paying attention, it was easy to let open applications, tons of browser tabs, and background tasks slow the computer down, with the main bottleneck being the 8 GB of RAM. Apple hasn't sold a MacBook with 8 GB of RAM since 2024, but the company has always insisted that its unified memory system means it doesn't need as much capacity as a Windows PC. But is that really true? Now that we have a very comparable Windows system with 8 GB of RAM as well, it'll be easy to test just how true Apple's claims are.
The bad news is that both devices took very little effort to use up the available memory. Playing a YouTube video with various news sites open in six Google Chrome tabs was enough to use over 90 percent of the 8 GB. Neither Windows nor macOS feels optimized for a computer with just 8 GB of RAM these days, no doubt from all the AI-infused tasks running in the background. Now, just because you're getting dangerously close to reaching 100 percent of the memory utilization, that doesn't mean your computer instantly freezes up. It takes a lot to get these systems to grind to a halt, but with a 16-GB laptop, you'll spend much less time managing what tabs and applications you have open. On the other hand, if you're a student coming from a cheap Chromebook or hand-me-down computer, these laptops will feel like a nice upgrade.
The XPS 13 has a fan inside, while the MacBook Neo is passively cooled. Under a heavy load you can hear that fan spin up in the XPS 13, whereas the Neo is completely silent. Both laptops get excellent battery life—enough to get through a full day of class or work. That's another area where laptops at this price tended to suffer in the past.
But the big difference between these two laptops is how you can configure them. Both start at $700 ($699 for the Neo, to be exact), and you get one upgrade option. For an extra $100, you can move up to the MacBook Neo with 512 GB of storage and Touch ID built in. On the other hand, the Dell XPS 13 has a $900 model that's identical to the base model, except it has 16 GB of RAM. So yes, the 16-GB version of the XPS 13 is $100 more expensive. But it's better in nearly every way, and it's likely the best laptop you can buy for less than $1,000.
And even when comparing the 8-GB model, the XPS 13 handily beats the MacBook Neo in tons of small ways. It has a better display, a backlit keyboard, two USB ports—one on each side—that support charging and 4K monitors, and it's more portable. It does all that while looking super sharp and feeling just as premium as the Neo. While I think everyone should buy a 16-GB laptop, at the 8-GB level, the Dell XPS 13 is the better laptop no matter how you slice it.

There’s a Very Simple Reason Why You Love the Slate Truck
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Tisha Johnson is a rare anomaly in the car world: a design leader for an automaker who is not a man. In a resolutely testosterone-fueled industry where, traditionally, women have seemingly been given positions of authority in design labs as long as they focus on interiors, colors, or material selections, very few have been afforded free rein on the most important visual element of the car, the exterior, let alone promoted to run the entire aesthetic show. Johnson has.
As head of design at Slate, this gender-specific fact might be why the world has fallen in love with the Jeff Bezos–backed truck. Casual observers might put the Slate EV's popularity down to its low price. Starting at $24,950, the Slate arriving later this year won't just be the cheapest EV on the US market; it will also be the cheapest pickup truck of any power flavor.
But people buy cheap all the time. Be it a pickup or portable speaker, cheap doesn't mean they love the product; it usually means a compromise. And it's hard to love a compromise. The real trick is in creating something beautiful and accessible.
It's a hard task—ask Jony Ive, who has fashioned the best-looking automotive interior in decades for the $640,000 Ferrari Luce. Even though you could buy 25 (and a half) Slate trucks for the same price as a Luce, the Ferrari's exterior has been met with a frosty reception, to say the least. The budget Slate, meanwhile, has won multiple awards for its looks, not just for how much it costs. Johnson and her team have nailed beautiful and accessible. The TL;DR secret sauce? Ditch the testosterone and bring in a woman's perspective, and, perhaps more importantly, lack of ego.
Johnson has been working toward getting people to love the Slate for 27 years. Her final-year thesis at California’s Art Center College of Design in 1999 focused on the genuine need for a useful, affordable, and hopefully desirable vehicle for a single mom. It has taken two long spells at Volvo (a 17-year tour in total), with stints in between as head of design at Whirlpool and Herman Miller, to realize her vision.
Toward the end of this year, Slate's first customers will get behind the wheel of Johnson's dream of an astonishingly affordable vehicle—one that can transform from an electric truck to a traditional “squareback” SUV to a jeep-like “fastback” SUV, thanks to a genuinely ingenious modular design. Complete color changes will be possible in two days and cost just $500. Panels can be swapped out; decals, roof racks, and $60 grille plates can be bought from Slate or, as the company is going to publish a load of its 3D files, tweaked and printed by owners themselves. Many companies talk about genuinely democratic design; very few deliver.
I sat down with Johnson to discuss this rare and laudable woman-centric approach to the Slate, and exactly how it's brought about an EV that the design world, auto trade, and the general public (180,000 preorders and counting) all love.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
JEREMY WHITE: Pickups are trapped in a hyper-masculine, aggressive design language. Giant grilles, towering fronts, hostile postures. As a woman leading the truck's design team, was stepping away from that intentional pushback against car-guy tropes or a byproduct of creating a utility vehicle with empathy and affordability?
TISHA JOHNSON: We were always intentional in what the expression would be. There were definitely things that we didn't want it to be. We didn't want it to be a jerk. We literally said that. First and foremost, we wanted the vehicle to be truly approachable. Friendly but very confident. We all attach to the vehicles we drive. They represent our personality, our self-expression. This vehicle, the ability to personalize, is a cornerstone of the thinking here.
We talked about—before we actually ever had one line sketched—that you're walking through the parking lot; you've been shopping, and you look and see your vehicle. How do you feel? How do you feel when you see a Slate? You feel like you cannot wait to get back to that vehicle, and it's a vehicle you can count on. It's someone you can trust. These were the kinds of things we wanted to see. We didn't want it to be cliché or look at the past. We said it would be familiar, but at the same time feel very relevant today.
Having written your thesis on designing a vehicle for a single mom with kids, starting from a different goal than a male designer, what tangible design decisions does your team bring to the Slate to create a truck for everyone, not just men? Did a different design language have to be established?
I want to make sure I'm super clear with you: We absolutely rejected an overly aggressive, hyper-dominant look. We didn't want it to look like a beast on the road. No way. Look at the front fascia, where the headlamps are. The face of the vehicle—it has eyes wide open. Round headlamps. There are reasons why this is good for accessorizing; it's very easy to get to and put different headlamps there if you want—but it also has an alertness to it that we wanted. But if you look at where that hood line is, it strikes across part of that headlamp, and that is so that there is definitely an expression of overt confidence.
Look at the side mirror; there's an area there where we put a little landing pad for a small decal. If you had only a few bucks in your pocket, and you just wanted to give a little pop of expression or color right there, you could. I just love that.
I would argue that a woman is not looking for a vehicle designed for her. Research shows our buying behaviors are not focused on anything clichéd, that's for sure. So we made that face come off as confident, fair, and modern, and with more product-like attributes than other vehicles.
Then you go from there. On the surface, there's a really nice strong shoulder. That is a cue that there's a vehicle there that's safe and reliable. We didn't get into a lot of surfacing that is swoopy and arrowed. The angle of the windscreen is fairly upright. We didn't go all super-fast there. These are decisions rejecting the tropes expected in a vehicle today. These modern clichés, we just left those behind.
Considering you rejected the design clichés, are you surprised at the plaudits that Slate’s looks have garnered from the male-dominated auto design world?
I'll give you a little bit of behind-the-scenes. We started with some assumptions that you would find any design group considering, like putting precious materials in the front area; and this is where we'll put the name mark, the DNA, and it is placed there beautifully, never to be touched, just to be admired. That's what goes on in a design studio.
As we were looking at designs and testing internally, we could see what people were attracted to. But as a design group, we kept saying, “This isn't right yet.” Then finally we realized the problem: We were using the exact playbook that has been handed down from generation to generation. We literally said, “This is all wrong. We cannot do this.”
So we literally threw out that playbook and said, if this is Slate's DNA, then we're going to put a plate right there between those two headlamps that has exposed fasteners. Yes, it holds the main brand mark, but we designed it in such a way that it's easy to remove, easy to replace. Yes, we offer some different designs, but we're saying this is easy enough for you, as the owner, to 3D-print something to put here if you want to. Now, that's outrageous. That is different.
Absolutely we wanted to forge a new path. We just did not know that it would be recognized. We didn't think it would be. We weren't considering it being appreciated so quickly and by so many. That's been an honor for us as a team.
EV development has been hijacked by tech-bro posturing. Ludicrous acceleration; giant screens. Is stripping away unnecessary tech bloat fundamentally an exercise in empathetic, less ego-driven design? And how do you take the ego out of auto design when it seems to be impossible at almost every other car brand?
Yes, I wish I could say it better. Before we had the design, we had some principles that were core, and one of those was to take away all of the unnecessary tech. It drives up the cost, yes, but I was driving in a car with my niece and her friends, a mix of twentysomething men and women, but mostly women. They were taking jabs at the tech-bro culture and talking about how it was getting in the way of the simple pleasures and things that you could appreciate. They said, “Like all of these screens everywhere. I don't use them. I'm not interested in it at all.” I was in heaven hearing it.
We considered radical things like, do you really need an HVAC unit? It wasn't a provocative idea that somebody put on the table to make a point. It was fiercely debated, and it won for good reasons. But the integrated stereo system did not win. We did a cost analysis on the window crank against a power pack, and the window crank won.
I infused a word into the design process. It wasn't overtly in the first description of the Slate, but it was there, between the lines. The word was “love.” That's a word we felt in the design studio, because we understood that as we were starting—the descriptions of the vehicle being affordable, easy to own, personalized, something that was robust and something that you wanted that was cool. You put that all together? That spells love.
So we wanted to be very open that we wanted people to love the vehicle. It requires real commitment on all of those levels at the same time. These are natural tensions that, in any other program I've ever worked on, at some point you let go of one of those big ideas to get to the goal on time. We said no.
In so much other car design, the word is not love; it's sex. Phallic fronts, power bulges. Car designers generally don't talk of lovable cars, do they?
Just being candid, I've been in design reviews in my earlier years where I would feel the conversation completely left my point of view out—the point of view of actually most people. We know that a female in the household is driving decisionmaking around a car purchase. She doesn't want to be classified or catered to in a way that is cliché. She does want to be considered, and that's important, because a woman will be inclined to consider the needs of everyone in the household. Letting all of that “gender” into vehicle design? I've always thought it was kind of silly. Love is so much more stable, Jeremy.
And lasts longer.
It does. You would see female designers more likely to be color and material designers on the interior. More and more, you are seeing a more equal distribution of men and women around different topics in car development, and that's great. But the conversation used to go, “Well, once you get inside of the vehicle, then you have the emotional bond, and it's more of an animal attraction on the outside.” I really push back on that. Yes, there is an attraction [with the Slate]. But that attraction that draws you toward it is based on something that is very lasting from the inside out. It's a deeper emotional connection.
How do you think you'll feel when you see your first mom driving around with two kids in the back of her Slate?
Emotional. It's very emotional to think about that. It's something I wanted to do, and I just hated that I didn't do it. And so, every day, I'm motivated because I'm involved in the act of doing that, of realizing that. It's incredibly rewarding.

French MEP Raphaël Glucksmann gears up to announce presidential run
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19

PARIS — Center-left MEP Raphaël Glucksmann will announce that he’s running in next year’s presidential election in France in the next few days, most likely with a prime-time TV interview on Sunday, according to three people close to him.
The trio, granted anonymity to speak candidly about Glucksmann’s plans, said he plans to take part in a closed primary being organized by the Socialist Party that currently includes Ségolène Royal, the Socialist presidential candidate in 2007 who lost to Nicolas Sarkozy, and MP Philippe Brun. Socialist Party leader Olivier Faure has also said he is considering running.
While a win would guarantee Glucksmann the support of the Socialists, the main center-left force in France, the party has been struggling to make inroads with voters and is beset by infighting.
Advertisement
Several high-profile Socialists, including former President François Hollande and former Prime Minister Bernard Cazeneuve, have publicly hinted at plans to sit out their party’s primary and launch independent presidential bids.
However, polls show that Glucksmann, the leader of his own small political party, Place Publique, is the best-placed presidential hopeful on the center left after leading the Socialists and their allies to a strong third-place finish in the 2024 European elections.
Yet he and the rest of the field still lag significantly behind far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen, according to most surveys. France’s presidential election goes to a runoff if no candidate scores more than 50 percent of the vote, and if the polls hold, Le Pen is all but guaranteed to nab one of the final two spots.
To advance to the second round, Glucksmann will have to see off centrist and center-right rivals like Edouard Philippe and the firebrand anticapitalist Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
Mélenchon, who announced his plans to run in May, is currently polling slightly ahead of Glucksmann, but both are within striking distance of making the runoff.
The two are bitter rivals whose divisions are reminiscent of those across left-leaning parties in the Western world, including the U.S. Democratic Party.
Advertisement
Glucksmann hopes his centrist brand of politics can win over former Socialist voters who backed President Emmanuel Macron. Mélenchon’s hardline messaging is more targeted at low-propensity voters, including younger voters and those from working-class, multicultural communities in major French cities.
Glucksmann and Mélenchon disagree on issues ranging from France’s participation in NATO, — which Mélenchon opposes and Glucksmann supports — to pension reform.
Mélenchon has pledged to lower the minimum retirement age to 60 if elected president, while Glucksmann believes some workers should be required to work longer and that France should move toward a system where retirement age would be based on life expectancy and individual working conditions.

When aid institutions fail to protect their own: The moral test exposed by Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:27:04 UTC
19:27:04 KST

Share & more
The 2026 Aid Worker Security Report confirms what many in the humanitarian community have long feared: 2025 was again the worst year on record for humanitarian workers. A staggering 1,187 aid workers were killed, wounded, kidnapped, or arbitrarily detained while carrying out humanitarian work.
While the horrors of Gaza and Sudan account for the greatest loss of humanitarian lives, Yemen now stands as the world's worst crisis for the arbitrary detention of humanitarians.
Nowhere is this more visible than in the case of the UN's own staff, dozens of whom have been arbitrarily detained by the Houthis for two years now. Many have endured physical violence, solitary confinement, incommunicado detention, coercive interrogations, and restricted access to food, water, and sanitation. Their families don’t know whether they’re alive, or if and when they will return home.
This year's World Humanitarian Day is not only a reminder of those still detained. It is a defining test of the United Nations: After two years of such limited progress, is the institution now ready to honestly re-evaluate its approach and demonstrate an unequivocal commitment to protecting and coming to the aid of those who risk their lives in its service?
Those detained are national staff, the local professionals who form the backbone of every humanitarian operation. They understand the language, the culture, and the communities they serve. Without them, humanitarian assistance would simply not function. Yet their central role in UN work is not reflected in the urgency of the response.
Those closest to the crisis are starting to ask an uncomfortable question: Would it have unfolded differently had those detained been international staff? If the answer is yes, or even possibly yes, then the problem extends beyond institutional weakness.
The arbitrary detention of humanitarian personnel is not simply an attack on individuals. It is an attack on the principle that humanitarian action must remain possible, even in war.
Those detained are neither combatants nor political actors, but professionals dedicated to serving communities affected by conflict, deprivation, and insecurity.
This is not a single incident. Across the world, state and de facto authorities are increasingly criminalising humanitarian work. When humanitarians are detained, entire communities lose access to lifesaving assistance. Protecting those who deliver aid is therefore inseparable from protecting the civilians who depend on it.
The international community has recognised the urgency of this challenge.
UN Security Council Resolution 2730 reaffirmed the obligation to protect humanitarian personnel and strengthen accountability for attacks against them. The European Commission's recent Communication on Humanitarian Action likewise places the protection of humanitarian workers and accountability at the heart of humanitarian policy. Australia's Declaration for the Protection of Humanitarian Personnel builds on these commitments by calling on states to translate international law into practical action and stronger protection.
Humanitarian workers and their families expect these commitments to be matched by visible leadership, accountability and decisive action. Yemen is where those commitments are now being tested.
A dangerous precedent
That a number of UN staff arbitrarily detained in Yemen now face death sentences sets a dangerous precedent that takes the erosion of humanitarian protection and the principle of functional immunity to the next level.
In November 2025, a Houthi court sentenced 17 humanitarian-affiliated staff – three of them from the UN and all of them national staff – to death by firing squad on espionage charges; the sentences remain under appeal.
If left unanswered, this risks normalising the prosecution and sentencing of humanitarians simply for doing their jobs. Coming after the unprecedented killing of UN personnel in Gaza, these sentences send a terrifying message: Humanitarian workers can be detained, prosecuted, and even sentenced to death with impunity.
If the international community allows this precedent to stand, every UN mission and humanitarian operation around the world becomes exponentially more dangerous. The UN's senior leadership must recognise that what is unfolding in Yemen is not a country-specific crisis. It is a challenge to the safety, independence and future protection of UN personnel and humanitarian workers everywhere.
Yet the institutional response to date has been more procedural than reflecting urgency. Typically, across the humanitarian system, responsibility becomes dispersed across departments and reporting lines. Procedures multiply, committees are formed, and decisions move slowly. No organisation consciously designs such a system, but too often process replaces leadership.
One decision, in particular, came to symbolise the perceived failure of visible commitment of UN leadership. The senior leadership for Yemen proceeded with previously planned summer leave shortly after the mass arrests. There may have been entirely legitimate reasons, and many undoubtedly continued working remotely. But institutions communicate through symbols as much as through decisions. For colleagues and families desperately seeking reassurance that the UN fully grasped the gravity of the crisis, the message it sent was devastating.
History repeatedly shows that institutions are judged not during routine periods but in moments of profound uncertainty. Rwanda, Sudan, Somalia, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, and now Yemen all remind us that moral leadership is ultimately measured by the willingness to act when the political costs are highest.
Every humanitarian organisation depends upon trust. Staff accept dangerous assignments because they believe their institution will stand behind them if the worst occurs. Once that belief begins to fracture, the damage spreads throughout the organisation. Cynicism deepens. Confidence erodes.
The detained UN personnel deserve far more than the repeated carefully worded statements of concern. They deserve visible leadership and relentless advocacy. They deserve to know that every diplomatic, political, and institutional avenue is being pursued until they are free.
The duty to stand by those who serve
Because the implications extend far beyond Yemen, the response must now be led at the highest political level of the United Nations. The Secretary-General should appoint a dedicated Under-Secretary-General as Special Envoy with a single mandate: to engage all relevant governments and parties to secure the immediate release of the detained humanitarian personnel.
Such an appointment would demonstrate that the organisation understands what is at stake; not simply the fate of those imprisoned today, but the protection of every UN staff member, and by extension every humanitarian worker, who may find themselves at risk tomorrow.
In conversations with affected family members and colleagues, there is a word that many are using privately, but that institutions have yet to reckon with publicly: betrayal. That word is earned in every week that passes without a meaningful update, in every unanswered question about what is being done, in every public statement that offers words of concern without evidence of action.
For a detainee, the fear that colleagues are going about their work, that institutional life continues, that no visible effort is being made to secure their release, is an unbearable daily reality lived inside a prison cell. It compounds the suffering of captivity with something arguably harder to bear: the sense of having been abandoned by the institutions they chose to serve.
For families, the experience is no less acute. They are left to navigate uncertainty alone, without information, without reassurance, and without any credible sense that the institution shares the urgency they feel every waking hour. Our work with former detainees and their families shows that the consequences of detention and prolonged uncertainty can continue to shape their lives long after release.
This is not a communications failure. It is a failure of duty of care. If humanitarian institutions cannot convincingly protect and stand behind those who serve in their name, the very real risk is the erosion not only of the confidence of their own staff but of confidence in humanitarian action itself. And unlike the detentions themselves, that failure is entirely within the power of the United Nations to remedy.
On this World Humanitarian Day, honouring humanitarian workers must mean more than remembering those killed or detained. It must mean standing behind those still serving – and proving that, when the worst happens, the institutions they serve will not abandon them.

He holds the diplomatic rank of Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary.
From 1997 to 1998, he served as attaché, third, and second secretary of the State and Legal Affairs Division of the Treaty and Legal Department at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine.
From 1998 to 2002, he was second and first secretary at the Embassy of Ukraine in Poland.
In 2002–2003, he served as first secretary of the Legal and Humanitarian Cooperation Division of the European Integration Department at the MFA; in 2003–2005, as acting head and head of the International Legal Cooperation Division of the Treaty and Legal Department; in 2005–2006, as head of the International Law and Foreign Policy Legislation Division of the Treaty and Legal Department; and in 2006, as deputy department director and head of the same division.

Nicchio Contrada breaks hoodoo to win Siena Palio
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
12:26:16 CEST
19:26:16 KST

The Nicchio (Sea-Shell) Contrada
broke a 28-year hoodoo to win Siena's Palio Tuesday night, the
iconic medieval bareback horse race around the Tuscan city's
central square.
                                    
                                       
				The Palio, meaning "banner", dating back to the 13th century, is
one of Italy's most colourful tourist attractions although many
newcomers to the event are shocked at how violent it can be and
how much deep-rooted intra-urban enmity it arouses, as well as
at the shameless haggling and negotiating that happens between
jockeys as the race gears to spring into life.
                                    
                                       
				Siena's trademark race, which formed the backdrop to the opening
chase sequence of the 2007 James Bond film Quantum of Solace,
takes place each year on July 2 and August 16, the day after the
'Ferragosto' Feast of the Assumption of Mary, although some
years have an extra one at the beginning of September.
                                    
                                       
				Jockeys from ten of Siena's 17 'contrade' or neighbourhoods
compete for the silk prize in the one and a half minute hurtle
around the Piazza del Campo.
                                    
                                       
				The only rule in the competition is that the jockeys, or
fantini, mustn't grab the reins of their adversaries. That means
whipping a rival's horse or even knocking a jockey off his steed
is allowed.
                                    
                                       
				Victory goes to the first horse to complete three laps of the
square, even if it arrives at the finishing post without a
rider,or 'scosso'.
                                    
                                       
				The chaotic and thrilling event attracts thousands of visitors
each year who are mostly oblivious to the punishment thehorses
take.
                                    
                                       
				But animal rights activists have long campaigned to get the
event banned, saying it is cruel, has little to do with sporting
skill and is dangerous for the horses, jockeys and spectators.
                                    
                                       
				More than 50 horses have died on the course since 1970.
                                    
                                       
				The Ferragosto Palio this August was postponed twice due to
heavy rain that had soaked the Campo's tuff track, making it too
treacherous for the horses to race.
                                    
                                       
				In the end veteran jockey Giovanni Atzeni aka Tittia prevailed
on the bay mare Anda e Bola, before falling off and suffering
concussion just after the finishing line.
                                    
                                       
				It was his 13th victory and the 43rd for Nicchio, which last won
on August 16, 1998.
                                    
                                       
				Atzeni's tally of 13 matches Trecciolino and move him within one
point of Aceto's 14, the most successful jockey of the modern
era.
                                    
                                       
				It was a second victory for Tittia's ride Anda e Bola, who
hadn't won since August 16, 2025, for Valdimontone, the rival
contrada of Nicchio, when it was ridden by Giuseppe Zedde, known
as Gingillo.
                                    
                                       
				Nicchio's victory was a resounding one, having started and
finished first without any other contrada threatening Tittia  in
the slightest during the three laps.

Why White House envoys cannot sway Israel’s war leader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:24:26 UTC
19:24:26 KST

Why White House envoys cannot sway Israel’s war leader
Any deal in any of Israel’s conflicts would be politically damaging for its prime minister.
On Monday, US Middle East envoy Jared Kushner visited Israel and met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The focus of the discussion was reportedly US President Donald Trump’s peace plan for Gaza, which the Israeli leader rejected last week after Hamas accepted it.
Despite claiming to have had a “good meeting”, Kushner did not seem to have achieved much progress. In an interview with Fox News, he seemed to downplay the Israeli rejection.
Unfortunately, such initiatives from the White House to try to jump start the stalled peace plan for Gaza amid growing criticism that the Board of Peace is failing are unlikely to work. Netanyahu will not step back from his insistence that Hamas has to disarm first before Israel fulfils any of its commitments. He holds the same position on Lebanon – a position that is seen as largely obstructive by those involved in the negotiations.
The ultimate goal of the Israeli prime minister is to delay future negotiations and especially the closing of any deal. This is because he does not gain anything politically from a concentrated effort to end Israel’s wars.
As long as Netanyahu is able to keep Israel fighting in any conflict – whether with Iran, the Palestinians, Hezbollah or Syria – he can pass himself off as “Mr Security”, the only one capable of dealing effectively with the multifront security threat. Maintaining this image before the elections in October is particularly important.
Opinion polls indicated that 45 percent of Israelis oppose a peace deal for Gaza, 37 percent want a return to fighting in the strip while 17 percent want the status quo to be maintained. Two-thirds of Israelis want Israeli occupation of parts of southern Lebanon to continue to retain a “security belt”. Nearly half of Israelis want major military action against Iran to continue. Many of these pro-war voters are part of Netanyahu’s potential supporters.
Does it matter to them that the prime minister has failed abysmally at nearly all of his plans and attempts to vanquish Israel’s enemies? Not so much. He is still seen as the only one with sufficient experience and toughness to face a broadly hostile world.
Many Israelis believe that the world at large has set its sights on the destruction of Israel. Anyone who does not automatically “stand with Israel” is Israel’s enemy. For his supporters, Netanyahu is the only Israeli politician to correctly identify this situation. They see him as the only one who would be able to separate the sheep from the goats and establish proper and effective defence alliances for Israel.
Netanyahu is also credited with a vast knowledge of American politics. Many Israelis believe he has taken everything Trump can give but has also allowed the Israeli public to see that even the US president is not to be trusted.
The fact that Israel is generally considered to have lost the United States as a significant partner is in many ways irrelevant to Netanyahu’s image. Now, as his rejection of the peace plan shows, he is the only one who can say “no” to the US.
Undermining any progress towards ending any of the conflicts is important for Netanyahu also because it allows him to shape his criminal trial. He can request recesses for “important political meetings”, for example. His legal team can claim it must break because of a scheduled office trip just as he can claim medical examinations and other such interruptions. War breeds anomalies and irregularities. Who but the prime minister would be responsible for seeing to the proper resolution of such interruptions?
While Netanyahu keeps pushing for perpetual war, he does not seem to be too worried about the Israeli economy. Indeed, conflict has proven beneficial for business, especially defence companies. The Israeli stock exchange is seeing record highs while the shekel has appreciated. Projected growth for 2027 is 5.6 percent.
But a report released in June by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) predicted that any return to intense military activity would exact “large fiscal costs” on the Israeli economy as businesses are forced to shut down and reservists are mobilised.
But OECD warnings can do little to dissuade a prime minister who has hedged his political survival on war. Nor can apparently special visits of White House envoys.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Amazon set to expand drone delivery of lightweight packages to 500 US cities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:23:02 UTC
19:23:02 KST

Amazon set to expand drone delivery of lightweight packages to 500 US cities
Millions more people may be able to get smaller, lightweight Amazon packages delivered by drones by the end of the year under a plan the company announced Thursday to expand the airborne shipping to suburban areas in nearly 500 U.S. cities.
Customers could receive the drone deliveries in as fast as 30 minutes, Amazon said in a news release. The drones can carry packages up to 5 pounds.
The plan will intensify the battle between Amazon and Walmart to provide consumers with the fastest delivery times. Both giants rely on a mix of drones and drivers to deliver everything consumers have ordered.
Amazon’s plan would expand its drone delivery operation more than sixfold nationwide into hundreds of new communities, including the Chicago, Atlanta, Cleveland and Boise metro areas. The drones will primarily fly in the suburbs well away from skyscrapers and major airports that could cause problems.
Drone delivery is growing fast but remains a small factor
Hundreds of thousands of packages have already been delivered by Amazon drones this year, but even after this expansion drones will still only handle a fraction of the hundreds of millions of package deliveries each year. In addition to only being able to carry 5 pounds, the drones Amazon builds face countless challenges from tree cover to landscaping and inflatable pools that can make it hard to find a good drop zone.
There are also regulatory hurdles to overcome in every community where Amazon wants to set up operations. Noise concerns also pose a potential challenge.
“It’s still an experiment. It’s still in test and learn mode,” said Sucharita Kodali, who is a retail analyst with Forrester.
The novelty of drone delivery may attract orders at first
Initially, consumers might order something delivered by drone because they are curious about it, but it’s not clear how often they will continue to use the service, and Amazon is still working out the economics, Kodali said.
The service will be free for Amazon Prime members who are ordering more than $50 worth of goods, but smaller orders will cost members $2.99. Non-members will pay $4.99 for drone delivery.
Prime members get free deliveries while non-members pay a flat fee if the shipment is under $35 for standard delivery or up to $12.99 for same‑day shipments when available.
Kodali said drones could prove more useful for certain light-weight deliveries that are needed urgently like prescription medications.
DoorDash and other delivery companies also are experimenting with using drones to deliver foods and other goods.
Amazon CEO believes drone delivery will be part of the mix
Amazon’s CEO Andy Jassy told shareholders in his annual letter in April that the company has learned a great deal by flying drones in 11 sites across Arizona, Florida, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Nebraska, and Texas. In each location, the drones launch from an Amazon warehouse and cover about 175 square miles, so it takes multiple drone launching locations to serve a large metro area.
“Prime Air now has a design that’ll scale, plans to serve communities with 30 million customers by year-end, and expects to deliver half a billion packages by the end of this decade (with an aim to deliver inside 30 minutes),” Jassy wrote.
Amazon is also continuing to invest in its warehouses, smaller fulfillment centers closer to customers and its fleet of trucks as the company competes to deliver packages within minutes or hours instead of just days.
Amazon is already certified by the Federal Aviation Administration and the company has been awarded waivers to fly drones beyond the line of sight of the pilots. Amazon has invested in safety measures to help drones avoid collisions with anything else in the sky while they are making deliveries.
The federal government has proposed a rule that would allow more drone operators to fly beyond the horizon, but that hasn’t been finalized yet.

'There's a problem at the border': Rijiju admits delineation issue in Arunachal, rejects China incursion claim
Edited by: Vivek Dubey / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 19, 2026, 15:52 IST
Comments

Text Size

Rijiju explained that the lack of demarcation has led to Chinese claims over certain stretches of land
NEW DELHI: Union minister Kiren Rijiju on Wednesday rejected reports that China has made a 60-km incursion into Arunachal Pradesh, saying there is a problem at the border but only because the boundary has not been delineated. He said concerns raised by villagers living in the frontier state are valid, but warned against spreading misinformation about Chinese troops entering Indian territory."Those who say that China has entered 60 kilometres inside (India) and share various videos to defame us are wrong. There is a problem at the border. Some people from villages in Arunachal Pradesh have expressed concern about the border problem, and that concern is valid because the border has not been delineated," he told news agency IANS.Rijiju said the situation should not be interpreted as China having captured an Indian village. He explained that the lack of demarcation has led to Chinese claims over certain stretches of land."So, it is not like they (China) came and captured our village. That is not the case. On certain land, they have cast an eye because there is no demarcation. Our people believe that our land extends further ahead, while the villages situated on the China side, including Tibetan and local people, claim that their land extends deep inside here.
So, there is confusion," the Union minister said."But telling such lies that they have entered 60 kilometres inside, and posting unrelated photos from Bangladesh and elsewhere to claim that the Chinese Army has penetrated 60 kilometres inside Arunachal, spreading such misinformation lowers the morale of our Army personnel and security forces stationed there, and creates confusion in the country. This is not right," he added.He said India has strengthened security arrangements along the frontier, with the Army and the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) increasing patrolling in the area.His comments come amid renewed focus on the India-China border following the government's decision to formally identify 27 locations and geographical features in Arunachal Pradesh by their standard names on official Survey of India maps.
The move followed China's repeated attempts to assign its own names to places in Arunachal Pradesh.India has repeatedly stressed that Arunachal Pradesh is an inalienable part of India.The ministry of external affairs has also stressed that maintaining peace and tranquillity along the Line of Actual Control is essential for the broader India-China relationship. India has said the state of affairs along the border will have a bearing on the wider bilateral ties.“Let me reiterate this once again that Arunachal Pradesh is an inalienable and integral part of India and this is a fact that is self-evident. At the same time, let me also underline that nothing can change this indisputable reality,” the MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said in a media briefing on August 11.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Army’s Armor Training Command conducted a live-fire exercise on Tuesday as part of its tank leader specialist course.
Trainees first prepared ammunition and completed crew assignments on CM11 Brave Tiger and M60A3 Patton tanks, Liberty Times reported. Tank commanders conducted communications checks to ensure commands could be given without issue.

The tanks’ turret stabilization systems were deliberately turned off to simulate system failure. Trainees were required to fire while stationary and on the move, according to Liberty Times. They had to compensate for the tank’s movement and vibrations while continuously tracking targets at different positions.
They also rotated through roles as commander, gunner, and loader to familiarize themselves with all crew positions. The exercise was designed to ensure that even without electronic assistance, troops could still engage targets effectively and adapt to changing combat scenarios.
The tank leader specialist course lasts six months. Its curriculum includes equipment operation, staff planning, and leadership training, according to Liberty Times.

Skeletal remains believed to be ritual offering unearthed in Peru
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:19:31 UTC
19:19:31 KST

Skeletal remains believed to be person sacrificed during ritual unearthed by archaeologists in Peru
Archaeologists on Tuesday unveiled the skeletal remains of an adult they believe was buried as an offering near the base of Huaca Pucllana, an ancient adobe pyramid in Peru's capital of Lima.
The remains are believed to be those of a man who may have been sacrificed during a ritual in which a canal linked to a ceremonial pool was closed.
The discovery has been preliminarily dated to around A.D. 650, so it would be approximately 1,400 years old, Peru's culture ministry said in a statement, while releasing multiple images of the excavation site.
Gladys Paz, the archaeologist who led the excavation, said the bones will help researchers better understand "the rituals of the Lima culture" and reconstruct ceremonies performed hundreds of years ago.
Paz said that the body was buried inside a canal, resting on its left flank, with the skull facing the pyramid and the Pacific Ocean.
"One of the most significant aspects of the discovery is the architecture of the ceremonial well," the culture ministry said. "Unlike other known structures at Huaca Pucllana, characterized by the use of small mud bricks, this well was built with river stones."
The Lima culture flourished between the first and seventh centuries along Peru's arid central coast, about 700 years before the rise of the Inca Empire.
Huaca Pucllana was one of the most important ceremonial and administrative centers of the Lima culture, which disappeared centuries before a group of Spanish conquistadors founded Lima in 1535.
Today, the pyramid is surrounded by parks, leafy streets and upscale apartment buildings in the districts of Miraflores and San Isidro.
Huaca Pucllana is open to tourists, with a restaurant serving Peruvian specialties like ceviche, stir-fried beef and roasted alpaca meat.
According to Peru's government, there are more than 400 archaeological sites across metropolitan Lima. Pieter Van Dalen, an archaeology professor at the National University of San Marcos who was not involved in the excavation, said that it's common to find tombs, mummified remains and other burial-related items along Peru's coast. Such discoveries have also been made while construction workers dig canals to install gas pipes.
In July 2025, utility workers excavating trenches to expand an underground gas network in Peru's capital unearthed two pre-Incan tombs that were over 1,000 years old. A month before that, utility workers found a 1,000-year-old mummy of a child while installing pipes.
In April 2025, archaeologists announced they found the 5,000-year-old remains of a noblewoman at the sacred Peruvian city of Caral, in an area that for decades was used as a garbage dump.

Taiwan needs stronger spy laws and better military pay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:19:30 UTC
19:19:30 KST

President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) has announced plans for a record defense budget while also proposing an “AI dividend” — a universal cash payment of NT$10,000 (US$315) to eligible residents.
The proposed 2027 defense budget, including regular and special allocations, would exceed NT$1 trillion for the first time. Yet new investments in the armed forces will not by themselves resolve one of the country’s most serious national-security vulnerabilities.
The combination of lenient espionage penalties and inadequate compensation for military personnel is a significant issue. Taiwan needs both the hardware to deter or repel a People’s Liberation Army attack and the legal and personnel reforms necessary to protect that hardware from Chinese infiltration.
Taiwan is repeatedly shaken by Chinese espionage cases, many involving the sale of military secrets for surprisingly small sums. Earlier this month, prosecutors indicted a 34-year-old sergeant from the Yilan Reserve Command for allegedly leaking classified military documents to a Chinese spy group over several years. Prosecutors said he received as much as NT$800,000 since 2022 in exchange for information related to the Hengshan military command-and-control system, the Patriot missile tactical handbook and Air Force operational intelligence.
The sergeant also allegedly recorded pledges of surrender and allegiance to China. In May 2024, prosecutors said, he accessed the military’s internal system and downloaded or photographed 60 classified electronic records related to military operations.
In April, six active and retired military personnel received prison sentences for leaking military secrets to China and helping form a spy organization. The lightest sentence was six months. The sentences could also be appealed, an outcome that underscores how inadequate penalties for military espionage can appear compared with those in other established democracies.
Spy sentence
The average sentence for military espionage is reportedly about 18 months. By contrast, comparable offenses in the US and the UK can result in sentences averaging roughly 20 years.
Su Tzu-yun (蘇紫雲), director of the research division at the Institute for National Defense and Security Research, has said courts imprison convicted traitors for periods 12.7 times shorter than those imposed in other democracies. The harshest sentence to date, he noted, was 7.5 years for a former Army colonel. A former major convicted of attempting to form a spy network for China received a suspended sentence of nine months.
In the same month, prosecutors indicted nine active-duty and discharged junior military officers for allegedly disclosing military secrets to China. One officer reportedly agreed to provide sensitive information for only NT$3,000 per month, plus a paid trip to China. The officers allegedly used smartphones to record base activities and transmit classified documents.
These cases reveal not only the reach of Chinese intelligence operations but also the ease with which vulnerable personnel can be recruited. If vital military information can be purchased for the price of a modest monthly allowance, Taiwan’s security system has a serious structural problem.
Chinese infiltration has also reached other critical parts of government. In June, a court sentenced a Chinese collaborator for leaking details of presidential and Air Force travel. That same month, opposition KMT legislators criticized reduced prison terms for aides to mainly ruling DPP legislators who had leaked confidential diplomatic information.
The information reportedly included details relevant to Chinese efforts to monitor then Vice President-elect Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) during her 2024 European travels, an operation that nearly led to a staged car collision involving Chinese embassy officials in the Czech Republic.
Time for change
As the saying goes, even a broken clock is right twice a day. The KMT has long advocated higher pay for military personnel, arguing that underpaid troops cannot adequately defend Taiwan. Given the DPP’s central message — “Resist China, Protect Taiwan” — the ruling party should be willing to support such a policy.
If the administration can distribute an AI dividend to residents, increasing compensation for the people responsible for operating the nation’s advanced weapons should also be within reach. The government could raise basic salaries, introduce special allowances, including an allowance comparable to the proposed cash dividend, and expand benefits for service members and their families.
Better compensation would serve several purposes. It could improve retention, help address the nation’s military personnel shortage and reinforce the social status of military service. It would also make military careers more competitive with other professions, reducing the financial vulnerability that Chinese intelligence services exploit.
Japan, arguably Taiwan’s most important regional partner, has also begun discussing better support for its armed forces. Facing the same strategic challenge from China, Japan’s Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro is considering the creation of a dedicated government agency as early as the next fiscal year. The agency would focus on post-retirement benefits, medical services and other forms of support for Self-Defense Force personnel and their families.
Hostile foreign power
Taiwan must pair better military pay and benefits with stronger deterrence against espionage. Major political parties should cooperate on a comprehensive overhaul of laws governing espionage across government agencies.
Penalties should reflect the grave harm caused by transferring military and diplomatic secrets to a hostile foreign power, while appeals procedures should not allow convicted spies to benefit disproportionately from delays or suspended sentences.
The KMT must also match its rhetoric with action. If the party is serious about improving military compensation and strengthening national security, it should work with the DPP rather than allow political disputes to delay essential defense measures. The KMT and its opposition partner, the TPP, delayed passage of the national budget for 266 days, the longest such delay in Taiwan’s legislative history.
Taiwan urgently needs tougher espionage penalties and comprehensive salary reforms to match its rising investment in military hardware. Without them, it will remain difficult to counter China’s increasingly asymmetric methods.
These reforms are neither extravagant nor unattainable. They would bring Taiwan closer to the standards and practices of other democracies while reducing the incentives for Chinese intelligence services to recruit Taiwanese personnel.
Only by making espionage costly and military service adequately valued can Taiwan better defend itself against the gray-zone pressure that China can impose at minimal cost.
Rath Wang is a political commentator based in Taipei who focuses on Taiwan’s politics, media, civil society and issues influencing the country’s future. He is a media producer and host of current-affairs talk shows and podcasts. He has worked on political campaigns and lived in Taiwan, Japan, Thailand and the US.

studio lievito carves MARMIFERE as urban furniture
Drawing inspiration from the historic Ferrovia Marmifera di Carrara — the 19th-century railway built to transport marble from the Apuan Alps down to the port of Carrara — Marmifere is a modular urban furniture collection designed by Studio Lievito. Conceived as a deliberate homage to Ugo La Pietra’s radical experimentation and Archizoom’s avant-garde vision, these sculptural stone elements act as symbolic bridges between the quarry and the city. Designed to inhabit public squares, parks, and pedestrian zones, they transform ancient geological memory into interactive urban landscapes that encourage rest, play, and contemplation.
Marmifere are an invitation to rest, relax and contemplate, but also to talk, play and explore
all images courtesy of Studio Lievito
modular modules form miniature railway tunnels
The first module of the Florence-based studio‘s Marmifere reinterprets the Ravaneti, the massive mounds of marble waste left behind by quarrying activities. One side of the module features a concave, hollowed profile that mimics the steep erosion of the mountain, revealing a reclined seat with an organic shape that invites passers-by to relax. On the opposite side, the surface remains intact, functioning as an inclined climbing wall fitted with recycled plastic holds for children to explore. Running through the interior is a hollow cavity referencing the railway’s entrance tunnels. When modules are aligned, these cavities connect to form miniature tunnels for children to crawl through.
Marmifere are a series of monolithic microarchitectural pieces for contemporary urban settings
recycled marble prompts discovery, play, and community
The second module takes its cues from quarry terraces, replicating the geometric succession of ledges and steps carved into the rock face. This translates into staggered levels offering diverse seating perspectives within the urban landscape. Like the first block, its rear wall serves as a spontaneous climbing structure, while the integrated tunnel cavity continues the theme of discovery and play. By blending raw industrial history with tactile interactivity, Studio Lievito crafts an intimate account of Carrara’s mountain landscape, inviting citizens to reconnect with the authentic heritage of Italian marble.

Easements on private land for military structures — Parliament adopted the bill in the first reading
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
13:18:53 EEST
19:18:53 KST

Easements on private land for military structures — Parliament adopted the bill in the first reading
Kyiv • UNN
Parliament supported a bill on easements on private agricultural land for fortifications. The fee will amount to 12% of the assessed value and will be paid after the war.
The Verkhovna Rada adopted as a basis a draft law on the use of the right to a land servitude for military needs. A total of 274 members of parliament voted for the document, UNN reports, citing the parliament’s press service.
Details
The draft law proposes granting regional military administrations the authority to establish land servitudes on privately owned agricultural land for the placement of engineering and fortification structures.
The fee for establishing a land servitude is proposed to be set at a fixed rate of 12% of the normative monetary valuation. This amount corresponds to the minimum market value of the annual lease of agricultural land plots. The fee for the land servitude will be paid to the landowner within two years after the end of martial law
According to members of parliament, this legislative initiative is prompted by the fact that, during martial law, a significant area of agricultural land is occupied by military engineering and fortification structures, making it impossible to carry out agricultural work there. At the same time, landowners and land users continue to be obliged to use land plots for their intended purpose and pay land taxes.
Additionally
A land servitude is the right of an owner or land user to limited paid or unpaid use of another person’s land plot. It is needed when it is otherwise impossible to satisfy one’s own needs (for example, to get to one’s house or lay pipes).
Reminder
In Ukraine, the right to receive land free of charge remains, but during martial law, a ban on most new transfers is in effect. The exceptions concern owners of buildings on land plots and real estate destroyed as a result of Russian aggression.

Harvard reaches $53M settlement over body parts sold by morgue manager
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:16:03 UTC
19:16:03 KST

Harvard University has agreed to pay $53 million to settle claims stemming from the theft and sale of body parts donated for scientific research, with a Boston court giving preliminary approval to the plan on Tuesday, US media reported.
Cedric Lodge, who managed the morgue at Harvard Medical School before being fired in 2023, was sentenced to eight years in prison in December after pleading guilty to trafficking stolen human remains.
Investigators said Lodge and his wife took body parts from the school "without the knowledge or permission of his employer, the donor, or the donor's family" and shipped them to buyers in other states beginning in 2018.
Harvard said on Monday it would seek court approval to establish "two class action settlement funds totaling $53 million."
"We are grateful to be working together with the plaintiffs to move forward in a way that prioritizes support for families and the (organ donation program) and avoids prolonged litigation," Harvard Medical School Dean George Daley and Dean for Medical Education Bernard Chang said in a letter.
They described Lodge's actions as "despicable, abhorrent, and a flagrant betrayal of our values as a medical community."
"We reaffirm our deep sorrow and empathy for the families of donors who may have been impacted," they said.
Settlement includes reforms
A Boston state court judge granted preliminary approval to the settlement plan on Tuesday, according to US media. Harvard said distributing the funds is expected to take several months.
Lodge's wife, Denise, was previously sentenced to one year in prison. Six other people who bought remains from Lodge also pleaded guilty and received sentences.
Harvard Medical School will establish an annual financial aid scholarship beginning in the 2027-28 academic year "in appreciation and in honor of all of our anatomical donors."
The settlement also includes a pledge by the school to issue a statement to claimant families condemning Lodge's actions and outlining improvements made to its organ donation programme.

At United Nations headquarters in New York, Stephane Dujarric, spokesperson for U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, addressed the incident during a daily press briefing.
