====================================================================================================

Many Russians who left because of the war had to start over abroad. Some found careers they never expected.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:14:16 UTC
19:14:16 KST

Many Russians who left because of the war had to start over abroad. Some found careers they never expected.
People who left Russia after the start of the full-scale war have had to start their lives over from scratch. They’ve had to learn a new language, absorb the local culture, traditions, and bureaucracy, adjust to the climate, and make new friends and acquaintances. Many lost their jobs during the move or after arriving in a new country and were forced — despite having a college degree and a strong portfolio — to take low-paying jobs. But some have learned new professions in emigration and are happy with them. Meduza tells the difficult, but in some ways even inspiring, stories of these Russians.
Ksenia Borovinskaya, 37
From a copywriter in Moscow to a bar founder in Buenos Aires
Before I emigrated, I was never idle — I was always finding good freelance work through people I knew. I wrote copy for Afisha Daily and Mel, and for shampoo and wet-wipe packaging. In 2018, an acquaintance helped me land a job at RusTransplant, a project for organ transplant patients, where I wrote guides on eating right, exercising, and having sex safely after a transplant.
The Moscow Health Ministry funded the project. In the war’s first few days, our director told us the ministry had set a condition for continued funding: staff members and the project itself had to publicly support the war on social media. Everyone refused.
I left Russia in March 2022 with my two young children and our dog. It was hard on the kids, but they understood why we left. In the war’s first days, my older son drew a tank with a line through it at school; his teacher handed me the drawing and asked that he not do it again. We wouldn’t have been allowed to live in peace in Russia.
We flew to Armenia first. Armenian turned out to be so difficult that in two months I learned only a few letters. I hadn’t expected Armenia to be so cold, and I was a wreck, unable to pull myself together.
At some point, a friend called from Argentina and said, “Come here: there’s no war, and people drink wine.” I thought Argentina might help me reset and recover, so I decided to move. Just before that, I learned I’d been fired from RusTransplant for working remotely. I used my last paycheck to buy tickets to Buenos Aires.
In Argentina, I applied for political asylum, citing my antiwar stance and the risk of persecution in Russia — police, for one, had already come looking for me at my registered address. I was issued a temporary residency certificate that let me live and work in the country legally.
I got my first job in Argentina out of pity, a month after I arrived. I walked into a bar and said, in broken Spanish, “Me want work. Please, sir.” The owner told me to come back that evening, and that’s how I became a waiters’ assistant. Over the following year and a half, I took on small repair jobs, worked at a carpentry shop, and translated for a crypto exchange.
My planning horizon stretched no further than a single day. I was desperately short on money and decided things couldn’t go on that way. Maybe everyone secretly dreams of opening their own bar. I spent a long time talking the idea over with my kids. I have two sons — the younger is 8, the older 12 — and they’re up for anything: “Should we move to Argentina? Let’s do it!” “Should we open a bar? Let’s do it!”
My kids’ confidence rubbed off on me, and at the end of 2024 I borrowed $15,000 from my ex-husband to open the bar. With interest, I owed him $18,000, of which I still have $4,000 left to pay back. The money went toward paperwork, equipment, and furniture — though I dragged a lot of it in from the trash. I hauled a board off the street once and hammered together a stool out of it.
When I found a space for the bar and was on my way to sign the lease, someone stole my bag, with my passport inside, right on the street. All I had left in my pocket was a certificate showing I’d applied for residency. When the agent saw it, he tried to talk the landlord out of renting to me, pointing at the door and saying, “That door has more rights than this girl does.” But I told them my story honestly, and I talked them into it.
Opening the bar and signing contracts required a residency number I didn’t yet have, which meant a lot of bureaucratic hassle. I ran from one office to another, and somehow a solution always turned up. I managed to get everything registered with nothing more than a certificate of temporary residency.
I wasn’t issued my DNI, Argentina’s residency document, until two years after I moved. My case took a long time to review, and I had to renew my pending-asylum certificate several times.
I got really lucky with the space. The bar is upstairs, and I live in the basement with my kids. Things happen, of course — two months ago, the building’s sewer pipe clogged, sewage came pouring out of the sink, and everything flooded. It would have made a fittingly symbolic end to my story: climbing and climbing only to drown anyway. But by evening I’d found a way to fix everything and open the bar.
My kids came up with the bar’s name, Babushka. It’s less a bar than a cultural space where you can grab a drink and a bite. We have one of the largest Russian-language poetry libraries on the continent. As soon as the bar started turning a profit, I shipped four cubic meters of books over from Russia. There are books in other languages too; all sorts of things end up with me. Once, a regular customer’s mother died at the age of 100, and I inherited her library.
The bar also has homeless friends. In the evening, if there’s food left over, I feed them, and in return they bring me books they find in the trash. Some books are gifts from the authors themselves, since Argentine writers regularly perform at the bar. We hold book launches, poetry nights, film screenings, and concerts, all in Spanish.
The bar started making money almost right away. I hadn’t even finished getting all the permits, and I was already earning money hosting parties and cooking food. Even then, it was enough to get by.
For my wedding to my ex-husband, my grandmother gave me a recipe book she’d kept her whole life. I cook from it, though I sometimes improvise. I also love Asian food, so Babushka serves everything from Thai-style fried cucumbers to borscht. We make classic cocktails too, from gin and tonic to Argentina’s signature Fernet con Coca.
Only my kids and I work at the bar. I’d never actually worked at a bar before — my only prior experience was a year as a waitress in college. My older son handles the accounting spreadsheets; he’s better with finances than anyone else in the family. Friends help out too — they hang out at the bar, and when they see I’m swamped, they’ll make a sandwich or pour coffee for customers.
Two months ago, my landlord told me the rent was about to triple because my old lease was expiring. Somehow I talked him down, and the rent only doubled.
I also raise prices at the bar almost every week. That’s not my choice — everything in Argentina keeps getting more expensive, and when my supply costs go up, I have to charge customers more. Even so, by Argentine standards the bar is inexpensive — locals constantly comment that we have “nice prices.”
Over the past few years I’ve realized that stability is an illusion. This has been a time of fucking adventures. The 2000s were an anomaly — 15 fat years when everyone had great jobs and carefree travel. It’s really painful to remember that life. Back then it felt like stability had always existed, but it wasn’t so long ago that we were trying on knockoff Nikes on a piece of cardboard at the market. Now I try to appreciate the small things, like having a roof over my head and food on the table.
Mikhail Tkachevsky, 33
From a bar manager in Moscow to a photographer in New York
In college, I studied to be a paramedic and worked part-time at Il Patio. By the end of my studies, I’d realized I wanted to be a bartender instead — there was more money and more room to grow than in paramedic work. I sought out contacts in the bartending community, went to lectures, and competed in bartending competitions. In the end, I spent 12 years in the bar industry.
I worked as a bartender in Moscow at Strelka, Mendeleev Bar, and Simach, and as head manager at the bistro bar Mentalitet, where I ran the team and came up with cocktails. The war started while I was working at the bar Ess-Thetik on Patriarch’s Ponds. I immediately bought a ticket to Yerevan on the next available flight, but it was canceled, and I stayed in Russia until October — I needed to deal with a worsening anxiety disorder, save up some money, and hand off my work. Maybe it’s some Soviet instinct: the world’s on fire, but you try not to let your boss down.
After the collapse of the USSR, my parents moved to the U.S., where I was born. I don’t remember my childhood there — we came back when I was 4 — but I had an American birth certificate. I never thought much of it, since I loved Moscow and wanted to live only there; I dreamed of an apartment on Trubnaya Street. But when the mobilization started, I remembered the birth certificate. I dug around online, found out I could get an emergency passport, went to the U.S. embassy in Moscow, filed an application, and within two hours had obtained [a passport].
In November 2022, I decided to move to the U.S. I flew to New York with $5,000 I’d saved while working as a bar manager. For the first 10 days, I stayed at an expensive hostel and paid $60 a night. Then I moved to a cheaper one, sharing a three-room apartment with one shower and one toilet with 11 other people. I spent four months there, paying just $400 a month.
The whole time, I was actively job hunting. I was sure that with my experience I’d quickly land a job at a good bar, but it turned out to be very difficult. Everywhere in New York I was told that experience alone wasn’t enough — I needed experience specifically at New York bars, because everything here was “special.” Though what I remember most about that “special” treatment is going to Employees Only, one of the best bars in the U.S., and waiting 25 minutes while the bartender chatted with a friend. He finally came over and told me the only non-alcoholic drink they had was tonic water. In New York bars, it’s better to be the bartender than the customer.
My money was running out fast, so I widened my job search to other cities. I got lucky and found a job as a bar manager in Washington, convincing them I had extensive experience even though my English wasn’t perfect. The owner spoke Russian, so we were able to work things out. I moved to Washington and settled into another hostel. The work was hard because the staff had such a casual attitude toward the job — one bartender would drink heavily on shift, then not show up the next day because of a hangover, and I’d have to cover for him.
Employees showed up late, took their duties lightly, and left the workspace dirty. It was hard for me, given the OCD I’d developed behind the bar in Moscow. On top of that, the city itself struck me as boring.
After three months in Washington, I quit and went back to New York. For a couple of months I lived off the money I’d made in Washington and rented a room with my savings. I looked hard for work, but no one was hiring. Then I got lucky and landed a job at a good bar — but it was terribly dirty, which weighed on me. I felt depressed, looking for an alternative while also getting sucked into Instagram reels. My feed kept showing me beautiful reels from cinematographers and professional photographers.
I loved that kind of content, and soon I started taking photos myself on my phone. I realized I was living in the most cinematic city in the world. You walk out of your building, and there are Latin American preachers praising Christ through a crackling speaker; across the street, students are recruiting for the Communist Party; and on weekends, Ecuadorians hold volleyball tournaments. All around are supermarket carts converted into grills, with chicken wings sizzling on them.
Through Facebook, I found an American bartender who had mutual acquaintances with me from Moscow. He was just launching a bar in New York, and on the recommendation of people I knew from Moscow bars, I got hired onto the team. But the project didn’t take off — there were almost no customers. A month later, half the team was let go. I was fired too, from one day to the next with no explanation — I think because of my weak English.
I was furious and decided I no longer wanted to depend on anyone and would make my living through photography instead. I bought a camera on credit for $2,500, even though borrowing money from a bank without a credit history or steady income is pretty difficult. All I could get approved for was an Amazon credit card with terrible terms.
I lived and breathed photography: watching lectures, interviews, podcasts, trying to understand not just the technique but how good photographers think. I needed money, so I didn’t waste time — I quickly put together a portfolio from what I’d shot while learning, started posting about myself in all kinds of chats, and signed up for client-finding services. Sometimes I’d approach people on the street and say, “Want me to take your portrait?” That’s how I earned my first $40 from photography: a random passerby liked his portrait and paid me for it.
A few months after I put together my portfolio, orders started coming in through Thumbtack, a service that helps find clients for a small commission. One of my first jobs was on Long Island, shooting a business portrait, and I was paid $330 for it. Getting there and back, though, took nearly five hours. That’s when I first understood that photography isn’t just the shoot itself: it’s also endless travel, negotiations, client hunting, and knowing how to run a business.
Gradually, I developed my own style. At first I was scared to approach people and photograph them, but I quickly realized people don’t get angry when you photograph them — they smile instead. It was as if photographing them was a compliment to their looks. I started photographing people on the street at New York’s Italian culture festival.
I submitted my festival photos to a street photography contest and unexpectedly took first place, winning $1,000. What’s more, the head of the jury was none other than Bruce Gilden himself. But what made me happiest was finally being able to pay for my room. I later posted an ironic reel from the festival about photographing people without asking their permission, and it unexpectedly racked up 27 million views.
After the video blew up, I got a strange message on Instagram. The person said he really liked my style and asked me to shoot his wedding. I figured he was a scammer, since his account was empty and he’d agreed to my price without haggling. He then wrote that if things worked out, we’d fly to Las Vegas, where he’d need a photographer too.
I suggested we meet in person, and he agreed and turned out to be a real person. A few days later I shot his wedding, and then we really did fly to Las Vegas, and later to Stockholm too, for events tied to his startup, where I worked as the photographer.
Photos from his wedding were even published in Vogue, since his wife is an influencer. Since then I’ve occasionally shot events, which is how my photos also made it into Dazed. But most of my income comes from personal photo sessions. Half my clients are Russian-speaking, half English-speaking.
I haven’t gotten rich off photography. In the two years I’ve been doing this, I’ve borrowed a lot from friends and worked side jobs at catering gigs and events as a bartender. I was investing in the future more than earning money.
Only now am I starting to earn enough to cover all my expenses, and even then it’s not always enough to pay down my debts. The income is unpredictable — sometimes you land a traveling project, like the one in Stockholm, where I made $2,500 in four days; other times you won’t make that much in an entire month. Right now, to keep growing as a photographer while staying financially secure, I combine shoots with working at a cafe two days a week.
At one point I really needed money, so I worked at a bar for three months. After a shift, I had no energy left to go anywhere with my camera, so I decided it was better to earn less for now than give up photography, which brings me more joy, and I quit again.
I loved Moscow, but now I feel at home in New York. Sometimes I grab a couple of wings from an Ecuadorian food stand near my place. They call me “amigo,” and even though they barely speak English and I don’t speak Spanish, we manage to chat a little. Every time, those conversations leave me with really warm feelings — like the city has finally accepted me.
Viktoria, 42
From a farmer outside Moscow to a baker in Serbia
In the 2000s, I worked as a secretary handling document flow at a company that sold appliances. Then I moved to HR, and later I processed and issued loans at a bank. The pay was low, and the work was boring and far too monotonous.
In the early 2010s, my husband and I wanted to change something. We’d had a child with health problems, and we started thinking about moving to the countryside since our son needed clean air. We’d long wanted to start our own business so we wouldn’t depend on a boss, could plan our own days, and could earn more. So we decided to raise broiler chickens.
In 2012, we found a small house in a village in the Moscow region and left Moscow. We’d never farmed before. We figured: if it worked out, great, and if it didn’t, at least we’d have enough meat to feed ourselves.
My husband had always been building things — he worked in metalworking, assembling and fixing machines at factories — and he was excited to set up chicken production. He built a henhouse, put together a watering system, and made a brooder for the chicks. Pretty quickly we went from 50 chicks to several hundred.
Then Russia annexed Crimea. I wanted to emigrate, but my husband wasn’t ready. Life got harder — prices for feed and hatching eggs shot up several times over, and income dropped too, because people started buying less farm-raised meat.
In 2018, I finally convinced my husband that we needed to leave. We sold our equipment and moved back to Moscow to save up money for emigration. My husband got a job as an engineer at a metalworking plant, but two months later he died in a workplace accident. I spent the whole next year recovering, supporting our three children and my mother-in-law. Then COVID hit, and I was sick the whole year — emigration was the last thing on my mind.
Then the war started. My middle daughter, who was in third grade, came home from school one day and said, “It’s such a shame I can’t go to Ukraine to help our guys.” I realized my kids were being brainwashed and needed to be saved. The last straw was the growing pressure on LGBTQ+ people. My oldest child, who’s 15, is queer. Fortunately, he hasn’t run into problems because of his orientation, but I knew he wouldn’t hide his identity.
My family had already been touched by repression once before. A firing squad executed my great-grandfather in 1936. My grandfather was sent to a labor camp at 21, and my grandmother too, for “spikelets”. So I had no illusions about what could happen when the state cracks down. I couldn’t afford to delay emigrating, and nothing was keeping me in Russia anyway: my mother and husband were both dead.
Emigrating to Serbia was the simplest option. Serbia is great because, until you find a way to legalize your status, you can just do visa runs. To pay for the move, I sold my car and left in February 2023.
At first, I planned to live on the children’s survivor’s benefits. I didn’t have any specific plans for earning money — I was confident I could find some basic job.
I searched for work for several months through Telegram chats where people posted job listings, and that’s where I came across a baker position. I applied, even though I’d never worked as a baker. The bakery took a chance on me because of my farming experience and my volunteer work at a church outside Moscow, where I used to cook in the dining hall on Sundays. In June 2023, the bakery brought me on for training.
My coworkers trained me right there on the job. For three months, my training was in Serbian, even though at the time I only knew a couple of phrases. Sometimes I could guess the meaning from context. Sometimes the words resembled Russian ones. When I really didn’t understand, I used a translator.
I really loved working at the bakery, even though the pay isn’t the highest. At first I made just $500 — combined with the children’s benefits from Russia, it was enough for a modest life. But now my salary has gone up by a couple hundred dollars.
Five coworkers and I make bread and various sweet and savory pastries. The workday can run up to 10 hours, depending on how much needs to be baked. My coworkers have welcomed me, and we get along well. Overall, I like Serbia — the people are friendly, and it feels calm and safe. Plus, there’s no insane propaganda in the schools that could affect the kids.
At first, our emigration was complicated because my oldest child started having serious health problems, brought on by the change in climate and the hormonal changes of adolescence. For two years we searched for specialists and tried different treatments for him. It turned out he has high-functioning autism, and, as a result of a case of swine flu he had in 2009, narcolepsy. Compared to that, all the other “minor” problems — the lack of money, the uncertainty, being in an unfamiliar country — aren’t problems at all.
Almost all my time goes to taking care of my kids. My older son’s treatment, for example, requires frequent doctor visits and monitoring his condition. Because of that, I barely follow what’s happening in Russia. And I don’t miss it, since I don’t have any close relatives left there.
I never give up hope, though sometimes I get tired and angry. There’s no one to share the responsibility with, but I know that problems can be broken down into tasks and solved. The cost of despair is too high for me — my children’s health and lives are at stake.
Alexander Balashov, 36
From a photographer in Kemerovo to a handyman in Seattle
Before emigrating from Russia, my wife and I did wedding and commercial photography and made good money at it. The work was such that we could often sleep in until noon, though there were weeks when we only got two to three hours of sleep a night. At the same time, I worked as a brand manager, running ad campaigns and dealing with clients.
I didn’t like the situation in the country. I volunteered at Navalny’s campaign office in Kemerovo, and in 2018 I was called in for questioning in connection with the case against the office’s coordinator. A lawyer advised me to show up but invoke Article 51 of the Constitution and say nothing. A few days after the questioning, my wife and I decided to leave Russia for a while and went on a trip through Southeast Asia. We visited Thailand, Vietnam, and Cambodia.
When we came back, no one bothered me for a while. But in 2021, I started getting calls from the prosecutor’s office and the police, inviting me in for questioning without a formal summons. I refused, telling them that if they wanted to talk, they should send an official summons. But of course it was frightening. We sold our apartment in a hurry, below market price, and went into hiding.
First we went to Altai, then to Sheregesh, a small town in the Kemerovo region. I turned off my phone so I couldn’t be tracked. We then decided to leave Russia for Kyrgyzstan and plan our next steps from there. But shortly before our flight, Russia launched its war against Ukraine.
I couldn’t stay silent, so I went back to Kemerovo and staged a one-person picket with a sign reading “No to War.” I understood this was a direct path to prison, but I couldn’t act otherwise. I was detained and sentenced to 12 days. Then a cycle began: after the 12 days, I was released, but I was detained again on my way out of the holding facility for another 10 days, and then again for 13 more days. I was charged with inciting hatred “against the social group of ‘police officers’” over an old comment I’d made on [the Russian social media platform] VK, in which I harshly criticized police.
While I was in the holding facility, an officer from the Interior Ministry’s Center for Combating Extremism, known as Center E, came to see me. He said I could either go to prison or cooperate, and offered to pay for my flight and expenses in Georgia in exchange for me spying on a friend who ran Navalny’s campaign office. I realized this was my chance to escape Russia and agreed. They didn’t ask me for any guarantees. I turned down the money for tickets and expenses, saying I’d rather submit receipts afterward.
Of course, I didn’t fly to Georgia. My wife and I decided we should fly straight to a country where we could stay, so we chose the United States, where we could apply for political asylum. We flew from Moscow to Qatar, then to Mexico, and from there to the U.S. border.
We took some of the money left over from selling our apartment in Kemerovo: $8,000. We decided not to take the rest so as not to draw attention at the border, fearing we wouldn’t be allowed to leave. We put some of the money into crypto and gave the rest of our savings to friends, family, and animal shelters.
We showed up at the U.S. border six times, and each time we were turned back. You can only request asylum right at the border or after you’ve crossed it. But American border agents stand before the border itself, thoroughly checking documents and vehicles, and if they suspect you might be an asylum seeker, they send you back. Our seventh attempt succeeded because the cars in the lane we were driving in weren’t being checked.
We applied for asylum, and after that, my wife and I were sent to separate immigration detention facilities, since asylum applications are always reviewed individually.
I was in immigration detention for almost four months. I spent a lot of time in the facility’s law library, where I learned about immigration law and found phone numbers for law firms. I called around and that’s how I found a free lawyer.
One of the conditions for getting out of immigration detention is having a sponsor in the U.S. — someone who will vouch for you and provide housing and food. I got lucky and found a sponsor while still detained: a guy in the facility with me had a friend who’d moved to the U.S. from Ukraine long ago, and that friend became a sponsor for both me and my “cellmate.”
After getting out of detention, I still had to get my wife out. While I was detained, I’d had almost no contact with her. I looked into it and learned she’d only be released on bail of $35,000. I didn’t have that kind of money.
I was preparing for the hearing that would decide whether my asylum petition would be approved, while also looking for money to get my wife released. My sponsor let me stay with him and offered me work with him on a construction site. I agreed and searched for other work at the same time — checking job listings online, asking people around me, and reaching out to friends of friends.
I soon found work on a skyscraper construction site, even though I’d never done anything like that in Russia. With money from that job, I moved out from my sponsor’s place and rented a room. But there was no way to quickly earn the $35,000 for my wife’s bail through construction work. So I turned to a company that specializes in exactly these situations — it pays your bail for you, and you pay it back later with a fee on top.
My wife was eventually released, after spending six months in detention. I kept working on the skyscraper construction site in Washington, while she got a job as a cleaner, cleaning apartments for pay. We had almost no free time — I’d sometimes wake up at three in the morning, work all day, and go to bed at ten at night. My wife was exhausted too. We lived like that for several months.
In early 2023, the skyscraper was finished, and I started looking for other ways to make money. In Russia, I’d never worked with my hands — I’d only done things around my own house. But I do have an engineering degree, so figuring out repair work wasn’t hard for me.
On Facebook, I found a Russian-speaking woman who’d moved to the U.S. with her parents as a child. She bought old RVs, fixed them up, and sold them. I got a job with her doing repairs and made about $25 an hour. That went on for several months, and then she moved on to other pursuits, leaving me without work.
I started looking for jobs on sites offering small repair services. I replaced toilets, installed doors, and painted rooms. Life in the U.S. is very expensive, so I had to grab anything that brought in income and work without days off.
My wife and I got lucky — in December 2024, we won our case and received a document allowing us to stay in the U.S. We wanted to get back into photography, which meant buying equipment and investing in marketing. But our marriage gradually started falling apart. My wife and I had built up mutual resentment, partly because of the drastic lifestyle change and the enormous stress. We tried to save the relationship, but it was hard to hear each other out. Little by little we stopped talking, even though we kept living together. I was the one who initiated the divorce. Attempts to reconnect didn’t work, and we didn’t have the energy to keep trying. Technically, though, we’re not divorced yet — we’re still working through the paperwork.
Soon after we split up, I moved to Seattle, focused on repair work, and became a “jack of all trades,” or handyman, as it’s called here. In the U.S. there are several platforms where you can hire workers like that.
Some jobs are simple: changing a lock or a faucet. But sometimes there are trickier ones, like framing a house. The work varies widely: laying tile, installing a bathtub, replacing a toilet, fixing a gate. Sometimes the job isn’t building something but tearing it down — a wall, say.
I realized that working with your hands is great. On top of that, it’s quite profitable for people without local degrees or certifications. I make between $8,000 and $12,000 a month, depending on how much work I take on. Usually I have up to six small jobs a day, but sometimes there’s one big job that takes a whole day or even several days.
I prepare for jobs in advance. For example, I knew nothing about installing automatic garage doors, but I researched it all online, showed up, and did it as if I’d been doing it my whole life. There’s tons of information online now about how to do repairs — there’s a YouTube video for almost any problem, or you can ask an AI. Prep usually takes a little time, anywhere from half an hour to an hour. Sometimes I just figure it out myself, working out logically how something is put together.
A typical summer workday runs 10–12 hours, so I make my own food and bring it with me. Travel eats up some of my time too — I might spend an hour getting from one job to the next.
Sometimes I work without days off — it’s easier for me to put in a lot of hours all at once so I’ll have more time later to relax somewhere beautiful. Ideally, I’d like to work a couple of weeks a month, or every other month, and spend the rest of my time traveling.
I feel like I belong in the U.S. now. Americans, in general, are a lot like Russians — just more successful and kinder. I don’t miss Russia much, since most of my friends have scattered elsewhere. They live all over the world: in England, Australia, the European Union. Some live in the U.S. too — by coincidence, some old friends of mine from Kemerovo now live in the town next to mine. But I keep close track of what’s happening in Russia and get into arguments about it on social media.
I love my work and consider myself a very happy person. Though I do hope that my ex-wife and I will get back into photography together — if not as a married couple, then as business partners.

Lithuania would not make ‘emotional’ investments into airBaltic – minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:14:00 UTC
19:14:00 KST

Lithuania has received no new proposal from Latvia to invest in its struggling national airline airBaltic and would reject any such offer, Transport Minister Juras Taminskas said, calling such an investment an “emotional act” that would not be in Lithuania’s interests.
“In my opinion, money must be placed where it creates added value for taxpayers: defence, road infrastructure, salaries, educational institutions, hospitals. It should not go towards buying an emotion, in this case airBaltic, which would demand more and more funds every single day,” Taminskas said in an interview with BNS.
The minister described airBaltic’s financial situation as a “long-standing issue” that must be addressed by the Latvian government without interference from other countries.
The comments follow news that the Latvian airline will suspend flights from Vilnius to Berlin and Dubai, and from Palanga to Tenerife, for the upcoming winter season. Frequencies between Vilnius and Tallinn will also be reduced.
airBaltic has millions in debt, plans to reduce its fleet, and is cutting routes. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has stressed the need for sufficient flights ahead of the Lithuanian EU Presidency and plans to discuss this in Latvia. What is your position?
The financial situation of airBaltic is not news; it did not happen yesterday. Their financial capacity has been a recurring public issue for years. A point must come where the company and the Latvian government review the business model. This is their field of operation, and certainly not a matter for interference by Lithuania, Estonia, Poland, or other countries.
airBaltic is an important partner, carrying nearly 12.6 percent of passengers in Lithuania. While some routes are being cut, they are opening new ones, such as to Switzerland for the skiing season. This is absolutely a normal process. Political opponents want to mix facts with politics to suggest something major has happened. Nothing has happened; it is a normal carrier practice based on market needs.
Regarding accessibility for the presidency [of the EU Council], Brussels is served by four direct flights per week, and there are 20 connecting flights a day from Vilnius. This is not just an airBaltic issue, so there is no need to mix political emotion with facts.
The prime minister could not say if Lithuania would consider buying airBaltic shares. Have you received such an offer?
We have not received an acquisition proposal. There was an offer previously when Gintautas Paluckas was prime minister [in 2025], but not currently.
I believe taxpayer money must be spent rationally. The budget is tight, with funding needed for everything from national defence to healthcare and education. The question is simple: do we spend money on priorities or on something that just gives us an “emotion”?
My view is that funds should go to infrastructure and services, not to purchasing airBaltic shares and holding onto an emotion that will require constant further investment. That is my firm opinion.
So even if airBaltic’s situation worsens and Latvia asks for help, you will not consider to respond?
Such a decision would be made collectively by the government, but my opinion as transport minister is that we should not waste taxpayer money on an emotion, but to invest where there is a direct return and immediate need.
How are preparations going for flight connectivity for the 2027 European Union Presidency?
We must not conflate two different things. The finances of airBaltic and seasonal schedule changes are separate from the [EU] presidency. For the presidency, we assess current flights and potential demand. Ministers from European countries do not only fly from Brussels; they fly from their own capitals.
It is vital to ensure connectivity with major hubs for transfers. Currently, we have four direct flights a week to Brussels and 20 daily connections. For example, one can reach Brussels within two to four hours via Warsaw, Copenhagen, Riga, Vienna, or Tallinn.
The scale of connectivity has changed fundamentally since Lithuania last held the presidency in 2013. Even without the presidency peak, current passenger numbers to Brussels are nearly identical to those seen during the 2013 presidency.
But is it not a matter of prestige for a presiding country to have direct flights for visiting diplomats?
Again, these are two different topics. Is it low prestige to have a transfer? Should we have direct flights to every European Union capital just for show? Ministers and members of the parliament already fly via Warsaw. Does that change anything? We must separate taxpayer funds from the desire for “prestige”.
Is our goal diplomatic relations and a successful presidency, or is it to show off? I believe it is not to show off, especially if those flights disappear the day the presidency ends. Our goal is sustained, better connectivity for Lithuania, not a six-month show paid for by taxpayers.
Today we have excellent connections with major hubs: Frankfurt, Warsaw, Copenhagen, Helsinki, Vienna, Amsterdam, and Stockholm.
Are there connections to other capitals that need to be secured?
One always wants more routes and shorter transfer times, and we work on that daily. However, compared to 10 or 13 years ago, Lithuania’s accessibility has fundamentally improved for the better.

Germany charged a Ukrainian for the Nord Stream blasts—Kyiv is now investigating if Russia staged the attack to frame Ukrainians

10:12:05 UTC
19:12:05 KST

Ukraine has opened its own criminal investigation into the 2022 destruction of the Nord Stream gas pipelines, months after Germany charged a Ukrainian over the blasts, Suspilne reported. Prosecutors in Kyiv registered the case on war-crimes grounds and say they will test whether Russia staged the sabotage to discredit Ukraine. Serhii Kuznietsov is due to stand trial in Germany in October.
Kyiv will test a Russian false-flag version
Ukraine's Security Service, under the Prosecutor General's Office, opened proceedings on 9 July under the article on violations of the laws and customs of war. Kuznietsov's Ukrainian lawyer, Mykola Katerynchuk, told Suspilne about the case.
The Prosecutor General's Office confirmed it is supervising a probe into the "possible commission in September 2022, amid the international armed conflict between Russia and Ukraine, by citizens of Ukraine, of actions connected to the undermining" of both pipelines in the Baltic Sea. It said the case was registered after the "independent discovery in the media" that Germany had charged a Ukrainian citizen.
Given Russia's use of hybrid methods, investigators will also examine whether Russians organized the explosions as a "false flag" operation, using Ukrainian citizens or imitating their participation to discredit Ukraine.
The office said it used the laws-and-customs-of-war charge because it matches the qualification chosen by Germany's Federal Prosecutor's Office.
Russia laid Nord Stream to bypass Ukraine amid preparations for war. Four years after it exploded, Kyiv says it had nothing to do with blasts
The case against Serhii Kuznietsov
The pipelines exploded on 26 September 2022. On 8 August 2025, Germany's Federal Court of Justice issued an arrest warrant for Kuznietsov, alleging he led a group of six who mined the pipelines and detonated them remotely.
Italian police arrested him on 21 August 2025, and Italy's Supreme Court later confirmed his extradition to Germany. A Polish court, by contrast, refused a German request for another Ukrainian suspect, Volodymyr Zhuravlov.
On 2 July 2026, Germany's Federal Prosecutor's Office published its charges — an attack on civilian objects, causing an explosion, and destroying structures. Kuznietsov denies guilt.

A fire covering approximately 5,000 square meters has been reported at the Progress plant, which was hit by Flamingo
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
13:11:46 EEST
19:11:46 KST

A fire covering approximately 5,000 square meters has been reported at the Progress plant, which was hit by Flamingo
Kyiv • UNN
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine confirmed the striking of the production workshop for assembling engines for Soyuz-type launch vehicles and the aircraft maintenance workshop of JSC "Aviakor – Aviation Plant"
The Progress Rocket and Space Center was hit by FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles on August 15. The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported that the strike caused a fire at the plant covering approximately 5,000 m², UNN writes.
"During the analysis of additional data, the August 15, 2026, strike on the production workshop for assembling engines for Soyuz-type launch vehicles and the aircraft maintenance workshop of JSC Aviakor – Aviation Plant was confirmed. In addition, a fire covering approximately 5,000 m² was recorded as a result of the strike on the Progress Rocket and Space Center in Samara, Samara Region, Russian Federation," the General Staff said in a statement.
The Progress Rocket and Space Center is one of the key enterprises in Russia’s rocket and space industry, involved in the production of the Soyuz family of launch vehicles. The enterprise’s products are used, among other things, to place spacecraft into orbit and deploy Russian satellite communications constellations in the interests of the Russian army. This also includes satellites from the Rassvet project.
"The destruction of facilities of this level significantly reduces the military and technological capabilities of the Russian aggressor," the General Staff emphasized.
OSINT analysts reported that, as a result of the strike by Flamingo missiles, a crater 85 meters long and 35 meters wide was formed.
The hit struck Building 106A. It is part of the production complex for Soyuz launch vehicles. Building 106A operates under a high cleanroom classification: onboard electrical equipment, instruments, and printed circuit boards are installed here—in effect, the launch vehicle’s "nervous system": the control system, cable network, and instrumentation compartment. Building 106B, which houses final assembly, is located nearby. Analysts emphasize that this is a high-class cleanroom, and contamination by combustion products means requalifying the clean zones, recertifying the production process, and conducting repeated dust-control inspections—months, not weeks.
Against the backdrop of the confirmed strikes on Russian missile production facilities by Flamingo missiles, Russians are already comparing it with the Tomahawk missile. In terms of flight range and warhead weight, the Ukrainian missile manufactured by Fire Point even surpasses the American one—creating significant problems for the Russian rear and forcing the enemy to resort to information countermeasures and actively promote the claim that the FP-5 is not highly effective at overcoming air-defense systems. At the same time, in the case of Progress alone, the missiles had to cover at least 900 km to reach the target—that is, pass through air-defense systems along the entire route.

Juhan Kivirähk: How to explain pictures to a (half)dead government?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:10:00 UTC
19:10:00 KST

Juhan Kivirähk: How to explain pictures to a (half)dead government?
Although politicians in power treat initiatives made outside the Riigikogu chamber dismissively, I believe the next president should take social and economic studies and their use in governing the country under his or her wing and become the patron of creating Estonia's future convention, Juhan Kivirähk writes.
The headline "How to explain pictures to a (half)dead government?" is a paraphrase of German avant‑garde artist Joseph Beuys's famous performance "How to Explain Pictures to a Dead Hare," in which the artist tried to interpret the relationship between the artist and the audience and how the public understands a work of art.
But just as artistic values remain elusive to a dead hare, our government, frozen in a strange lethargy, also seems unable to understand or interpret the information scientists and experts provide about the state of Estonian society and its development opportunities.
Many studies have been conducted in Estonia and development strategies have been created that could and should help guide society's development wisely. Unfortunately, political decision-makers seem to live in a kind of parallel reality, ignoring social facts and forecasts that do not fit party ideology. Instead, governments tend to base their work on coalition agreements put together voluntaristically.
Estonia currently has the strategic development plan "Estonia 2035," and work has begun on the nationwide plan "Estonia 2050." The government's website offers sixteen sectoral development plans. In addition, various institutes and think tanks have produced thorough development scenarios at different times.
Since 1995, Estonia's best social scientists have compiled human development reports that include in‑depth analysis of social life and policy recommendations. From 2006 to 2017, the Development Fund did very valuable work identifying social problems and offering solutions, but it likely became too inconvenient for politicians and was shut down.
The understanding that policy must rely on research has nevertheless been accepted. Each year ministries commission social studies for significant sums. Unfortunately, they do not know how to use the results, and most end up sitting on shelves.
On June 13, Postimees published a programmatic article by well‑known and respected social scientists Erik Terk, Mati Heidmets and Marju Lauristin titled "Estonia needs a new comprehensive future strategy." It largely revisited the principles of the sustainable development strategy "Sustainable Estonia 21" (SE 21), approved by the Riigikogu in September 2005. Had the state followed the principles and proposals set out in SE 21 since its completion, we would undoubtedly be living in a much better Estonia today.
SE 21 was based on a holistic approach to managing social life. It stated that to accelerate development in Estonia, we must run in four directions at once: strengthen the Estonian cultural space, ensure people's well‑being, keep society cohesive and maintain environmental balance. These four goals form an interconnected system. They cannot be developed one by one or at each other's expense, but all at the same time. When making changes in one field, it is necessary to consider what changes this will cause in the others.
At first it seemed politicians took the strategy seriously, and even national statistics began tracking sustainable development parameters. Unfortunately, following the strategy proved too difficult for politicians, because it is much more pleasant to deal with everyday fine‑tuning.
Terk, Heidmets and Lauristin propose creating a new form of political cooperation that uses modern technology to shape Estonia's long‑term development — the Estonia Future Convention. The convention would not be a place for final decisions but for forming agreements and drafting proposals. What is agreed in the convention would become input for the Riigikogu and the government.
A similar proposal already appeared in SE 21: the idea of a future convention corresponded to a national development network operating on similar principles, with a development committee in the Riigikogu as its partner.
Two decades have been lost, and there is reason to fear that politicians will stare at this latest proposal — a kind of last cry for help from social scientists — just as indifferently as dead hares. In any case, the three professors' initiative has received no response. Our political system is not designed to promote social good but to reproduce only party power. And for achieving that, strategy naturally offers no helping hand.
Entrepreneur Andres Inn, who ran as an independent candidate in the European Parliament elections, described Estonia's political modus vivendi very aptly:
"Political loyalty is rewarded instead of expertise, short‑term coalition compromises are preferred over long‑term strategy, and ministers are accountable upward to the party leadership rather than outward to the public. Ministries operate like semi‑autonomous fiefdoms, poorly coordinated and often working against each other. Major reforms, whether in health care, education or taxation, arrive half‑planned, over‑promised and poorly executed. When things go wrong, responsibility dissolves into the familiar fog of 'collective decision‑making.' This is not governance. This is political career risk management."
Unfortunately, there is no hope of changing the current electoral system, which, as Guido Viik said, continues to bring to power "vain but not competent" politicians. So the only option is to rely on initiatives made outside the Riigikogu chamber.
Although many believe the president is merely a high state official appointed by politicians, citizens have a different understanding of the presidency and different expectations for it.
The president has the power to launch important social initiatives. SE 21 itself was born in the social atmosphere created by Arnold Rüütel's election as Estonia's president. With support from entrepreneur Aadu Luukas, the The Social Agreement Foundation was created in the early 2000s. It was during this time that work began on SE 21, completed in 2005. This was followed by the creation of the Development Fund in 2006.
Toomas Hendrik Ilves, elected president in 2006, also tried to involve civil society in political decision‑making. In addition to being the patron of the first People's Assembly in 2013 and bringing its proposals to the Riigikogu, he regularly held "president's gatherings." In these debates, involving society's opinion leaders, many current social issues were discussed and solutions proposed.
Although politicians in power treated initiatives outside the Riigikogu dismissively then and still do now, I believe the next president should take social and economic studies and their use in governing the country under his or her wing and become the patron of creating Estonia's future convention. Perhaps the president can show politicians a picture that truly describes society's real condition in a way that makes them ask the question Mari‑Liis Lill posed at the Riigikogu during the 25th anniversary of the creative unions' plenary: "What is wrong with this picture?"
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon

Iran labels California its ‘new territory’ after Trump’s Hormuz claim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:09:54 UTC
19:09:54 KST

Sahin Demir
19 August 2026•Update: 19 August 2026
An official Iranian social media account labeled California a “new territory” of Iran on Tuesday in response to US President Donald Trump posting an image portraying the Strait of Hormuz as “NEW U.S. Territory.”
Trump shared the image on his Truth Social account Tuesday, showing a map of the Strait of Hormuz with the strategic waterway circled beneath the words “NEW U.S. Territory,” following up on his earlier remarks saying the strait would be made US territory after the war ends.
The White House later reposted Trump’s post on its official account on US social media platform X.
In response, the official Iran in Hyderabad account on X posted a map of the US showing California highlighted in blue, with the words: “NEW TERRITORY OF ISLAMIC REPUBLIC OF IRAN.”
Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s deputy foreign minister, also hit back at Trump’s post, writing on X: “His delusion regarding the Strait of Hormuz will soon either be corrected, or we will correct the delusions of this delusional man.”
California, particularly the Los Angeles area, is home to the largest concentration of people of Iranian descent outside Iran. An estimated 141,000 Iranian Americans live in Los Angeles County, according to the Iranian Diaspora Dashboard hosted by UCLA’s Center for Near Eastern Studies.
The Iranian community in Southern California expanded significantly following Iran’s 1979 Islamic Revolution, with the Westwood area of Los Angeles becoming a major center of Iranian diaspora life, commonly known as “Tehrangeles.”
The exchange comes amid heightened tensions between Tehran and Washington following months of conflict.
Iran and the US signed a memorandum of understanding in June aimed at ending the war and paving the way for a broader agreement, but talks have since stalled amid disputes over its implementation and navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.
Negotiations involving Iran and Oman over arrangements for navigation through the strategic waterway, meanwhile, have continued without a breakthrough.

Over 4,000 candidates registered for State Duma polls in federal, single-member districts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:08:02 UTC
19:08:02 KST

MOSCOW, August 19. /TASS/. More than 4,000 candidates have been registered for the elections of deputies to the State Duma in federal and single-member constituencies, Central Election Commission Chairwoman Ella Pamfilova told a meeting of the commission.
"A total of 4,436 candidates have been registered for the elections of deputies to the State Duma of the Federal Assembly of the Russian Federation of the ninth convocation in the single-member and multi-member constituencies," Pamfilova said.
Federal lists were registered, put forward by political parties: The Communist Party – 329 candidates, New People – 295, United Russia – 389, LDPR – 243, Just Russia – 259, Communists of Russia – 265, Party of Pensioners – 254, Rodina – 295, Party of Direct Democracy – 236, Greens – 251. Registration for the State Duma elections concluded on August 16.
According to Pamfilova, 1,723 candidates submitted documents for nomination to the district election commissions and were nominated.
"82 people lost their status as nominees; of these, 11 were nominated by six parties, and 71 were self-nominated. Registration was denied to 16 applicants, of whom eight were nominated by three parties and eight were self-nominated," Pamfilova said.
"1,622 candidates were registered, of which 1,616 were nominated by 11 parties, and four candidates were self-nominated. Five people from four parties withdrew after registration: LDPR (the Rostov Region), A Just Russia (Moscow), based on a personal application – Yabloko (the Kaliningrad Region), Greens (the Tver Region) – due to the loss of passive electoral rights, Greens in the Samara Region – based on the party’s decision."
She said that the Commission registered 39 candidates from eight political parties for the elections of the heads of eight constituent entities.
She added that 40 candidates were put forward for the elections of the highest officials of the constituent entities by the regional branches of nine parties.
"As a result, 39 people were registered – they were put forward by eight parties," Pamfilova said.
She also said that 18,478 candidates were registered for the elections to 39 legislative assemblies, which will be held in September 2026.
According to her, a total of 19,438 candidates were nominated, and 18,478 were registered, of whom 14,007 were elected in the single-member constituencies and 4,471 in multi-member constituencies.

"I have instructed the relevant authorities to conduct a thorough, transparent, and exhaustive investigation,” in a post on X.

HANOI, Aug. 19 (Xinhua) -- Three people were killed in a fire at a wood-processing workshop in Chuong My ward in Hanoi, capital of Vietnam, on Wednesday, the Voice of Vietnam reported.
The fire broke out at about 10:05 a.m. in the workshop's paint room and mezzanine, rapidly spreading and sending thick black smoke over the facility, with about 30 workers inside at that time, according to the report.

Authorities continued searching the site, while verifying information about the victims and investigating the cause, the report added. ■

Trump put thousands of soldiers on Washington’s streets. They seldom stop crime
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:07:09 UTC
19:07:09 KST

Trump put thousands of soldiers on Washington’s streets. They seldom stop crime
WASHINGTON, Aug 19 - Well past midnight one day this spring, three police officers pulled up to a nightclub where a man was stomping on a young woman lying on the sidewalk.
The officers stopped the attack and arrested him, according to a police report. It was the kind of assault police might encounter on almost any night in almost any city.
But one detail stood out to police officer Xavier Jimenez, who wrote the report: “There was approximately 15 national guard members in the area on routine patrol who did not take any action.”
President Donald Trump deployed thousands of National Guard troops to Washington last summer as the centerpiece of what he describes as a no-holds-barred effort to combat crime, especially in cities run by Democrats. Every day, small clots of soldiers in camouflage and body armor patrol tourist-heavy areas of the U.S. capital, including national monuments, subway stations and the area around its professional baseball park.
What the soldiers seldom do, Reuters found, is fight crime.
Since their arrival last August, the National Guard soldiers Trump ordered to Washington have been mentioned in only a tiny fraction — about 1.3% — of the criminal cases filed in the Superior Court of the District of Columbia, which handles nearly all the city’s criminal prosecutions. In dozens of cases, the soldiers appear not as people making the arrests but as victims of crime.
The roughly 4,500 soldiers currently deployed to Washington outnumber its 3,200 police officers. And they cost more: The Trump administration last year told Congress that sending guardsmen to the capital cost about $1.65 million a day – before officials doubled the number of troops this summer. The city’s most recent police budget was about $1.5 million daily.
The administration told Congress it plans to keep sending soldiers to Washington – though it has not said how many – until the end of Trump’s presidency in 2029 at a cost of $1.4 billion.
To gauge the impact of that deployment, Reuters reviewed every publicly available charging document filed in Superior Court and interviewed lawyers, residents, service members and others who are familiar with their work.
The soldiers mostly responded to minor incidents in neighborhoods that are wealthier, whiter and less dangerous than the rest of the capital, Reuters found after comparing court records to the city’s demographics and crime information. Reuters could find no reference in court records to soldiers doing any kind of law enforcement in the neighborhoods where about 82% of the city’s 859 murders occurred over the past five years.
The White House did not respond to questions about soldiers’ work. Spokeswoman Lauren Bis said Trump’s efforts in the city have “driven down crime, beautified the city, and improved quality of life for countless individuals.”
D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser, who has called the deployment “problematic,” declined to comment, as did the city’s police department.
The National Guard taskforce managing the Washington deployment did not respond to questions about its work or its cost. A spokeswoman, Leona Hendrickson, said soldiers were too busy to be interviewed.
Although soldiers have sometimes broken up fights or assaults, many of the crimes for which they detained people have been minor. In October, soldiers chased down a man who had taken two slices of pizza and offered $2 as partial payment, according to police records. A week later, they stopped a man who threw a rock at a bus. In April, they detained a man who allegedly stole two beef jerky sticks worth about $7 from a pharmacy, according to the report. Last month, six soldiers held a woman who drank a bottle of root beer without paying.
The Rev. William Young, who lives in the Navy Yard neighborhood where soldiers patrol frequently, laughed when asked whether the troops made him feel safer. “It’s a way of keeping fear in all of us,” he said. “This is not how a capital of democracy should be protected, by having soldiers marching to protect the streets.”
‘THEY COULD HAVE DONE MORE’
Reuters found 217 criminal cases in Washington in which police mentioned the involvement of the National Guard. In about a quarter of them, 62 cases, soldiers single-handedly stopped people suspected of a crime, often for things like shoplifting or jumping turnstiles to avoid paying subway fare. In another 43 cases, soldiers helped police officers arrest someone.
Videos obtained by community groups also show troops in groups of 20 or more stationed outside subway stations at night, blocking teens from descending the escalators to enforce a city curfew.
“It’s like they brought people here from all across the country, just to be here. And they harass people a lot more than they are actually doing police work,” said the Rev. Norman Nixon, the pastor of the Union Temple Baptist Church.
Although the guardsmen have been deputized as U.S. Marshals, according to government records, they have limited law-enforcement power. The Defense Department has described their work as “presence patrols,” a show of force meant to deter crime rather than respond to it. They can detain suspects, but then must call police officers to make a formal arrest.
Court records describe 35 instances in which the troops were witnesses to crimes, sometimes simply watching until police officers arrived. They have told officers about a drug deal, a man urinating in public, another who exposed himself to a subway policeman and two men writing with chalk on a monument outside the city’s train station, one of them wearing a banana costume.
Evelyn Jones said she wonders whether soldiers could have saved her nephew, Keon Jones, who was stabbed to death in April near a trendy strip of hotels and restaurants on the city’s waterfront.
The soldiers called emergency services after finding Jones unresponsive after a fight. They later told police they thought Jones was merely intoxicated. They did not realize, until after officers reached the scene, that he had been stabbed so severely his intestines were spilling out. He died in hospital about two hours later.
“They could have done more to help him,” his aunt said.
The service members themselves have often been victims, a fact underscored last year when two soldiers from West Virginia were shot not far from the White House, killing one of them.
Reuters found 62 cases in which people were charged with pushing, punching or threatening soldiers. Nine were accused of spitting on the soldiers. One man allegedly tried to grab a soldier’s pistol as the soldier tried to arrest him for stealing baseball caps in a subway station. Another man was charged after he told a group of soldiers that he wanted to “shoot you, in between your balls, with a bazooka,” according to a police report.
And twice, police in Washington arrested off-duty soldiers for violating the city’s firearms laws, though the U.S. Attorney’s Office dropped the charges against both of them.
This summer, they took on a new mission: guarding the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, which the Trump administration spent millions of dollars to renovate only to see it turn green with algae as its liner peeled away. Trump claimed the pool was sabotaged by vandals. But U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro eventually conceded that a government contractor “botched” the job.
PATROLLING SAFER NEIGHBORHOODS
The U.S. has long used National Guard soldiers to respond to disasters, help secure major events like the Super Bowl and occasionally quell riots, but they haven't been used for everyday crime-fighting. Trump also authorized smaller deployments in Memphis and New Orleans and has mused about sending soldiers to other cities.
“You do not want armed soldiers on the streets of America,” said Gen. Randy Manner, who retired in 2012 as the second-in-command of the National Guard Bureau. He said soldiers are ill-prepared for police work and more expensive than hiring more police officers.
Determining the soldiers’ impact on crime in Washington is not straightforward. In addition to the soldiers, the Trump administration sent hundreds of extra federal agents into the city, who largely functioned as local police officers.
The number of murders in Washington fell for the third consecutive year. But homicide numbers also dropped in cities where the government has not sent soldiers or additional federal agents. And the total number of violent crimes — serious assaults, robberies and sex offenses in addition to homicides — reported by city police between January and mid-August is marginally higher than last year, about 4%.
A study in May by the nonpartisan Niskanen Center found that sending soldiers into Washington led to fewer stolen cars but had no impact on violent crimes.
Charles Stimson, a senior fellow at the pro-Trump Heritage Foundation, said the soldiers’ visibility served as a deterrent. “When you’re speeding and you see a cop, you slow down,” he said. “If those National Guard went poof and left town tomorrow, crime would go up.”
The Reuters review of court records found little evidence of soldiers’ presence in high-crime neighborhoods where they might have responded to more serious crimes.
Instead, the court records show soldiers were more likely to be mentioned in arrest records in city neighborhoods that have higher incomes, in which more people have college degrees, and where more people are white. Most of the arrests in which soldiers participated were either near the city’s core or its subway stops.
Reuters used the location of incidents in court records to identify the areas in which soldiers were either assisting the police or seeking help from them, then compared those neighborhoods to the rest of the city. That does not account for places soldiers might have been sent if they did not interact with law enforcement there. But it suggests that their presence was not aimed at quelling the violent crime that had ravaged parts of the city in the past.
Salim Adofo, an outreach coordinator with the Anacostia Coordinating Council, a nonprofit operating in a low-income part of the city, said that matched his experience.
“I haven’t seen them all year,” he said. REUTERS

KUALA LUMPUR, Aug. 19 (Xinhua) -- Malaysia's manufacturing capacity utilization rose 1.2 percentage points year on year to 83.7 percent in the second quarter of 2026, compared with 82.5 percent a year earlier, official data showed on Wednesday.
All manufacturing sub-sectors recorded utilization rates above 80 percent, led by transport equipment and other manufactures at 87.2 percent, up 1.2 percentage points from a year earlier, the Department of Statistics Malaysia said in a statement.
Electrical and electronics products followed at 85.3 percent, an increase of 2.6 percentage points.
On a quarterly basis, overall manufacturing capacity utilization increased 0.9 percentage point from 82.8 percent in the first quarter.
Export-oriented industries recorded a 1.3 percentage point year-on-year increase to 82.9 percent, while domestic-oriented industries rose 0.8 percentage point to 85.2 percent.
Low demand, insufficient material supplies, and machinery and equipment repairs and maintenance remained the main factors behind capacity underutilization, it said. ■

The government will table Budget 2027 in parliament on Oct. 9, 2026, after consultations with stakeholders and the public. ■

US families, healthcare providers under strain after Trump crackdown on Haitian immigrants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:06:51 UTC
19:06:51 KST

US families, healthcare providers under strain after Trump crackdown on Haitian immigrants
NEW CITY, New York, Aug 19 - Richie Rosen, 43, was born with a rare genetic condition called Williams syndrome. His hands are weak and unreliable. He longs for human connection but gets anxious in social situations and is easily upset.
For four years, a Haitian caregiver named Tassy helped him navigate day-to-day life at a group home for developmentally disabled men in upstate New York – cooking for him, driving him around and making difficult chores more manageable.
But on July 27, Jawonio, the nonprofit that runs the facility, terminated Tassy’s contract after the Trump administration ended Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and the work authorization that came with it.
"I miss him a lot," Rosen told Reuters last week, sitting in his room at the home in Rockland County, a leafy suburb north of New York City. “I miss him just saying hi to me all the time."
Around 21,000 of the 330,000 Haitians in the United States under TPS worked as caregivers and nursing assistants as of last year, serving around 77,000 patients, according to an analysis of U.S. census data by Philip Connor, a research fellow at Princeton University.
Their abrupt removal from the healthcare industry has placed additional strain on a system already struggling to meet the needs of the fast-aging U.S. population. It also came as a shock to families that relied on them.
Richie's mother, Sharan Rosen, said Tassy was “like family” to her son, who never got the chance to say goodbye to his longtime aide.
“My heart is breaking for him and for my son,” she said.
Reuters was unable to reach Tassy for this story and is using only his first name due to his vulnerable legal status.
Jawonio was forced to lay off nearly two dozen Haitians last month, totaling 7% of its staff. Most of those affected provided round-the-clock care for disabled patients for around $20 per hour, just a few dollars above New York’s minimum wage.
"These are among the most difficult positions to fill," Jawonio's CEO, Randi Rios-Castro, told Reuters in response to emailed questions.
“This has never been just an immigration issue,” she wrote of the decision to end TPS. “It is a healthcare workforce issue for us and our country.”
‘PATIENT CARE SUFFERS’
The United States granted humanitarian protection to Haitians following a devastating earthquake in 2010.
The Trump administration cited improving conditions in Haiti as a reason for ending the program, though the country remains among the most unstable in the Western Hemisphere.
Haiti has not held elections since 2016; its last president was assassinated in 2021. Gang violence has convulsed the capital. 1.4 million people are displaced from their homes, the U.N. said last year, and about 6 in 10 live in poverty.
No longer able to legally work in the United States, former TPS holders can now return to Haiti voluntarily -- or try to stay in the U.S. and risk arrest and deportation.
New York state had the second-largest number of Haitian TPS holders after Florida, one of the country's most popular retirement destinations.
Weeks before TPS was set to expire, Emmett Reed, CEO of the Florida Health Care Association, sent a letter to Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin urging him to consider an exemption for long-term caregivers.
"Florida is home to one of the nation's largest and fastest-growing older adult populations, and demand for long-term care services continues to increase each year," Reed wrote in the letter.
The loss of Haitian workers risked “causing a ripple effect that could overwhelm our local hospitals and the entire healthcare system,” he continued.
Nancy Hagans, president of the New York State Nurses Association, moved to the U.S. from Haiti as a child and works at a hospital in Brooklyn. At an August 5 vigil held outside Maimonides Medical Center to protest staffing shortages, she compared the impact of ending TPS to the workforce deficit during the COVID-19 pandemic.
“When healthcare workers live in fear of going to work, patient care suffers,” Hagans told the crowd.
Responding to questions from Reuters, the Department of Homeland Security said it was “grossly false and lazy” to assert the healthcare industry relied on immigrants, adding that “for too long, TPS has been allowed to function as a de facto amnesty program."
Jawonio has appealed for help to Republican Congressman Mike Lawler, who represents Rockland County in New York's lower Hudson Valley, home to an estimated 11,000 Haitians.
Lawler, facing a competitive race in November’s midterm elections, has opposed stripping Haitians of protections despite being a backer of Trump and his hardline immigration agenda.
His office said he is working with Jawonio and other local groups to find alternative legal statuses for Haitian TPS holders.
"Losing these experienced workers creates real staffing challenges for providers who were already facing shortages and risks disrupting care for vulnerable residents,” Lawler's spokeswoman Caroline Hunt wrote in an email to Reuters.
FAMILY FILLS IN
At the group home in Rockland County, staffers are picking up extra shifts after the departures of Tassy and Marc, another former Haitian caregiver.
For the Rosens, the loss feels personal.
Sharan, 77, said she told her son that Tassy might have to leave because of new immigration policies. But she didn’t expect it to happen overnight.
Now, she and her 81-year-old husband are trying to help fill the gaps, including driving him to his job at a nearby grocery store.
Rosen, asked to recall the moment he learned his aide was gone, didn’t want to discuss it.
"I hope one day I can see him again," he said. REUTERS

Myanmar designates century-old air compressor station as heritage site
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
18:06:44 CST
19:06:44 KST

YANGON, Aug. 19 (Xinhua) -- Myanmar's Ministry of Hotels, Tourism and Culture announced on Wednesday it has designated a 138-year-old air compressor station in Yangon as an ancient heritage site.
The compressor station is not only a historic building, but also evidence of the country's technological and industrial development, the ministry's Department of Archaeology and National Museum said, calling for the site to be studied, preserved and maintained for future generations.
The air compressor station, also known as the blower station, was officially designated a heritage site on Tuesday, marked by the installation of a commemorative bronze plaque, the ministry said.
Located in Botahtaung township in Yangon region, the facility is operated by the engineering department of the Yangon City Development Committee.
Built in 1888, the station used air pressure to discharge sewage collected from households in downtown Yangon into the Yangon River. As electricity was not yet available in the early years, it initially relied on coal-fired boilers and compressor engines.
The equipment was upgraded in 1961 with electric air compressors, which remain in use today. The original coal-fired compressors have been preserved and are displayed for educational purposes, the ministry said. ■

Colombia’s New Government Seeks to Review JAS 39 Gripen Contract
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:06:30 UTC
19:06:30 KST

Colombia’s new government is seeking to review the terms of the deal to purchase Swedish JAS 39 Gripen E/F fighter jets.
According to Defensa, it is not a matter of canceling the purchase, but rather an attempt to renegotiate the terms agreed with Sweden.
The Colombian government is reportedly assessing the cost difference compared to similar contracts signed by other countries, particularly the agreement to supply Gripen aircraft to Thailand.
Such comparisons have raised questions about the final cost of the Colombian contract and may serve as one of the arguments in favor of revising its terms.
The contract covers the purchase of 15 single-seat Gripen E and two two-seat Gripen F fighter jets, as well as weapons, personnel training, equipment, maintenance, and other elements required to bring the new fleet into service.
These aircraft are intended to gradually replace the Kfir fighter jets, which for many years have formed the backbone of the Colombian Aerospace Force’s combat capabilities.
Colombia may seek more favorable financial terms, increased industrial compensation, technology transfer, expansion of personnel training programs, and the involvement of national companies in the program’s implementation.
The last point is particularly important, as the agreement with Sweden creates opportunities to strengthen Colombia’s aviation and defense-industrial capabilities.
However, revising the contract does not allow Colombia to simply cancel the purchase with no consequences.
The agreement has already been signed and sets forth the financial and legal obligations of the parties. Therefore, any changes will have to be coordinated directly with the Swedish government and Saab.
The contract for the purchase of fighter jets was signed in November 2025.
Its value is estimated at ₱16 trillion ($4.24 billion). The aircraft are scheduled to be delivered between 2027 and 2032.

Parents of euthanasia teen go to court over prosecution letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:06:28 UTC
