Drought forces Swiss cows to descend early from Alpine pastures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:43:57 UTC
18:43:57 KST

Drought forces Swiss cows to descend early from Alpine pastures
Some Swiss farmers have already brought their livestock down from the mountain pastures earlier than planned due to drought conditions.
The Jura Arc, French-speaking Switzerland and parts of eastern Switzerland have been particularly hard hit, said Selina Droz, director-general of the Swiss Alpine Economy Federation (FSEA). The situation is critical across the whole country.
+ Why Swiss cows climb mountains
The FSEA does not have precise figures on the number of farms that have had to bring forward the descent from the mountain pastures. According to Droz, the vast majority of the mountain pastures affected have, however, brought only some of their animals back down to the valley, in order to conserve drinking water and fodder there too.
This year’s “highly exceptional situation” is also taking its toll on lowland farms, whose fodder reserves are equally limited due to the drought. The only alternative is the early slaughter of livestock, a measure to which some have already resorted.
The shorter summer grazing period is also having an impact on production. The FSEA forecasts below-average production of alpine cheese for the current year. For Gruyère d’alpage, for example, the trade association expects a drop in production of around 10% compared with the previous year.
More
The difficult search for real Swiss cows
Given climate change, dry summers are set to become more frequent in the future. However, early descents from the alpine pastures must remain an emergency measure. According to Droz, transporting water by road or helicopter only makes sense if, for example, the farm in question has even less fodder available.
All alpine farms should therefore review their own water infrastructure and adapt it where necessary. The implementation of projects such as new reservoirs or the tapping of springs requires further funding from the Confederation and the cantons.
According to the FSEA, Switzerland has around 6,600 alpine pastures, of which around a third of the usable agricultural area is farmed in summer, producing 5,500 tonnes of alpine cheese each year.

Italy is facing a fresh femicide wave
with six women killed by their partners or exes since the
mid-August Ferragosto holiday on Saturday.
                                    
                                       
				The latest two were on Tuesday, a 72-year-old woman stoned to
death by her 74-year-old husband in a field near Cosenza in
Calabria and a 50-year-old Polish woman stabbed to death by her
69-year-old Tunisian husband at Colleferro south of Rome.
                                    
                                       
				Previously, on Monday, a 39-year-old woman was killed by her
43-tyear-old ex husband near Venice after having reported him to
police several times for domestic violence, and after it emerged
that he had been reported by three other women since 2002.
                                    
                                       
				Femicide has been classed as a national emergency in Italy with
murderous violence against women hitting new heights.
                                    
                                       
				A specific new offence of femicide has been put onto the
country's law books.
                                    
                                       
				A campaign of education for young males towards healthy
relationships was partly stymied when the government made it
conditional on parent approval to take part.in courses in
Italy's schools.

Behind the Scenes: The Kyiv Independent's July digest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:42:31 UTC
18:42:31 KST

Welcome to the Kyiv Independent’s July digest where we share what we’ve been up to as a company — the work that goes into keeping our journalism independent and how it connects with our global community of readers and supporters.
What’s new at the Kyiv Independent
The biggest news of the month is that after a sold-out debut in New York last year, the Kyiv Independent is bringing another live event to the UK for the first time. On October 2, we’re hosting an event at Kings Place in London, with Editor-in-Chief Olga Rudenko hosting live storytelling from CEO Daryna Shevchenko and reporters Francis Farrell, Dominic Culverwell, and Olena Zashko. The evening will also include a curated photo exhibition, "The War They Live," an audience Q&A, and a meet-the-team reception.
As Olga Rudenko put it, "we spend most of our time reporting from Ukraine for an audience we don't actually see. Evenings like this mean a lot because they help close that gap."
Tickets are available now, with a livestream option for those who won’t be able to see us in person but would still like to attend.
Outside of the landmark events such as this one, we often organize meetings with our members whenever we travel. These are intimate gatherings over coffee, and an opportunity to connect with someone on our team and have a meaningful dialogue. To get a heads up when we come to your city, join our member community. Support of our members lets us scale our journalism and bring it to more people around the world. In turn, we offer many exclusive benefits, such as these meetups, Ukrainian language classes, merchandise store discounts, and more ways to connect with our team.
Over in our store, we launched Old Patterns, New Stories, a new collection built around Ukraine's centuries-old tradition of embroidery. It brings together two collaborations: a limited-edition vyshyvanka made with Ukrainian embroidery brand Gaptuvalnya, and several pieces created with Kyiv-based illustrator Kateryna Stepanishcheva (known as myfabstory), each representing Kyiv's past, present, and future.
With this collection, we also released the Kyiv Independent’s first-ever family look, with matching pieces for kids and their parents. You can build your own family bundle here, and the whole line is available here.
Vyshyvanka is one of the items that carries Ukrainian identity, and some of our team members, including our Editor-in-Chief Olga Rudenko, shared their stories connected with this traditional shirt which you can read here.
We also have a story we're especially glad to share. Ukrainian photojournalist George Ivanchenko, who lost his leg in the same Russian drone strike that killed his colleague, French journalist Antoni Lallican, in October 2025, has completed his recovery. Nearly 1,500 Kyiv Independent readers funded his fully functional electronic prosthesis, and George recently graduated from the Superhumans Center in Lviv wearing it for the first time. "I didn't think it was possible to walk this easily. It's incredible," George said. He’s now putting his prosthesis to a test on a camping trip to France with his wife, where he also intends to visit Antoni's family. It's a powerful reminder of what our community can do when it rallies around a shared cause — you can read the full story here.
Finally, we're excited to share that we partnered with The Atlantic to offer our community members a new benefit as a gesture of appreciation for their support. We teamed up with the Atlantic to offer the Kyiv Independent members based in continental Europe $30 off a yearlong digital subscription — unlocking The Atlantic's full archive, narrated articles, podcasts, and more.
In other media
July kept us on our toes as Ukraine's political situation shifted following the dismissal of Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov. Deputy Chief Editor Oleksiy Sorokin joined Pod Save the World, the Crooked Media podcast hosted by Tommy Vietor and Ben Rhodes, to break down the protests over President Volodymyr Zelensky's military staffing decisions and the latest Russian ballistic missile strikes on Ukraine. Oleksiy also appeared on the inaugural episode of Battleground: The Big Picture, the Goalhanger military history podcast, discussing the founding of the Kyiv Independent, the pressures facing Ukraine's free press, and the shifting balance of power within the Zelensky administration.
Deputy Chief Editor Toma Istomina spoke with NPR's Here & Now, about the wave of protests that followed Fedorov's dismissal and what it could mean for Ukraine's war effort.
And London-based think tank Chatham House drew on our reporting in its own analysis of the reshuffle, citing our coverage of Fedorov's record in office, the appointment of his successor, and the timing of his departure.
Special recognition
We're also glad to share that the Kyiv Independent has been shortlisted in two categories at the Press Gazette’s Future of Media Awards: Newsletter of the Year (National/International) category with Ukraine Weekly, authored by our Editor-in-Chief Olga Rudenko, and Reader Revenue Strategy category for our community-first approach in building a successful independent newsroom from Ukraine.
Thank you for reading. As always, there's a lot happening behind the scenes at the Kyiv Independent, and we're glad to have a way to bring you along for more of it. We'll keep sharing these updates every month, and we'd love to hear what you'd like to see more of.
If you're a member of the press looking to connect with us, or a reader who knows journalists we should connect with, email us at press@kyivindependent.com.

Ukraine anti-graft agencies uncover alleged laundering group tied to presidential official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:42:17 UTC
18:42:17 KST

Zelensky fires top presidential aide after anti-graft agencies reveal corruption probe
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Wednesday dismissed his deputy chief-of-staff Iryna Mudra after the country’s anti-graft agencies announced they were raiding the homes of a senior official from the president's office and a sitting member of parliament as part of a corruption probe.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Wednesday fired a top aide reportedly targeted in a corruption investigation, just a day after an ousted defence minister issued a surprise call for wartime elections.
Zelensky issued a decree to remove Iryna Mudra, his deputy chief of staff, after the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) said it was raiding the homes of a senior official from the president's office and a sitting member of parliament.
The agency, which did not name Mudra, said the investigation was linked to allegations of money laundering over a multimillion-dollar bail payment for a suspect in a major corruption case brought last year.
Ukrainian anti-corruption agencies earlier on Wednesday said they had launched a special operation against lawmakers and presidential advisers.
The NABU and SAPO agencies said in a YouTube video they had launched a special operation against lawmakers and presidential advisers. The anti-graft bodies said the group comprised a deputy head of the presidential office, a former lawmaker, heads of the management and supervisory boards of a state-owned bank and others.
They did not name the individuals, in accordance with Ukrainian law.
The probe poses a fresh headache for Zelensky after ousted defence chief Mykhailo Fedorov called for wartime elections in a bombshell statement late on Tuesday.
Read moreUkraine's sacked defence minister Fedorov calls for wartime presidential elections
Lawmakers on Wednesday approved the appointment of Yevhenii Khmara, a former top special forces operative, as Ukraine’s new defence minister after weeks of political turmoil over Fedorov’s ouster.
His removal had sent thousands of protesters on to the streets in rare wartime protests over the past month demanding that Zelensky reinstate the 35-year-old politician, whose supporters credit him with trying to reform the ministry.
The crisis had also forced Zelensky to replace Ukraine’s top military commander with the younger Mykhailo Drapatyi, who was backed by protesters for his allegedly more troop-friendly approach, which they hope will lessen losses on the front line.
Read moreUkrainians welcome new army chief but seek return of fired defence minister
Ukraine’s anti-corruption agencies have waged a high-profile war against graft while Kyiv’s military fights Russia, targeting senior officials in a campaign they say is critical to preparing for Ukrainian membership in the European Union.
Late last year, Zelensky's top aide and eminence grise Andriy Yermak resigned after being linked to a $100 million graft probe into the energy sector, which has been battered by Russian attacks throughout the war.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)

Russia, Ukraine conduct prisoner exchange in Belarus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:42:00 UTC
18:42:00 KST

GOMEL, 19 August (BelTA) - An exchange of prisoners of war between Russia and Ukraine was conducted on the territory of Belarus, BelTA has learned.
 
 
Belarus continues to fulfill its humanitarian mission and once again served as a place for the prisoner exchange. Russia and Ukraine swapped over 103 people each.
The Belarusian side arranged the necessary logistical chain creating the conditions for the safe landing of the aircraft at Gomel airport and for the movement of a convoy of buses to the Novaya Guta border checkpoint where the exchange took place.
Each person was provided with hot meals. Adding a touch of tradition, the dry rations included apples and honey, the symbolic offerings of the Orthodox Savior's Feast which is marked on 19 August .For people who had spent a long time away from their families and loved ones and had experienced stressful situations, faith became a true salvation.
Ambulance teams were on hand, ready to provide medical assistance.
Natalya Masterskaya, Deputy Head of the Main Healthcare Directorate of the Gomel Oblast Executive Committee, emphasized that the presence of medical personnel is a necessity during such exchange operations. There were more than 70 of them. Over nearly 2.5 years, medical assistance has been provided to more than 1,500 prisoners of war from both sides. “For us, this is a great responsibility because prisoners of war arrive with various health conditions ranging from satisfactory to extremely severe. We provide each person with the necessary medical care in full right on the spot, and if necessary, we hospitalize them in healthcare institutions of the region. If surgical intervention is required, we perform it or transfer the patient to a higher-level facility, to national healthcare institutions in Minsk,” she said.
Medical assistance is provided equally to prisoners of war from both Russia and Ukraine. Most of the patients have sustained injuries.
“Therefore, we perform primary surgical debridement, carry out surgical interventions, and treat complications since these are typically severe patients. We also receive people with strokes; they are hospitalized in intensive care units and undergo rehabilitation treatment. We provide the full spectrum and the entire range of necessary medical care,” Natalya Masterskaya said.
Each ambulance crew is equipped with everything necessary. “We already have experience and are aware of what to expect. So each team carries the necessary stock of medical supplies and medications. Of course, we have a supply of bandages, painkillers, and antiemetics and also blood pressure-lowering medications, antipyretics, and others. We have all the necessary drugs,” Natalya Masterskaya assured.
The main desire of every prisoner of war is to return home as soon as possible and embrace their loved ones.
Belarus consistently adheres to a peace-loving position, providing safe humanitarian channels, corridors and venues for organizing and conducting exchanges between Russia and Ukraine. More than 70 such events have already been held on Belarusian territory.
/More to come/

Bilateral ties in focus as Syria's top diplomat makes trip to Pakistan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:40:00 UTC
18:40:00 KST

Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani was set to arrive in Islamabad Wednesday evening for a two-day visit to Pakistan, a Pakistani Foreign Ministry source said.
Al-Shaibani will be in Pakistan on Aug. 19-20 at the invitation of his counterpart, Ishaq Dar, said the source, who asked not to be named.
The trip will mark the highest-level visit by a Syrian official to Pakistan since the overthrow of Bashar Assad in 2024, although other Syrian ministers have visited Islamabad since then.
It will also be the first visit by a Syrian foreign minister to Pakistan in 19 years.
In addition to talks with Dar, al-Shaibani is expected to meet Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and other ministers.
The last Syrian foreign minister to visit Pakistan was Walid al-Mouallem, who traveled to Islamabad in May 2007.
A Pakistani delegation met al-Shaibani in Damascus in June last year.
In March, the Pakistani prime minister discussed the ongoing escalation in the Middle East with Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa during a telephone call.
Al-Shaibani was appointed foreign minister under President al-Sharaa's administration following the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024.
His visit comes as Islamabad on Wednesday "strongly" condemned Israel's unprovoked attack on the Abu al-Duhur Airbase in Syria's northwestern Idlib province.
The two sides are expected to discuss ways to revive and expand cooperation in various fields, including the economy and defense, according to the source.
Islamabad and Damascus have maintained decadeslong relations, strengthened by military cooperation and training exchanges.
Pakistan's Embassy in Damascus remained open following Assad's overthrow, although bilateral cooperation between the two countries has remained limited over the past two years.
Pakistan and Syria formally established diplomatic relations in December 1949, two years after the creation of Pakistan.
Bilateral trade between Pakistan and Syria remains modest, totaling just $8.49 million.

Albania protests escalate as fight over land and power deepens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:39:56 UTC
18:39:56 KST

Breadcrumb
'What happens in Palestine does not stay in Palestine': Albania's Flamingo Revolution and the fight over land, power and sovereignty
Since mid-May 2026, protesters have gathered every day in cities across Albania, making the mobilisation one of the longest-running continuous protest movements in recent years.
The protests began as opposition to a luxury tourism development on the uninhabited island of Sazan, while developing into a national and transnational campaign challenging the Albanian government's model of development, the privatisation and exploitation of the land, and the country's increasingly political alignment with Western and Israeli interests.
The demonstrations, now widely known as the Flamingo Revolution, have brought together an unusually broad coalition of environmental activists, students, artists, architects, trade unionists and civil society groups.
Among the movement's most interesting voices is Fioralba Duma, an activist with Palestina e Lirë (Free Palestine in Albanian), who has participated in the protests since day one.
Over the past two years, Fioralba became the most important activist against Prime Minister Edi Rama's migration agreement with Italy, the externalisation of European borders through migrant detention centres in Albania, and what she describes as the growing convergence between environmental dispossession, colonial politics and solidarity with Palestine.
Speaking to The New Arab, Fioralba argues that the protests are no longer simply about Sazan, but have become a broader struggle over who owns Albania's land, who benefits from its development, and how global political conflicts increasingly shape domestic politics.
The origins of the movement
While the movement exploded onto the international scene over three months ago, opposition to the project dates back several years.
Activists say concerns first emerged around 2021, when plans for large-scale tourism projects began to surface for Sazan Island and other protected coastal areas.
For Fioralba Duma, the controversy reflects a much longer process.
"People had been talking about it since at least last year, I'd actually say since around 2021, when we first started noticing development initiatives that would later become connected to the project. We all knew the island was going to be handed over to private investors," she tells The New Arab.
"Today, the island is uninhabited, although during the communist period it had a school, a cinema, and other public facilities. It is, however, a strategically important island, both geographically and environmentally."
The controversy intensified after the Albanian parliament approved legislation allowing the construction of tourism infrastructure, including resorts, in certain categories of protected areas.
The decision came shortly after Albania and Italy ratified the migration agreement, prompting demonstrations against both measures.
The turning point, however, came after private security guards assaulted protesters near the fenced-off construction site in Zvërnec. Videos of the violence quickly spread across Albanian social media, transforming it into a national political issue.
"The footage provoked widespread indignation," Fioralba recalls. "The following day, we organised a demonstration in Tirana."
As the demonstrations continued, the focus quickly expanded beyond Sazan itself. According to Fioralba, the movement has become a broader challenge to Albania's development model, raising questions about who controls the country's natural resources and the country itself.
"At the heart of the mobilisation is a broader debate over ownership and the public interest. It is not simply about private versus public property, but about protecting places that belong to society as a whole rather than to oligarchic interests," she says.
Protesters have also focused on Law No. 21 of 2024, which allows new tourism developments in certain protected areas.
Activists argue that the legislation, together with the dismantling of protections for several protected areas, reflects a wider shift in Albania's approach to environmental governance.
Fioralba pointed to the Vjosa River, where, although the river itself remains protected, parts of its surrounding ecosystem lie outside the protected area.
She also situates these facts within the "Albania One Euro" model. The initiative was launched in 2006 under former Prime Minister Sali Berisha to encourage investment through favourable concession terms.
During the protests, activists also turned to The Albanian Files: Freedom and Architecture, an almost 800-page publication documenting hundreds of architectural and urban development projects across the country.
Copies of the book were scanned, shared and discussed during demonstrations as protesters sought to map connections between political power and what is happening on their land.
A struggle over Albania's future
The movement has also placed renewed scrutiny on corruption, money laundering and the role of foreign capital in reshaping Albania's landscape.
Fioralba argues that major developments increasingly benefit international investors while sidelining local communities and Albanian architects, who, she says, are routinely excluded from the projects.
For many protesters, this has also shaped the meaning of patriotism: defending forests, rivers and coastlines has become inseparable from defending Albania itself against economic dispossession and the enclosure of the commons.
"The fence represented the physical and symbolic enclosure of a place that people felt belonged to everyone," she explains. "It made visible the broader struggle over who has the right to the country's land and future."
One of the most widely shared images was an AI-generated illustration depicting a fictional border between Albania and Israel — a deliberately provocative piece that linked Jared Kushner's investment projects to wider debates about settler colonialism, land dispossession and Israel's ongoing genocide in Gaza.
"Although the protest did not initially receive widespread public support, the reaction to that image and to the demonstrations showed that Palestine, colonialism and the role of Israel already resonated deeply with many people," Fioralba adds.
As demonstrations continued day after day, the movement rapidly spread throughout the country, while solidarity actions were organised by Albanian diaspora communities in Italy, elsewhere in Europe, the United States and Australia.
At its peak, organisers estimate that around 100,000 people participated — a remarkable mobilisation in a country of roughly 2.3 million inhabitants.
One of the defining characteristics of the Flamingo Revolution has been its ability to unite movements that had long operated separately.
Environmental campaigners, artists, architects, students, designers and long-time political activists have found themselves marching together, transforming what began as an environmental campaign into one of the broadest social coalitions Albania has seen in years.
For Fioralba, that convergence did not happen by chance. "If you look around the protests today, you see environmental activists, designers, artists, students — people who have spent years working on very different causes," she says.
"A friend once joked that it feels as though all of us spent years participating in small, isolated protests simply to prepare for something like this. In a way, that's exactly how it feels."
Rather than creating a new movement from scratch, the protests became a meeting point for struggles that had been developing independently.
Environmental justice, anti-corruption campaigns, artistic activism and grassroots organising suddenly found a common political language through the defence of Sazan and Albanian land.
"We were building experiences, relationships and political awareness separately, until a moment arrived when all of those struggles suddenly converged," Fioralba continues.
"That is why this movement is different. It is not only about one project or one environmental campaign. It has become a space where many different political and social struggles have found a common language."
Fioralba also believes the unprecedented global mobilisations for Palestine helped reshape Albania's protest culture.
While she acknowledges that Albania has experienced major demonstrations before — notably the student movement — she argues that Palestine contributed something different: it normalised public protest for a new generation and offered a political framework through which many people interpreted the developments unfolding in their own country.
"Palestine acted like a kind of fuel. It helped people overcome a certain attachment to the dominant narrative of 'development.' It offered a different lens through which to understand what was happening in Albania," she says.
Palestine in the Albanian Revolution
If the movement has challenged Albania's development model, Fioralba believes it has also begun to reshape how many Albanians imagine the country's future.
One of its most significant achievements, she argues, has been opening a public conversation that would have been almost unthinkable only a few years ago.
Albania's post-communist history, she says, produced an almost unquestionable attachment to private property. After nearly five decades of state socialism, ownership became synonymous with freedom, making criticism of privatisation or large-scale investment politically difficult.
"There are still people who take the microphone during demonstrations and feel the need to clarify: 'We are not against private investors. We are not against wealthy people. We are against those who destroy the environment, who operate without transparency, and who act with impunity.'"
Yet Fioralba believes the Flamingo Revolution has begun to erode those assumptions.
Many protesters have begun questioning an economic model centred on speculative investment, environmental destruction, and the privatisation of public goods, while demanding stronger public education, healthcare, and social protections.
"I would never have expected this from a society that experienced one of Europe's harshest communist dictatorships. Yet this is exactly what I have witnessed. After 35 years of what we call 'turbo-capitalism,' more and more Albanians are beginning to imagine a different future," she says.
For Fioralba, that political transformation also explains why Palestina e Lirë became deeply involved in these struggles. Although the collective was founded in solidarity with Gaza, its members soon concluded that the mechanisms they opposed in Palestine could also be recognised elsewhere.
"We quickly realised that what happens in Palestine does not stay in Palestine," Fioralba adds.
According to the activist, a series of political developments reinforced that conviction: the expansion of Albania's defence industry following Antony Blinken's 2024 visit, the Rama-Meloni migration agreement, the deepening strategic relationship between Tirana and Rome, Prime Minister Edi Rama's growing engagement with Israeli political leaders, and what activists perceive as an increasing alignment of Albania with broader Western geopolitical interests.
Taken individually, she says, each event might appear unrelated. Viewed together, however, they reveal what the movement considers a broader political trajectory.
The result has been a growing debate over what Palestina e Lirë calls Albania's "complicity."
Rather than treating Palestine as a distant foreign policy issue, the collective argues that the same political and economic relationships destroying Gaza also influence decisions about land inside Albania.
"People kept asking us: 'Why do you care so much about Palestine? Why don't you care about Albania?' For us, that has always been a false distinction," she explains.
Fioralba argues that Albania's own history — marked by foreign intervention, the partition of Albanian-inhabited territories by the European Powers, and collective memories of genocide and displacement — has fostered the idea that promises of external investment are crucial to the country's stability.
Yet she believes projects proposed for Sazan, Zvërnec, and Lake Butrint changed this perception.
"We see them as different expressions of what we describe as the 'Israelisation' of Albania — a model in which territory, strategic assets and public resources are increasingly subordinated to external political and economic interests," Fioralba concludes.
Dalia Ismail is a Palestinian-Italian independent analyst and journalist
Follow her on X: @Dalia_dalla_pal

Nuclear material found at site will remain in Syria: Syrian FM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:38:59 UTC
18:38:59 KST

Breadcrumb
Nuclear material found at site will remain in Syria, right to civilian use: Syrian FM
Nuclear material discovered at an undisclosed site in Syria is not dangerous and will remain in Syrian custody, subject to guarantees from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani said on Tuesday.
During a joint press conference in Damascus with IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi, the foreign minister added that Syria had the right to use this material for civil and peaceful purposes.
"On July 17, we sent an official letter to the agency, in which we voluntarily declared the presence of nuclear materials at an undeclared site, part of the legacy left by the old regime", Shaibani said.
"According to technical assessments, these materials present no risk", assured the Syrian minister. "These matters will remain in Syria's custody, while being subject to the agency's supervision system", he said.
The head of the UN's nuclear watchdog said on Tuesday its inspectors had found several tons of nuclear material in Syria, at a site Damascus reported to the agency last month.
The inspectors visited two sites, one in Deir Ezzor and "a second location related to the nuclear material identified by Syria recently", according to a joint statement.
Speaking at a news conference in Damascus, Rafael Grossi, the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), praised Damascus's "courageous decision" to report the undisclosed site, which dates back to the rule of ousted former dictator Bashar-al-Assad.
"We are talking about a few tons of nuclear material that could be put to bad use," he said, promising that it would be put under international safeguards.
Grossi said "this material will be accounted for, will be put within the international safeguards system".
Syrian and IAEA experts will work together to safely store the materials, he said.
"We are starting to turn a page, and turning a page does not mean forgetting the past," he added.
Likely from reactor
Grossi also visited a site in Deir al-Zour in the east, which has been shut for 18 years after an Israeli attack on the site.
In 2008, less than a year after the strike, US officials accused Syria of having sought to build a secret nuclear reactor and acknowledged that Israel had destroyed it in the raid.
The UN atomic watchdog declared in 2011 that the Syrian site was "very likely" to have been a nuclear reactor, adding that information provided to it suggested that it was being built with North Korean assistance.
Pierre Razoux, academic director of French think tank the FMES Institute, told AFP the nuclear materials found on Tuesday are "most likely... linked to the Syrian nuclear program, which was halted in 2007 after the Israeli raid on the Al-Kibar site" in Deir al-Zour.
He said, however, that Syria may also have nuclear materials that Iraq rid itself of at the start of the 2000s.
Grossi said the find vindicated the IAEA's longstanding suspicion that Syria had been secretly building a reactor and that the agency was "at the... site of Deir al-Zour, where a very comprehensive work of excavation and exploration is taking place now".
The watchdog said last year that it had discovered uranium particles at the site during an inspection in 2024.
Grossi's visit came after news outlet Axios last week quoted US and Israeli officials as saying Washington and the IAEA reached an agreement to have the watchdog remove nuclear material stored at a clandestine site in Syria after having "reached understandings with Syria and Israel".
Axios said Israel, a nuclear-armed state, was closely monitoring a location called "Site 99", where Israeli officials say the Assad government stored nuclear material that was part of the Deir al-Zour project, also known as "Al-Kibar", and that Israel had threatened to bomb it.

The Verkhovna Rada adopts comprehensive support for children with disabilities on the second attempt
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
12:38:58 EEST

The Verkhovna Rada adopts comprehensive support for children with disabilities on the second attempt
Kyiv • UNN
With 331 votes, Parliament adopted a law on comprehensive support for children and persons with disabilities starting in 2027. The base amount will be at least 4,000 hryvnias.
The Verkhovna Rada, on its second attempt, adopted in the second reading and as a whole a bill providing for the introduction of comprehensive support for children with disabilities starting in 2027. UNN reports this, citing a parliamentary session.
Details
Draft Law No. 14191 "On Amendments to the Law of Ukraine "On State Social Assistance to Persons with Disabilities from Childhood and Children with Disabilities" Concerning the Formation of Comprehensive State Support and the Enhancement of Social Guarantees for Families with Persons with Disabilities" was supported by 331 members of parliament.
The bill establishes comprehensive state support provided to persons with disabilities from childhood, children with disabilities, their parents or other legal representatives, and includes cash payments and social services, as well as other types of social support, in particular a combined early intervention social service.
It is noted that persons with disabilities from childhood and children with disabilities under the age of 18 are entitled to state social assistance.
Under the bill, state social assistance is assigned and paid monthly in the following amounts:
-  for children with disabilities under the age of 18 - 200% of the basic amount;  
-  for persons with disabilities from childhood of Group I - 200% of the basic amount; 
-  for persons with disabilities from childhood of Group II - 100% of the basic amount; 
-  for persons with disabilities from childhood of Group III - 75% of the basic amount. 
The document stipulates that the "basic amount" is a statutory monetary indicator used to determine the amounts of state social assistance provided for by this law and, beginning in 2027, established by the Law on the State Budget of Ukraine for the respective year.
The bill stipulates that, from January 1, 2027, the basic amount shall be set at no less than 4,000 hryvnias.
State social assistance to persons with disabilities from childhood and children with disabilities, the care allowance for them, and funeral assistance are assigned and paid by the Pension Fund of Ukraine in accordance with the procedure established by the Cabinet of Ministers.
A care allowance is also established. Thus, persons with disabilities from childhood in Group I shall receive a care allowance in the following amounts:
-  for persons with disabilities from childhood classified in
subgroup A of Group I, - 200% of the basic amount;  
-  for persons with disabilities from childhood classified in
subgroup B of Group I, - 100% of the basic amount. 
The care allowance for a child with a disability in subgroup A under the age of 18 shall be set at 200% of the basic amount.
The care allowance for another child with a disability under the age of 18 who, in accordance with the procedure established by law, has been determined to require care and has received the relevant documentary confirmation from a medical advisory commission shall be set at 100% of the basic amount.
The document also proposes introducing a phased payment model for children with disabilities and persons with disabilities from childhood who are in full state care:
-  until January 1, 2028, such persons shall receive only 25% of the assigned state social assistance. The remaining 75% shall be transferred
to the institution to improve living conditions; 
-  from January 1, 2028 - 50% shall be paid directly to the person (or their legal representative), while the other 50% shall go to the institution to pay for social services under a contract. 
The bill shall enter into force on the day following the day of its publication and shall take effect on January 1, 2027.
By January 1, 2027, the Cabinet of Ministers is to draft and submit to the Verkhovna Rada for consideration a bill on amendments to the Budget Code of Ukraine concerning the establishment, by the Law on the State Budget of Ukraine for the respective year, of the basic amount as a unit for calculating the amounts of state social assistance.
It should be noted that on July 15, the Verkhovna Rada was unable to adopt the bill in the second reading (receiving only 163 votes), and by 283 votes "For" sent the document for a repeat second reading.
We remind you
The Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine adopted as a basis a bill providing for the introduction of a new type of state social assistance—the basic social assistance—in place of several payments.

Ukrainian UNWAVE EW System Was the Only One to Jam a UAV During Baltic Exercises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:38:55 UTC
18:38:55 KST

The Ukrainian UNWAVE electronic warfare system was the only one able to jam a UAV during NATO’s Baltic Trust 26 exercises in Latvia, the company told Militarnyi.
The exercise marked the final stage of NATO’s program to test counter-UAV systems.
During the Jamming Performance Challenge tests, an EW system from the Ukrainian company jammed a UAV, causing it to lose control and crash.
Due to its successful performance in countering UAVs, the Ukrainian system received a special award from the training organizers.
In addition, during the exercises, the company conducted tests of the Patelnia, Choven, and Shatro electronic warfare systems, as well as the Bashur UAV detection complex.
The Patelynia is a portable infantry EW system in a backpack configuration weighing 15.6 kg, designed to protect positions from munition drops and FPV drones. The system has an output power of 50W per channel, with a total output of 100W. It is powered by a 24V battery that provides up to 100 minutes of autonomous operation.
The Choven is a vehicle-mounted EW system in a roof-box configuration, equipped with 14 jamming modules with a combined output power of 3,200W (50W per channel). The system is designed to block UAV telemetry, video feeds, and navigation. It can be powered by the vehicle’s onboard electrical system or an external 28V battery and mounts on standard roof rails.
The Shatro is a multi-frequency dome EW system that creates a continuous 360-degree barrier against FPV drones and munition drops. Depending on the configuration, the system combines single- and dual-channel amplifier modules with an output power of at least 50W per channel.
The Bashur is a compact passive UAV detection and direction-finding system with power consumption of up to 20W. It detects FPV drones and analog video channels at distances of up to 2 km and sends a signal to automatically activate EW systems within two minutes of deployment.
Earlier this May, the company’s software demonstrated compatibility with NATO’s C-UAS digital architecture in accordance with STANREC 4869 during the Technical Interoperability Exercise 2026.
It has also been integrated with ten modules from other manufacturers.

Russia and Ukraine exchange 103 POWs – MOD (VIDEO)
Russia and Ukraine have conducted another prisoner of war exchange, returning over a hundred servicemen to each side, the Defense Ministry in Moscow announced on Wednesday.
In a statement published on social media, the ministry said that “103 Russian servicemen were returned from territory controlled by the Kiev regime.” In exchange, 103 Ukrainian Armed Forces prisoners of war were transferred to Kiev.
The returned Russian servicemen are currently in Belarus, where they are receiving psychological and medical assistance, according to the ministry. Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova is working with the freed soldiers.
Lantratova noted that of the 103 returned Russian soldiers, 31 are wounded. “Among those who returned are fathers of many children, and some are very young men,” she added.
The soldiers will later be transported to Russia for further treatment and rehabilitation at Defense Ministry medical facilities.
During the exchange, Lantratova met Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmitry Lubinets. The two sides exchanged lists of missing persons, as well as letters from relatives for servicemen who remain in captivity. They also agreed to arrange the delivery of parcels to POWs held by both sides.
The exchange was carried out with humanitarian mediation from the United Arab Emirates, the ministry added.
The swap is the latest in a series of prisoner exchanges between Moscow and Kiev despite the ongoing conflict.
The previous exchange took place on June 26, when the two sides returned 160 servicemen each, also with UAE mediation. Earlier that month, Russia and Ukraine also exchanged 185 POWs each, while another 205 servicemen from each side were released in May.
Moscow and Kiev have also continued exchanging the bodies of fallen soldiers. The UAE has repeatedly acted as a mediator in humanitarian contacts between the two sides.

The three men were accused of making calls for the violent overthrow of the Azerbaijani government, inciting ethnic hatred and issuing public calls for terrorism. The charges stem from comments they were said to have made during July and August livestreams for the YouTube channel “Chistota Ponimaniya.”

“Our expectation to take urgent and effective measures to end the provocations, threats and violent rhetoric against Azerbaijan in the information and media space was once again conveyed to the Russian side,” the ministry said in a statement.

“The logic behind my decision is straightforward: I don’t believe anyone’s personal expert opinion or public statements should impact interstate relations or create obstacles for joint government efforts,” Chadayev wrote on Telegram.

Relations between Russia and Azerbaijan have grown increasingly strained after a Russian missile accidentally shot down an Azerbaijani passenger plane in December 2024, killing 38 people. While Russia acknowledged responsibility for the deadly incident, tensions have persisted, accompanied by reciprocal arrests of each other’s citizens.
Earlier this week, Russian law enforcement authorities deported the head of an Azerbaijani diaspora organization in Moscow who had been stripped of his Russian citizenship last year, though official reasons for the deportation were not disclosed.

Nord Stream: Second suspect arrested over pipeline blasts
August 19, 2026
A second suspect has been arrested in relation to the Nord Stream gas pipeline explosions in 2022, German prosecutors said on Wednesday.
Croatian police, acting on a European arrest warrant, detained a Ukrainian national in Pula.
"The Federal Public Prosecutor's Office had Ukrainian Vladimir Z. arrested in Pula (Croatia) by local police forces," prosecutors said.
They said that the man, a trained scuba diver, "is strongly suspected of jointly causing explosions."
The prosecutors said they were pursuing the man's extradition from Croatia.
He is reported to have previously been detained in Poland in September 2025 but was released after an extradition request from Germany was turned down.
Another suspect, also a Ukrainian national, was arrested in Italy last year.
What happened to the Nord Stream pipelines?
The Nord Stream 1 and 2 pipelines were set up to deliver Russian gas to Germany and other countries in Europe.
Nord Stream 2 had yet to enter service when in September 2022, both pipelines were damaged by blasts that rendered them inoperable.
The blasts came just months after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Germany has said it believes the blasts were sabotage ordered by unspecified Ukrainian state entities but Kyiv has so far denied involvement.
Prosecutors have said the plot aimed to permanently disrupt gas deliveries via the pipelines and prevent Moscow from using the revenue generated from natural gas trading to finance its military operations.
Moscow had repeatedly reduced or suspended deliveries through Nord Stream 1 after starting the invasion, blaming Western sanctions and technical issues.
Europe, in its turn, accused Russia of weaponizing energy supplies.

TalTech rector concedes presidential race as Ülle Madise emerges as sole candidate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19

TalTech rector concedes presidential race as Ülle Madise emerges as sole candidate
Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise is likely the only candidate at the presidential elections, Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech) Rector and potential candidate Tiit Land said.
Land, who had been proposed as a candidate mostly by fellow academics, effectively conceded his candidacy at the presidential elections to be held at the Riigikogu on September 2-3.
Land had met with most Riigikogu party factions, but opposition Isamaa declaring in favor of Madise Tuesday afternoon and joining the Reform Party, Eesti 200 and the Social Democrats, tipped the balance.
"Today's arithmetic at the Riigikogu shows that only one worthy candidate is to be nominated for the vote there. I wish Ülle Madise success and perseverance," Land announced.
While Madise already saw 63 MPs sign in her favor as candidate even before Isamaa made its decision, Land currently only has clear backing from the Center Party, with eight MPs, plus "several" of the 20 independent MPs, but not enough to reach the 21 signatures needed to nominate.
Land added he had always been, and if necessary would continue to be, ready to engage in substantive debate on Estonia's future and to present his vision of the president's role in that future. This even included the presidential electoral process itself.
"For me, the meetings with the members of the Riigikogu were very valuable. There are many issues Estonia needs to discuss, including the procedure for electing the president – should the head of state continue to be elected at the Riigikogu with cross-party support, or should we opt for direct elections in the future?" Land added.
Land thanked all who had backed his nomination, particularly his fellow university rectors and the president of the Estonian Academy of Sciences.
Land was a latecomer to the list of potential runners, only emerging last week, but soon emerged as a potential challenger to Madise. The latter only declared her intention to run at the start of this week.
The candidate nomination window is August 21-24, with only those figures with 21 or more MPs' signatures to their name able to register. August 20 is a national holiday.
With Isamaa's backing, Madise now has more than 68 signatures, the number needed to elect a president in the 101-seat Riigikogu, though the three secret ballots are on September 2-3. If inconclusive, the process would move to the 208-member electoral college.
Center Party still sticking with Land
The Center Party parliamentary group chairman Lauri Laats told ERR that while Land will most likely be unable to secure the 21 signatures needed at the Riigikogu, this was the reason why "we like him even more, as he is able to put simple things together and logically deduce what is going to happen."
Land was also more likely to reach the 21-signature benchmark than other potential candidates who had emerged recently, notably diplomats Maive Rute and Hannes Hanso, and piano-maker Indrek Laul, Laats continued.
Both Center and Land still want a debate with Madise, Laats went on, adding he "hopes Madise takes advantage of this opportunity."
"We will not change our minds; the Center Party will not be pushed around," he said, noting that if the process goes to the electoral college, Laats will be in a stronger position then, having debated Madise.
Laats said his party had not made any final decisions on how to vote come September 2.
Editor's note: This piece was updated to include comment from Lauri Laats.

NASA releases first IMAGES of SpaceX lunar crash crater
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:36:02 UTC
18:36:02 KST

NASA releases first IMAGES of SpaceX lunar crash crater
NASA has released images showing a crater blasted into the Moon by a discarded SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket stage that struck the lunar surface at around 5,400 mph (8,700 kph) earlier this month.
The US space agency published an animated before-and-after comparison on Tuesday, using images captured by its Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) that show the previously undisturbed surface and a dark new impact scar.
NASA said the crater measures roughly 18 meters (60 ft) across and less than 3 meters (10 ft) deep.
The images also reveal bright and dark rays spreading outward from the crater. NASA said the darker streaks consist of weathered lunar dust and rocks that were blasted out from the upper 1.5 ft (0.46 m) of the lunar surface by the impact. The material had been altered over time by solar wind, cosmic rays, and micrometeorite strikes. Brighter debris near the crater rim came from deeper underground.
Spotted: Falcon 9 impact site 
NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) has captured images of a new crater on the Moon. The crater formed on Aug. 5, 2026, when a SpaceX Falcon 9 upper stage impacted the lunar surface. https://t.co/aqduBYwpmgpic.twitter.com/hE83yvzmIk
The 4-ton upper stage struck the Moon on August 5 after drifting through space for more than a year. The Falcon 9 launched in January 2025 carrying the US Blue Ghost and Japanese Resilience lunar landers. Its reusable first-stage booster returned to Earth, while the second stage remained in space.
SpaceX said the stage had initially been placed on a trajectory considered safe under existing rules. A combination of solar activity and gravitational forces later sent it toward the lunar surface.
Although the Moon is regularly struck by natural meteoroids, collisions involving man-made objects are much less common. NASA deliberately crashed rocket stages into the lunar surface during the Apollo era to collect seismic data.
Experts have warned that unplanned impacts could become a greater concern as human activity on and around the Moon increases. UK aerospace engineer Dean Sladen told Space.com last week that uncontrolled rocket stages could become a “tangible operational risk” as space agencies and private companies build permanent lunar infrastructure.

At the same time, Russian authorities were rushing to put out a small fire after a drone fell in an industrial area in the city of Ufa in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan, the republic’s head Radiy Khabirov said on Telegram.
Khabirov added that a drone hit an apartment building and a few cars in Ufa, an oil refining hub, injuring one person.

ECB chief warns Europe's post-war growth model eroding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:34:24 UTC
18:34:24 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
19 August 2026•Update: 19 August 2026
European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde warned Wednesday that Europe's post-war growth model is eroding as the international environment changes.
Lagarde, speaking during a discussion on the global economic outlook at the World Economic Forum in Geneva, said Europe's traditional growth model rested on expanding global trade, strength in mid-tech manufacturing and a stable global order underpinned by a US security umbrella.
She said expanding trade could no longer be taken for granted, noting that more than 2,500 trade restrictions were implemented globally from January to October 2025.
China now competes directly with the euro area in close to 40% of sectors where Europe has a comparative advantage, compared with around 25% in the early 2000s, she said.
European industry has also lost its advantage of relatively cheap energy, Lagarde said. EU electricity prices for energy-intensive industries averaged more than twice US levels and around 50% above Chinese levels last year.
Lagarde said the rules-based global order was under pressure from geopolitical tensions, adding that firms invest less when capital is seen as less safe.
Despite these headwinds, Europe retains substantial strengths, including the world's largest network of trade agreements and an integrated market of 27 member states with 450 million consumers, she said.
The euro area economy grew by 1.5% last year, driven entirely by domestic demand, she said. The economy posted quarter-on-quarter growth of 0.4% in the second quarter of 2026, with domestic demand contributing positively.
Lagarde called on Europe to make better use of the scale of its home market to support investment, innovation and productivity.
"Europe largely missed out on the first digital revolution, as the commercial gains from the spread of information and communication technologies were captured disproportionately elsewhere," she said.
"We cannot afford to repeat that experience with artificial intelligence, the second digital revolution," she added.
Survey evidence suggests euro area firms expect to allocate an average of around 9% of their total investment to artificial intelligence this year, Lagarde said.
She identified fragmentation in the EU single market and capital markets as two critical barriers to European firms' ability to scale.
Some 12% of EU scale-ups have relocated outside the bloc, most notably to the US, she said.
Lagarde highlighted "EU Inc.," a proposed optional EU-wide corporate legal form that would allow companies to incorporate once and operate under a single set of rules across the bloc.
She also said EU leaders have called for co-legislators to reach an agreement on a market integration package by the end of 2026, moving Europe closer to a genuine single market for capital.

The audience award winner was decided by an online vote in which viewers could rate films by five different emotions, and "Moulin Rouge" got the most votes in the "thrilling" and "touching" categories. It was followed by Maltese director Alex Camilleri's romantic musical drama "Żejtune," released this year.
Croatian director Igor Šereg's comedy "The Wedding" ("Svadba") was seen as the most feel-good film, Thea Sharrock's "Me Before You" (2016) as the saddest, and Pedro Almodóvar's Spanish black romantic comedy "Tie Me Up! Tie Me Down!" ("¡Átame!," 1989) won the "most stirring" category from the over 1,000 votes cast.

The 21st PÖFF Tartuff Love Film Festival took place August 8-15. A total of 11,000 people attended Tartuff's film screenings and events before the festival ended in the early hours of Sunday.
"Moulin Rouge" (2001) starred Nicole Kidman and Ewan McGregor and is the final installment of Luhrmann's Red Curtain Trilogy, following "Strictly Ballroom" (1992) and "Romeo + Juliet" (1996).

Anti-corruption agencies: MPs and presidential officials laundered US$3m to post bail for ex-energy minister
In the course of an investigation known as Operation Forrest Gump, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) have uncovered a scheme in which the participants allegedly laundered UAH 150 million (approx. US$3.3 million) through a state-owned bank in order to post bail for former energy minister Herman Halushchenko. They were allegedly acting on the instructions of a former and a current MP, and officials from Zelenskyy's Office are also said to have been involved.
Source: NABU YouTube channel
Quote from NABU detective Mykhailo Romaniuk: "As part of a special operation to eliminate high-level corruption, NABU and SAPO have exposed a group of individuals who organised and facilitated the laundering of criminally obtained funds.
The funds in question are UAH 150 million in cash which, according to the investigation, was laundered through a series of accounts belonging to shell companies in order to pay bail for a member of the criminal organisation in the Midas case."
Details: According to NABU, the group included a deputy head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, a former MP, and the chairs of the board and supervisory board of a state-owned bank.
Ekonomichna Pravda has learned that the individuals in question are Iryna Mudra, Deputy Head of the President's Office; Maksym Mykytas, a former MP; Vadym Stolar, an MP elected to parliament from the now-banned Opposition Platform – For Life party; Mykola Hladyshenko, Chair of the Supervisory Board of Sense Bank; and Oleh Stupak, Chair of the Management Board of Sense Bank.
The participants in the scheme have been served with a notice of suspicion under Article 209.3 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (laundering of proceeds of crime).
To implement the scheme, the organisers used Sense Bank and accounts held by controlled companies. The group gained control of the accounts at the bank in early June and involved senior management in the scheme.
Investigators also recorded a conversation between the scheme's organisers in which they discussed posting UAH 150 million in bail for someone involved in the Midas anti-corruption case, an investigation into large-scale embezzlement in the energy sector.
The bail discussed in the recordings may have been intended for former energy minister Herman Halushchenko, as the name "Herman" crops up in the conversation.
Background:
- Bail of UAH 150 million was posted for Herman Halushchenko, a suspect in the Midas case, at the end of June.
- Sources told Ukrainska Pravda that the funds had been deposited by four companies: Tetras Optima LLC – 54 million, Hiran Konstrakt LLC – 87 million, Skait Riteil LLC – five million, and Pelet Servis LLC – four million.
- In November 2025, it was reported that NABU was conducting searches at the premises of businessman Tymur Mindich, a close friend of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and the then justice minister Halushchenko. Sources told Ukrainska Pravda at the time that Mindich had fled abroad just hours before the searches.
- On the same day, NABU announced it had uncovered a large-scale corruption scheme involving embezzlement in the energy sector and published audio recordings of conversations between suspects in the case.
- Halushchenko, who along with Mindich is a suspect in the Midas case, was taken into custody in February.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s benchmark stock index fell below the 45,000-point mark on Wednesday as Middle East tensions weighed on sentiment and US stocks declined overnight.
The Taiwan Stock Exchange Capitalization Weighted Index, or TAIEX, closed down 589.33 points, or 1.3%, at 44,719.35. Turnover fell to NT$847.9 billion, compared with NT$958.4 billion in the previous session, according to Taiwan Index Plus and CTEE.
All of the market’s most heavily weighted stocks declined. TSMC fell 1.26% to NT$2,350.
Foxconn lost 1.61% to NT$245. Delta Electronics fell 3.02% to NT$1,765, MediaTek declined 1.03% to NT$3,845, and ASE fell 1.84% to NT$588.
Aspeed Technology, the highest-priced stock on the TAIEX, fell 7.18% to NT$15,830. King Slide Works declined 1.91% to NT$14,095.
The memory sector saw another session of selling pressure. Nanya Technology fell 6.6%, Winbond Electronics declined 4.82%, while Macronix International lost 2.46%.
Mercuries Life Insurance fell 1.22% to NT$9.7 on its final trading day before being merged into E Sun Financial Holding through a share conversion. E Sun edged down 0.79% to NT$37.8.
Passive component stocks moved higher against the broader market. Prosperity Dielectrics, Nichidenbo, Ta-I Technology and Taiwan Chinsan Electronic Industrial all reached their daily limit-ups, while industry leader Yageo closed unchanged.
The sector benefited mainly from expectations that inventory adjustments are nearing completion. As supply chain inventories decline, reports of potential price increases for some products have prompted expectations for a recovery in second-half orders and improving supply and demand, according to CTEE.
Shipping stocks also performed relatively well on heavy trading volume. Shih Wei Navigation reached its daily limit, while Sincere Navigation, U-Ming Marine Transport and Taiwan Navigation also gained.
Merida Industry hit the daily price limit at NT$88.6 on expectations for a stronger second half. The third quarter is the bicycle industry’s peak season, while the company expects 2026 earnings to recover as European and Chinese markets improve and foreign-exchange losses ease.
Ruan Hui-ci (阮蕙慈), analyst at Da-hwa investment consulting firm, said Wednesday was the settlement day for Taiwan index futures. Foreign investors held large positions that would benefit from a lower index, giving them an incentive to push prices down ahead of settlement, according to CTEE.
She said the market’s decline was likely to be temporary. After its recent rebound, the market is entering a period of consolidation, with technical indicators pointing to support at current levels.
Concord Securities investment director Liao Chi-hung (廖繼弘) said the TAIEX is facing resistance around 46,000 points, where investors who bought at higher levels are still holding positions. He expects the index to trade between 44,000 and 46,000 points in the near term as trading volume remains subdued.
Liao said Nvidia’s earnings report next week could provide an indication of whether its AI-related revenue and profitability are meeting market expectations, potentially supporting confidence in technology stocks. However, he said a sustained recovery in the broader market would require daily trading volume of at least NT$1.1-1.2 trillion, along with further improvement in weekly market indicators.

Taipei Zoo continues critical care for premature orangutan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:31:37 UTC
18:31:37 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei Zoo on Wednesday shared an update on Da Pao, a premature Bornean orangutan receiving intensive medical care, saying the infant continues to gain weight and shows signs of improvement but remains in critical care.
The update came on International Orangutan Day, as the zoo provided information about the twin orangutans born by cesarean section to mother Ke Yi at the end of June. The other twin, Hsiao Pao, died shortly after birth from respiratory distress syndrome, per a zoo press release.
The zoo said Da Pao was born with its lungs and other organs not yet fully developed. The infant required an endotracheal tube and ventilator to assist with breathing. Its ability to breathe independently has gradually improved, allowing medical staff to remove the endotracheal tube.
However, because Da Pao previously experienced lung collapse and inflammation, it continues to require oxygen support through a high-flow nasal cannula, the zoo said. The infant's digestive system is also not fully developed, and it has experienced bloating and other digestive problems.
Its overall physiological condition requires round-the-clock monitoring. A cross-disciplinary medical team, including support from the Neonatal Department at National Taiwan University Hospital, has been invaluable.
The zoo said Da Pao's weight has been steadily increasing. Activity level, including limb movements and responses to external stimuli, has also improved. Zoo staff have recently begun bottle-feeding to help it practice sucking and swallowing, per the press release.
The zoo also highlighted the conservation challenges facing Bornean orangutans, which are classified as critically endangered. Wild populations face threats including deforestation, habitat fragmentation, human-wildlife conflict, illegal hunting, and the wildlife trade.
Orangutans reproduce slowly, with females typically giving birth every six to eight years. Young orangutans depend on their mothers for an extended period to learn essential survival skills, including foraging and nest building. As a result, the zoo said, once orangutan populations decline, recovery can take considerable time.

Taiwan legislative speaker clashes with premier over refusal to countersign laws
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:31:17 UTC
18:31:17 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Legislative Yuan Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) clashed with Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) on Tuesday after Cho announced Monday that he would refuse to countersign two more bills passed by the legislature.
Han cautioned the Cabinet against refusing to countersign the Act Governing Savings Accounts for Future Education and Development of Children and Youth and amendments to the Cable Radio and Television Act, per Tai Sounds. He warned that if the Cabinet believes it can refuse to enforce or countersign legislation passed by the legislature, Taiwan’s constitutional order would be put in peril.
Han questioned the Cabinet’s legal authority to use the premier’s countersigning power as a veto over passed legislation. He stressed that the executive branch should not treat the Cabinet as the Constitutional Court, which serves as a mechanism for resolving disputes between Taiwan’s branches of government.
Cho responded by citing Article 37 of the Constitution, which states that laws promulgated or orders issued by the president require the premier’s countersignature, per Liberty Times. He argued that he has the authority to refuse to countersign legislation passed by the legislature.
Cho also cited Article 91 of the Budget Act and Article 70 of the Constitution, arguing that the legislature has no authority to pass legislation that would increase the executive branch’s fiscal burden, per UDN. He said the executive branch was forced to respond to what he described as “the legislature’s repeated attacks against Taiwan’s constitutional order under Han.”
Cho said he hoped to resolve the imbalance in the constitutional system. Sources close to Han suggested that after Han publicly criticized KMT Caucus Convener Fu Kun-chi (傅崐萁) to help push through the 2026 budget, the government’s refusal to countersign two more bills prompted his Facebook criticism, per UDN.
DPP Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) echoed Cho’s argument, saying the Constitution authorizes the premier to refuse to countersign legislation, per NOWNews. He said that while the executive branch is not above the Constitution, a legislative majority cannot violate the supreme law at will.
Kaohsiung Mayor Chen Chi-mai (陳其邁) suggested that the root of the dispute was the opposition’s boycott of Constitutional Court nominees, per CNA. While the Constitutional Court was briefly paralyzed by a lack of new nominees, it has since resumed operations following a controversial ruling.
TPP Legislative Caucus Convener Chen Ching-lung (陳清龍) criticized Cho’s use of the countersigning power, noting that under the Constitution, the Cabinet should request reconsideration of legislation it believes would be difficult to enforce, per Z.Media. KMT Legislator Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) argued that Lai should have intervened to resolve the legislative deadlock rather than allowing the conflict between the executive and legislative branches to worsen, per Tai Sounds.
On whether Cho has the authority to refuse to countersign legislation passed by the legislature, pro-DPP legal commentator and lawyer Huang Ti-ying (黃帝穎) argued that the opposition’s refusal to initiate a vote of no confidence legitimizes Cho’s decision, per SETN. If a vote of no confidence succeeds, Lai may dissolve the legislature and trigger a new legislative election.
Soochow University Professor Su Tzu-chiao (蘇子喬) said the countersigning mechanism was designed to check presidential power in a semi-presidential system, per UDN. However, former President Lee Teng-hui (李登輝) consolidated the power to appoint premiers under the sole discretion of the president, rendering the mechanism largely moot.
Su said the Cabinet should ask the legislature to reconsider bills it believes may be difficult to enforce. He stressed that the repeated use of the refusal to countersign, which was first used when the Constitutional Court was paralyzed, is a major concern now that the court is functioning again.
Su recommended that the Cabinet seek recourse through the Constitutional Court, adding that the legislature should also consider asking the court to intervene over the use of the countersigning power.
Retired Tunghai University Professor Lin Teng-yau (林騰鷂) noted that the constitutional provision concerning countersigning appears in the chapter governing presidential powers, per ETtoday. He said requirements such as countersigning or legislative authorization for certain presidential powers were designed as safeguards against potential presidential abuse of power.
Lin warned that before the Constitutional Court rules a law unconstitutional, the Cabinet does not have the authority to unilaterally declare it unconstitutional. He cautioned that reinterpreting a constitutional mechanism could become a means of expanding executive power.

US removes Nigeria from decade-long port security restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:29:05 UTC
18:29:05 KST

US removes Nigeria from decade-long port security restrictions
The US has lifted security restrictions on vessels arriving from Nigeria, ending a 12-year regime that burdened shipping companies with additional guards, inspections, and paperwork.
A US Coast Guard notice published on Wednesday said “recent assessments” had found that Africa’s most populous nation was maintaining effective antiterrorism measures at its ports, warranting the removal of restrictions known as Conditions of Entry (CoE).
The measures, imposed in June 2014, did not amount to an outright ban on Nigerian-flagged ships. They applied to vessels that had called at designated Nigerian ports during their previous five port calls, requiring operators to tighten onboard security, guard access points, and report their precautions. The safeguards were intended to prevent ships leaving poorly secured ports from being exploited to carry terrorists, weapons, or tampered cargo into US waters.
The conditions had long drawn complaints over higher insurance bills, added personnel costs, and delays. Abuja expects their removal to improve turnaround times and attract shipping lines, although congestion, corruption allegations, and Gulf of Guinea piracy remain obstacles.
The Nigerian Maritime Administration and Safety Agency said the US Coast Guard conducted four assessments of the West African nation’s maritime security systems and port facilities between March 2024 and April 2026.
The agency said in a statement on Tuesday that it expects the lifting of the CoE “to improve port competitiveness, enhance vessel turnaround and schedule reliability, reduce additional security-related costs and strengthen Nigeria’s position in global shipping.”
Nigeria’s minister of marine and blue economy, Adegboyega Oyetola, hailed the decision as “a major milestone” affirming Abuja’s progress in maritime security and implementation of the International Ship and Port Facility Security Code.
“We will sustain this momentum and ensure Nigeria remains a safe, secure and competitive destination for international shipping,” he wrote on X.
Nigeria was not the only African country subject to US conditions of entry. Similar vessel restrictions remain in force against Cameroon, Comoros, Equatorial Guinea, The Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Libya, Madagascar, Seychelles, Sudan, and Sao Tome and Principe. In February, the Coast Guard expanded the restrictions within Cameroon and Madagascar by revoking exemptions previously granted to certain port facilities.

Labour ‘could lose up to 50 seats’ to Greens if new drilling in North Sea approved
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:28:36 UTC
18:28:36 KST

Labour could lose dozens of seats to the Green party if the government allows new drilling in the North Sea, according to internal research shared with the Guardian.
Green party analysis suggests up to 50 Labour MPs, including Andy Burnham’s key ally Louise Haigh, could lose their seats at the next election if the government fails to make urgent climate action a priority or allows new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea.
The research found that voters in these key Labour v Green seats want bold action to tackle the climate crisis, which has contributed to record heatwaves, devastating wildfires and crippling droughts this summer in the UK – and say Labour MPs will pay the price if the demands are not met.
Rachel Millward, a deputy leader of the Green party, said: “If Labour won’t be swayed by the science or the moral imperative to leave all fossil fuels in the ground, perhaps they will listen to the polling. The data is clear: voters want more from our government on climate change, and they certainly don’t want our new prime minister to back away from his party’s bare minimum commitments.”
Labour dismissed the claims, pointing out that since Burnham took office the number of seats the Green party is projected to win at the next election had fallen from 20 to seven.
Last month, Burnham – who has been tight lipped about the climate crisis since tacking office – said he would be “pragmatic” about oil and gas and that decisions on new drilling would be made “in due course”. “The question isn’t whether Britain will still be using oil and gas, the question is where does it come from,” he said.
Many Labour MPs are increasingly worried about how support for expanded drilling will play with an electorate alarmed by the worst drought since 1976, record heatwaves, wildfires, and climate-related food inflation and potential supply shortages.
They say new drilling in the North Sea will do nothing to improve energy security or lower bills but will pour even more taxpayer money into the coffers of oil firms, which have already made record profits this year.
The Greens have stressed their opposition to further new licences for oil and gas drilling the North Sea, including the Jackdaw gasfield and the Rosebank oilfield, west of Shetland. A decision on these projects is due in the coming weeks and the Greens say they expect a new surge in defectors from Labour if the projects are approved.
Millward said: “Right now we are facing the worst crisis since world war two – and yet rather than step up to the mark, we have a prime minister who seems more interested in telling Donald Trump what he wants to hear on North Sea drilling than taking the bold action needed to keep us safe.”
Green party researchers identified the 50 seats held by Labour that require the smallest swing to be taken by the Greens. They then cross-referenced constituency-level polling carried out by Friends of the Earth in October last year that included a question on whether the government should “go faster” in its efforts to tackle the climate crisis.
More than 50% of voters in every Labour-Green battleground constituency supported the idea that the government should do more to tackle the climate crisis, with more than two-thirds backing the idea in several constituencies. Thirty-seven of the 50 seats equalled or exceeded the England-wide average of 55.5% that favoured faster climate action, and 13 fell below that figure.
A Labour source dismissed the findings, saying: “This is utter fantasy from a party desperate for relevance. Back in the real world Labour is delivering lower bills, energy security and good jobs.”
Luke Tryl, from the polling group More in Common, warned that urgent action on the climate was “an important glue that unites much of Labour’s coalition”.
He said: “If Labour is seen to be rowing back on its commitment to tackling climate change and clean energy, it will undoubtedly deter some of the progressive voters Labour has been winning back under Burnham.”
Tryl said approving individual licences in the North Sea might not trigger a Green surge as long as voters believed Labour was sticking to its manifesto pledges on net zero.
He added: “A pragmatic approach that continues progress to net zero but which balances cost of living concerns is likely to be the best way for Labour to maintain and unite the different wings of their coalition.”
